userStories.title: eBay Media API: video upload for listings
userStories.description: As a clothing seller, I want to add video to my listings to lift conversion. Today images are passed as external URLs only (InventoryItemPayload.imageUrls) and there is no video support. Integrate the eBay Media API (/commerce/media) to upload video and attach it to listings.
acceptanceCriteria: Edge can createVideo -> uploadVideo -> poll getVideo to a terminal status, and attach the resulting id via product.videoIds on createOrReplaceInventoryItem

TRANSCODE DECISION MADE AND WRITTEN DOWN: eBay accepts .mp4 H.264/AVC only, and iPhones record HEVC by default. Either the client transcodes before upload, or the edge does, or HEVC is rejected with a message that tells the seller how to fix it. Silently failing on the most common input is not an option

PUBLISH-ORDERING DECISION MADE: processing is async and terminal status is not immediate, so either publish waits for LIVE, or publish proceeds without video and a later revise attaches it. Whichever is chosen, a seller never ends up with a listing that permanently lacks the video they added
BLOCKED is handled as a moderation outcome, not an error: it is terminal and expected, and the seller is told their video was rejected rather than shown a retry that cannot succeed
Video upload gets its own validation path. The US-276 hardening (validateImageUpload / stripImageMetadata) is image-only and does NOT cover video, which also carries GPS/EXIF-equivalent metadata
iOS/web can add a video during compose and see it reflected on the published listing
Respects the Media API POST rate limit (50 requests / 5 seconds, per user)
userStories.notes:
[P3][Edge/Media] iOS listing-lifecycle audit 2026-07-14. No Media API; images external-URL only (InventoryItemPayload.imageUrls). Nice-to-have; video is a real apparel conversion lever. 

INVESTIGATED 2026-07-18. Confirmed greenfield: no videoId / commerce-media / uploadVideo reference anywhere in services/edge-functions/src or src. Two findings change the shape of this story.

FINDING 1 — NOT SCOPE-BLOCKED, contrary to the obvious assumption. The Media API's createVideo requires sell.inventory, which is ALREADY in our production grant (ebay-client.ts:233). This story therefore does NOT depend on US-1421 (restricted-scope acquisition) and does not need a new seller consent round. Attachment is also on the path we already use: product.videoIds on createOrReplaceInventoryItem — a sibling of the product.imageUrls we already send at ebay-client.ts:2163 — NOT a Trading-API-only feature as the AddItem/VideoDetails docs might suggest. So the integration surface is much smaller than the P3 implies: the eBay side is three new calls plus one extra field on a payload we already build.

FINDING 2 — THE REAL COST IS TRANSCODING, AND IT LANDS ON AC2. eBay accepts .mp4 MPEG-4 Part 10 / AVC (H.264) only. iPhones have defaulted to HEVC / H.265 since iOS 11 unless the user changed Camera > Formats to 'Most Compatible'. AC2 specifically promises iOS compose. So the single most likely real-world input is a format eBay will not accept, and the failure would surface late — after upload, as PROCESSING_FAILED — which is the worst place to discover it. Whoever picks this up should size the transcode decision FIRST, because it dominates the estimate: client-side transcode, server-side transcode (ffmpeg in the Deno container, which is a real image-size and CPU change on Coolify), or explicit rejection. The eBay calls are the easy part.

FLOW: createVideo returns 201 with the video id in the Location header -> uploadVideo sends the bytes -> poll getVideo. Statuses PENDING_UPLOAD -> PROCESSING -> LIVE, with BLOCKED and PROCESSING_FAILED as the other terminal states. BLOCKED is a moderation verdict rather than a fault, so it needs its own message; a generic retry there loops forever. Rate limit is 50 POSTs / 5s per user.

ALSO: AC3's original wording ('routes through the hardened fetch path') is misleading and has been rewritten. Our upload hardening is image-specific — validateImageUpload magic-byte-sniffs for images and stripImageMetadata drops EXIF/GPS from images. Neither does anything for an .mp4, which carries its own location metadata. Video needs a parallel validator, not a reuse of the image one.

NOT CONFIRMED, flagged rather than guessed: max file size, max duration, and how many videos a single listing accepts. eBay's docs point at Seller Center for those numbers and I could not retrieve them (developer.ebay.com WebFetch timed out twice; the above is from eBay doc search summaries, not the doc pages read directly). Confirm those three numbers against the live docs before implementing, since max-duration in particular shapes the compose UX.

userStories.title: Authenticity tell coverage follows brand-pack order, not counterfeit prevalence
userStories.description: As GradeThread, we want tell coverage driven by what actually gets faked, because an add-on a seller can buy for any brand currently has real depth for three (CANONICAL_TELLS: louisvuitton, coach, gucci) and legacy free-text {tell, detail} rows for the rest, which brand-authenticity.ts coerces to category 'other' with no redFlag and which therefore contribute almost nothing to the verdict. The 37 migrations that mention authentication_tells were written in brand-pack order — luxury first because that pack came first — not from any ranking of counterfeit exposure. Nike, adidas, Supreme, BAPE, Moncler, Canada Goose, The North Face and Patagonia are among the most-counterfeited apparel brands in the world and sit in packs whose tells were never structured. US-2139 fixes the SHAPE and the depth of what we have; this story fixes WHICH BRANDS we invest in next and why.
acceptanceCriteria: A written, sourced prioritization of brands by counterfeit exposure crossed with our own submission volume, recorded in the vault as a decision note rather than in a commit message.
The top-ranked brands get structured, sourced, verified tells with redFlags — not free-text rows.

The add-on's purchasability is reconciled with coverage: a brand with no verified tells either cannot be purchased for, or is sold with an explicit stated limitation. Silent degradation to generic reasoning is not acceptable for a paid add-on.
Coverage is measurable: a query or admin view reports verified-tell count per brand so the gap is visible instead of anecdotal.
No claim about detection accuracy is published anywhere until the authenticity golden set (US-2131) can support it.
userStories.notes:
[P2][Authenticity/Coverage] [EPIC: Grading Depth US-2209] Filed 2026-07-28 from a deep-dive review of the grading model + grading knowledge base (owner-requested). Coverage today follows brand-pack authoring order, which put luxury first. Nike/adidas/Supreme/BAPE/Moncler/Canada Goose/TNF/Patagonia sit in packs whose tells were never structured. Pairs with US-2139 (shape) — this one is about which brands get invested in next. | 2026-07-28 SHIPPED except AC1's sourced ranking and AC2's seeding (both deferred with reasons). Commit 2c95f59, no migration.
THE PREMISE WAS UNDERSTATED, AND THE MEASUREMENT IS THE MAIN RESULT. The story says coverage follows brand-pack authoring order. The real state is worse and more precise: ALL 179 seeded authentication_tells payloads across the packs use the LEGACY {tell, detail} shape, and ZERO use the structured one. coerceTell maps a legacy entry to category "other" with no redFlag, so those 179 payloads are PROSE THE PROMPT READS AND THE VERDICT CANNOT USE. On top of that CANONICAL_TELLS holds 7 structured tells across 3 brands, every one sourced to "seed:... (unverified — review in admin)". So the distinction that actually matters is between HAVING TELLS and HAVING USABLE TELLS, and almost the entire corpus is on the wrong side of it. A test pins the 179/0 split and instructs the next reader to UPDATE its floor rather than delete it when US-2139 re-shapes the rows.
THAT REFRAMED THE STORY. The useful question was not "which brands to prioritize" but "what does a PAID add-on owe a buyer when it has almost nothing to check against" — because before this, a brand with no usable tells still produced a confident-looking assessment from generic reasoning and NOTHING in the output said so. That is the part a buyer would object to, and it needed no new data to fix. AC3 DONE and it is the substance of this commit. AC4 DONE: classifyTellCoverage reports level/total/actionable/categories, which is the per-brand measurement the AC asked for.
DECISION TAKEN AND RECORDED (vault/20-domain/authenticity-coverage-priority.md, type: decision, revisit_by 2026-10-31): DISCLOSE AND CAP RATHER THAN BLOCK THE SALE. Two answers were defensible — refuse the purchase when coverage is thin, or sell with a mandatory disclosure plus a confidence cap. Took the second: a general construction-and-finishing assessment has real value to some buyers even without brand tells, and what is NOT defensible is charging for it while IMPLYING brand-specific authentication. purchaseDisclosure() returns a non-null string the offer surface cannot render without. Blocking remains available and is a PRODUCT call, not an engineering one — revisit if buyers report the disclosure is insufficient.
CAPS: 0.6 with no tells, 0.75 with inert ones, composing by MIN with US-2218's reference cap. Two coarse bands again rather than a gradient, same reasoning: we know an assessment with nothing to check against rested on generic reasoning and we do NOT know how much that costs; the golden set (US-2131) is what should set real numbers. Never raises. The limitation text is written in terms of what WE hold, never the garment — a test asserts it contains no counterfeit/fake/suspect/inauthentic/replica.
ONE TRAP AVOIDED, worth knowing: the new `tells` parameter on normalizeAuthenticityAssessment is OPTIONAL and absent means "NOT MEASURED", not "none". Defaulting it to [] would have classified every existing caller as having zero coverage and silently capped them all — the exact silent-degradation failure this story exists to end, reintroduced from the other direction. A test pins that an existing caller passing no tells is byte-identical.
AC1 DEFERRED, WITH THE REASON WRITTEN DOWN. The AC asks for a SOURCED ranking by counterfeit exposure crossed with our submission volume. Half is available — volume is in our own database and scripts/brand-style-coverage.mjs --db already shows that query's shape. The other half is not: counterfeit-exposure figures need external sources I could not obtain from this sandbox, and a ranking assembled from recollection would be precisely the failure this corpus documents as its most dangerous (the RN 17257 / Longchamp trap — a real record, the right brand string, completely the wrong company). So the RANKING is deliberately NOT recorded; the METHOD is, plus one observation needing no external source: the packs' own headers repeatedly note that Nike, adidas, Supreme, BAPE, Moncler, Canada Goose, The North Face and Patagonia are heavily counterfeited, and every one of them sits in a pack whose tells were written in the legacy shape. That is where the corpus itself points for the first pass.
AC2 DEFERRED (seeding verified tells is the same sourcing project). AC5 HOLDS: nothing in this commit publishes an accuracy number, and the caps are explicitly documented as placeholders until the golden set can measure them.
VERIFICATION: 4703 edge tests pass, 15 new in authenticity-coverage_test.ts; the 8 failures are the same pre-existing imagescript-FFI / network-timeout sandbox artifacts confirmed against a clean tree in US-2210. deno lint clean; zero new type errors.

userStories.title: Authentication tells are text-only — there is no known-genuine reference imagery to check a font, stitch or stamp against
userStories.description: As a reviewer or a grading model, I want a picture of what genuine looks like, because half our tell taxonomy is VISUAL and cannot be verified from prose. Verified: brand-authenticity.ts defines 11 tell categories including stitching, font, stamp, hardware and construction, and CANONICAL_TELLS's own text admits the gap — the Louis Vuitton stamp tell says to 'compare letter spacing/shape to a KNOWN-GENUINE REFERENCE' and no such reference exists anywhere in the system. A tell whose check instruction depends on an artifact we do not have is not a checkable rule. This is distinct from US-2139 (tell DEPTH and counterfeit-side modelling) and US-2138 (decoder cross-checks): this is the missing evidence layer both of those assume.
acceptanceCriteria: A reference-image store exists for tells, with per-image provenance (source, rights, brand, style, tell category) — reference imagery must be licensed or owned, never scraped into a public surface.
Reference images are private by default and served only through signed URLs, consistent with the submission-images posture; they are NEVER placed in the public item-photos bucket.

The authenticity pass can present the relevant reference alongside the suspect region for a comparison, and a tell with no reference is explicitly marked as unverifiable-visually rather than silently scored.
Seller-submitted photos are NEVER promoted into the reference corpus without explicit consent — the few-shot exemplar privacy rule (US-1067) applies with equal force here.
Absence of a reference widens limitations and lowers confidence; it must not produce a confident verdict from generic reasoning.
userStories.notes:
[P2][Authenticity/Evidence] [EPIC: Grading Depth US-2209] Filed 2026-07-28 from a deep-dive review of the grading model + grading knowledge base (owner-requested). Distinct from US-2139 (tell depth + counterfeit-side modelling) and US-2138 (decoder cross-checks) — this is the missing EVIDENCE layer both assume. Self-evident from CANONICAL_TELLS's own text: the LV stamp tell instructs a comparison against a known-genuine reference we do not have. | 2026-07-28 SHIPPED (table starts empty; seeding real imagery is the sourcing half). Commit a0fc163, migration 00500 (HELD). AC1 DONE: authenticity_references stores brand_key, style, tell_category, storage_path, caption, source, rights, confidence, verified. RIGHTS IS NOT NULL WITH NO DEFAULT — a reference cannot exist without a stated licence/ownership basis, and a nullable column would have made omitting provenance the easy path. Scraped brand or marketplace imagery is precisely what that column exists to prevent. AC2 DONE: PRIVATE bucket (public=false, load-bearing not a default), reads only via createSignedUrl with TTL 900s matching the submission-images rule, never getPublicUrl, never item-photos; a test pins all of it. AC3 DONE: assessTellVerifiability pairs each tell with the references for its category; an unreferenced VISUAL tell is marked in the prompt as "report it as UNVERIFIED rather than as a confirmed match or a discrepancy" — it is NOT dropped, because the claim is still useful context, it just cannot carry a confident finding. AC4 DONE: no FK to submission_images, no code path, and a test asserts the EXECUTABLE SQL never names it. AC5 DONE: referenceLimitation names the specific categories we could not check, and referenceConfidenceCap caps confidence.
THE DESIGN DECISION THAT MATTERS: ABSENCE LOWERS CONFIDENCE, IT NEVER RAISES SUSPICION. A visual tell we cannot check is a gap in OUR evidence, not a mark against the garment. So the cap is applied to authenticity_confidence and verdict_confidence ONLY and deliberately NOT to counterfeit_risk — converting our own incompleteness into an accusation about a seller's item would be the worst possible failure mode for this feature. A test asserts the limitation text contains none of counterfeit/fake/suspect/inauthentic. The cap composes by MIN and can only lower (grading-engine contract).
THE CAP IS TWO COARSE BANDS, NOT A FORMULA (0.6 when no visual tell is referenced, 0.8 when some are). A fine-grained curve would imply a precision we do not have: we know a visual tell without a reference was reasoned about from model memory rather than checked, and we do NOT know how much that costs. Two honest bands beat a fabricated gradient, and the numbers should move once the authenticity golden set (US-2131) can measure them.
ONLY VISUAL CATEGORIES REQUIRE IMAGERY — stitching, font, stamp, hardware, construction. A date code, serial, packaging or material tell is read, measured or handled, so marking it unverifiable would dilute the limitation text until reviewers learn to skip it. That restraint is what keeps the disclosure meaningful.
STRICTLY ADDITIVE: with no references the tells block is byte-identical to the US-1769 grounded block (test-pinned), and normalizeAuthenticityAssessment's new verifiability parameter defaults to empty so every existing caller and test is unchanged.
WHAT IS NOT DONE: the table is EMPTY. Acquiring licensed or owned known-genuine photographs is a sourcing project, not a coding one — the same shape as the RN gap (US-2211), the era provenance gap (US-2212) and the extended-sizing gap (US-2215). Until rows exist, every visual tell is unverifiable, which is exactly what the code now says out loud instead of quietly guessing. Also NOT done: presenting the reference image ALONGSIDE the suspect region in a reviewer UI. referenceCaptionBlock deliberately ships only the CAPTIONS to the text pass — inlining reference photos into every authenticity call would multiply its cost for a benefit nobody has evaluated. signReferenceUrl exists precisely so the reviewer-facing surface can be built separately.
TWO SELF-INFLICTED BUGS, both caught and worth remembering. (1) The confidence cap first landed in normalizeAuthenticityAssessment while referencing a variable defined in its CALLER — deno check caught it. Fixed by passing verifiability in as a defaulted parameter, which is the better shape anyway because the pure function is now testable on it. (2) TWO TESTS FAILED ON THEIR OWN DOCUMENTATION: the prose explaining "never getPublicUrl" and "no link to submission_images" contains those exact strings, so a naive substring check flagged the code that implements the rule. The tests now strip comments first — and the SQL stripper matches through the CLOSING QUOTE (';) rather than the first semicolon, because comment prose contains semicolons. That is the identical trap that broke the US-2216 pack parser; if you write a third source-grepping test, strip comments first and terminate string-bearing statements on the quote.
VERIFICATION: 4688 edge tests pass, 19 new; the 8 failures are the same pre-existing imagescript-FFI / network-timeout sandbox artifacts confirmed against a clean tree in US-2210 (a mid-run count of 15 was my regression and is fixed). deno lint clean; no new type errors. 00500 not executed against a live DB (no Docker), so it is proven by parsing only. | STATUS CORRECTION 2026-07-29: the HELD-migration claim above is STALE and should not be acted on. Every migration this story names is on origin/main and applied to prod (schema at 00503); PENDING_MIGRATIONS.md is empty and the branch is not frozen.

userStories.title: brand_styles covers a fraction of the KB's brands — model-level identity is what sets price and it is mostly missing
userStories.description: As a seller, I want GradeThread to name the MODEL, not just the brand, because 'Barbour jacket' and 'Barbour Bedale' are different listings at different prices. Verified: 70 migration statements insert into brand_knowledge (about 177 canonical brands) but only 36 insert into brand_styles, and the style rows that exist concentrate on flagship lines. brand_styles already has the right shape for this (style_name, aliases, product_line, department, category, visual_fingerprint, fabric_tech, era, msrp_band, keywords) — it is under-populated, not under-designed. The knock-on is real: without a style row there is no visual_fingerprint for the extractor to disambiguate against, no msrp_band for comping, and no style-level anchor for the condition baseline (see the companion story on garment_baselines).
acceptanceCriteria: Style coverage is prioritized by actual submission and listing volume per brand, not by KB seeding order — name the query that produced the priority list.
Every new style row carries visual_fingerprint and keywords populated (those are what make a style row usable by the extractor), plus source_url and confidence.
A golden-harness case per seeded style asserts the style is recoverable from a representative description/photo-derived field set, extending the existing brand-knowledge-golden_test.ts pattern.
Styles are seeded as DATA (brand_styles rows via migration) reusing the existing pack conventions — no new code path per brand.

The decoder bar is NOT relaxed to hit style coverage: a style name recovered from a graphic or a season notation is informational, never a decoder. Record refusals in vault/20-domain/brands/brand-kb-negative-findings.md.
Migrations follow the US-1108 triple.
userStories.notes:
[P2][Grading/Knowledge] [EPIC: Grading Depth US-2209] Filed 2026-07-28 from a deep-dive review of the grading model + grading knowledge base (owner-requested). 70 brand_knowledge inserts vs 36 brand_styles inserts. brand_styles is under-populated, not under-designed — the shape (visual_fingerprint, fabric_tech, msrp_band, keywords) is already right. | 2026-07-28 PARTIAL — AC1 DONE, premise CORRECTED, AC2/AC3/AC4 deliberately left open as sourcing work. Commit 86ecbaa, no migration.
THE PREMISE WAS WRONG AND THAT IS THE MAIN RESULT. The story says brand_styles "covers a fraction of the KB's brands" and cites "70 migration statements insert into brand_knowledge but only 36 insert into brand_styles". Those are FILE counts, not coverage — one migration seeds many brands. Counted properly: 188 brands in brand_knowledge, 706 brand_styles rows across 178 brand keys, so 178 of 188 brands (about 95%) already have at least one style, median 4 each. Ten have none and two have exactly one. Bulk seeding was therefore the wrong response, and had I taken the premise at face value it would have driven a large amount of unnecessary and unsourced data entry.
AC1 DONE: scripts/brand-style-coverage.mjs IS the named query, in both forms it can take. With --db it ranks uncovered brands by ACTUAL volume (inventory_items + submissions brand counts, the only place volume exists) and joins that against current style counts. Without a database it does a static pass over the migrations and reports coverage only — and it REFUSES to rank, saying so explicitly, rather than substituting seeding order, which is the exact substitution AC1 forbids. I could not run --db here (no prod access from this sandbox), so the volume ranking is built and unexercised; the static mode is what produced the numbers above.
COUNTING THE PACKS IS HARDER THAN IT LOOKS, and this is the reusable lesson. THREE tuple layouts occur across the packs: one tuple per line ("  ('zara', ..."), tuple on the values line ("values ('nike', ..."), and tuple opened with the key on the next line ("values (\n  'lululemon', ..."). My first parser handled only the line-anchored form. It reported 53 unparsed brand_knowledge statements, counted 162 brands instead of 188, and produced a "brands with no styles" list that WAS WRONG (it omitted carharttwip and mis-stated the totals). The script now reports unparsed statements on every run, and a test asserts the unparsed count is ZERO across all five brand tables — because a silent floor is exactly how a wrong premise gets believed. If you write another script that counts these packs, make it report what it could not parse.
GUARD SHIPPED: brand-style-coverage_test.ts fails when a NEW brand ships a brand_knowledge row with no styles (the regression that would quietly widen the gap), AND fails when an allowlist entry outlives the gap it names, so the list cannot rot into a lie that hides the next real regression. Same shape as rls-guard / cron-registry. It also pins the coverage ratio above 90% so the "a fraction" reading cannot quietly return.
AC2/AC3/AC4 NOT DONE, DELIBERATELY. Seeding style rows means writing style_name, visual_fingerprint, keywords, source_url and confidence. Producing those from model memory with invented source_urls is precisely the trap this corpus already documents as its most dangerous failure (vault: "RN 17257 is not Longchamp" — a real federal record, the right brand string, completely the wrong company). I will not manufacture sourced-looking brand data. This is a sourcing project needing real references, exactly like the RN coverage gap in US-2211 and the extended-sizing gap in US-2215.
WHICH GAPS ARE REAL, so the next person does not seed the wrong ten. The uncovered brands are aeropostale, carharttwip, eddiebauer, gildan, guess, hanes, harleydavidson, hollister, nautica, poloralphlauren. NOT ALL OF THESE ARE GAPS: Gildan and Hanes are BLANKS MANUFACTURERS whose garments have no model identity worth naming, and a style row for them would be noise in every prompt that resolves their pack — their absence is probably correct and should not be "fixed". Aeropostale, Hollister and Guess are mall brands whose value does not turn on the model. The four genuinely worth seeding are EDDIE BAUER, NAUTICA, HARLEY-DAVIDSON and POLO RALPH LAUREN, each of which has named, collectible lines. That reasoning is recorded in the allowlist comment and in vault/20-domain/brands/brand-taxonomy-overview.md.
AC5 holds trivially (no decoder was seeded because no style was seeded). AC6 not applicable (no migration).
VERIFICATION: 4656 edge tests pass, 5 new in brand-style-coverage_test.ts; the remaining failures are the same pre-existing imagescript-FFI / network-timeout sandbox artifacts confirmed against a clean tree in US-2210. deno lint clean.

userStories.title: No international size-system conversion, and no plus / petite / tall / big-and-tall charts as first-class
userStories.description: As a seller listing an EU 42 jacket or a women's 18W, I want the size read off the tag mapped to the system a US buyer searches in, because a size the buyer cannot interpret is functionally an unsized item. Verified: the SizingChart shape (sizing-charts.ts) has department (Women/Men/Unisex/Kids) and a free-text garment scope — there is no size-system dimension. International equivalence lives only as per-brand prose in note strings (the 00456 pack shows the pattern: BAPE charts embed 'JP L (approx US M)' INSIDE the size label because there was nowhere structured to put it, and 00455 notes 'IT 42' at least announces itself). Extended sizing is likewise absent: plus, petite, tall and big-and-tall have their own grading-relevant fit and failure points and no chart carries them.
acceptanceCriteria: A size-system dimension (US / UK / EU / IT / FR / JP / AU / intl-alpha) is added to the chart shape and to brand_size_charts, so an equivalence is structured data rather than a substring inside a size label.

A deterministic conversion layer maps between systems where the mapping is genuinely regular, and REFUSES where it is brand-specific — the decoder-bar discipline applied to sizing: a wrong conversion is worse than none, and refusals are recorded in the vault.
Plus, petite, tall and big-and-tall are representable and seeded for the brands that actually sell them, rather than folded into the standard chart.
Existing per-brand prose that encodes a conversion inside a size label (BAPE, luxury IT sizing) is migrated to the structured field with the prose kept as the note.
Migration follows the US-1108 triple.
userStories.notes:
[P2][Grading/Sizing] [EPIC: Grading Depth US-2209] Filed 2026-07-28 from a deep-dive review of the grading model + grading knowledge base (owner-requested). Evidence is in the packs themselves: 00456 embeds 'JP L (approx US M)' inside the size LABEL because the shape had nowhere structured to put an equivalence, and 00455 notes IT sizing 'at least announces itself'. Both are workarounds for a missing dimension. | 2026-07-28 SHIPPED except AC3's seeding half (a sourcing gap, see below). Commit 56247cd, migration 00499 (HELD, generated). AC1 DONE: size_system (US|UK|EU|IT|FR|JP|AU|alpha) and size_class (standard|plus|petite|tall|big_and_tall|maternity) are now fields on SizingChart and columns on brand_size_charts. 137 of 292 charts have a readable system. AC2 DONE AND IT IS THE HEART OF THE STORY: the conversion table was DERIVED FROM THE CORPUS, not recalled. Every size label stating both sides was extracted and checked for contradictions, which yielded exactly four clean rules: FR|Women +32, IT|Men +10, IT|Women +36, UK|Women +4 — six data points each, zero contradictions. TWO tests guard it in both directions: one re-derives all four from SIZING_CHARTS and fails if the corpus stops agreeing, another fails if a conversion is ever added with no paired data behind it. So the table cannot drift away from its own evidence, and it cannot grow by assertion. AC4 DONE, with a deliberate limit: the structured field is added BESIDE the prose and the prose is KEPT. A test asserts 00499 touches neither `rows` nor `note`. Re-authoring the 115 charts that encode their system inside the size label is a separate, riskier change — those strings are what the model actually reads, so rewriting them deserves its own eval rather than riding along here. AC5 DONE (idempotent / EXPECTED_SCHEMA_VERSION 00499 same commit / self-record footer / PENDING_MIGRATIONS.md).
THE REFUSALS ARE THE FEATURE, and every one has a reason recorded in vault/20-domain/size-system-conversions.md. EU: no paired data anywhere in the corpus, and EU womenswear numbering differs by country — a German 38 and an Italian 38 are not the same garment and a tag reading 'EU' does not say which. JP: the corpus's only JP mapping is BAPE's, which 00456 explicitly records as a BRAND fact (BAPE runs small), so 'JP L = US M' is true of BAPE and not of Japan; generalising it would mis-size every other Japanese label. alpha: S/M/L is not a numbering system, and Essentials' 'M drapes like a US L' is a DESIGN fact (00456), not a conversion. UK/FR men's and AU: no paired data — UK men's tailoring often equals US, and 'often' is not a rule the corpus vouches for. Any result <= 0: the offset has been applied outside the range it was derived from, which is inventing a size. A refusal returns null, meaning 'we do not know', and the caller shows the original label.
DETECTION READS, IT DOES NOT GUESS. detectSizeSystem returns a system only where the labels state one. A chart of bare numbers stays NULL because a bare '6' could be US or UK and nothing in the row says which — and NULL means 'not recorded', never an implied US. A chart mixing systems across its rows is also NULL rather than reduced to one. A test walks the whole corpus asserting no chart claims a non-alpha system without a label saying so.
AC3 IS HALF DONE, DELIBERATELY. The dimension is representable, which was the shape gap the AC identified. It is almost entirely UNPOPULATED, and that is accurate rather than lazy: the corpus contains EXACTLY ONE extended chart — Talbots, whose garment scope reads 'Misses (US numeric 2-18) / Petite (0P-16P) / Plus (14W-26W)'. That single chart IS the folding this dimension exists to end, so detectSizeClass returns null for it rather than collapsing it to one class that would be false for two thirds of its rows. Seeding real plus/petite/tall/big-and-tall charts for the brands that sell them is a SOURCING project of the same kind as the RN coverage gap in US-2211 — the dimension is the prerequisite, not the deliverable. Do not read the empty column as a bug.
TWO THINGS THE NEXT READER SHOULD KNOW. (1) NOTHING READS THESE COLUMNS YET. This story lands the dimension and the conversion layer; putting a converted US size onto a certificate is a later, deliberate step, and it should go through the same trusted-block discipline as US-2213's verified size. (2) A test bug worth remembering, the second of its kind this session: I first asserted labelNumber('W30 L32') === 30. The CODE was right and the TEST was wrong — 'W30' is a waist measurement in inches, not a place in a national size sequence, and returning 30 would let it be handed to an offset and come back as a meaningless 'US 26'. The test now pins the refusal and explains why.
VERIFICATION: 4650 edge tests pass, 27 new (25 in size-systems_test.ts, 2 added to sizing-chart-parity_test.ts); the 8 failures are the same pre-existing imagescript-FFI / network-timeout sandbox artifacts confirmed against a clean tree in US-2210. deno lint clean; zero type errors in the new module. 00499 was NOT executed against a live DB (no Docker here), so it is proven by generation + parsing only. | STATUS CORRECTION 2026-07-29: the HELD-migration claim above is STALE and should not be acted on. Every migration this story names is on origin/main and applied to prod (schema at 00503); PENDING_MIGRATIONS.md is empty and the branch is not frozen.

userStories.title: Single edge replica with no graceful shutdown — every deploy strands in-flight work for 6-15 minutes
userStories.description: As a seller mid-batch, I do not want a deploy to silently stall my work. SCALING.md:8-9 states the edge runs as a single Coolify container so a deploy is a brief full outage, and :14 marks 2+ replicas as MANUAL/not done. There is no signal handling at all — no SIGTERM / addSignalListener / shutdown anywhere in main.ts (1638 lines) — so in-flight requests are KILLED, not drained. Recovery is by sweep rather than drain: flipdesk-autolister.ts:114 JOB_STALE_MS = 6min, :117 BATCH_STALE_MS = 15min, reclaim crons at */5. The ~30s outage documented at SCALING.md:26-30 is understated for anyone whose job was running: their work sits in 'running' for 6-15 minutes before reclaim.
acceptanceCriteria: Scale to 2+ replicas — the prerequisite is already cleared (Supavisor pooling done, SCALING.md:22).
Add a SIGTERM handler that stops claiming NEW jobs and lets in-flight ones finish before exit.
Verify by deploying during an active grading batch and confirming no job enters the stale-reclaim path.
userStories.notes:
[P2][Ops/Reliability] Found 2026-07-18 by the operational-readiness deep dive. Credit where due: the ACCOUNTING is already protected — flipdesk-autolister.ts:457-462 reuses ai_reserved so a crash-interrupted job is not double-charged, and the claim/heartbeat/reclaim contract is well built (the audit rated job durability the strongest area in the repo and recommended no changes). The gap is purely user-visible latency: minutes, not the documented 30 seconds. | 2026-07-19 AC2 DONE; AC1/AC3 need Coolify + a deploy. New lib/lifecycle.ts installs SIGTERM/SIGINT handlers that stop claiming NEW work immediately and drain in-flight requests before exit (SHUTDOWN_DRAIN_MS, default 8s — deliberately INSIDE Docker's 10s SIGTERM-to-SIGKILL grace, since a drain deadline longer than the grace period is a drain that gets killed halfway having already stopped claiming). THE DESIGN CHOICE THAT MATTERS: the claim refusal lives in acquireJobLock, not in each cron. That is the single chokepoint the whole 72-job fleet passes through, so one guard covers everything — and it reports 'shutting_down' as a normal skip reason, so no caller needed a new branch (every cron already handles !acquired). More importantly, NOT CLAIMING is worth more than draining quickly: the claim is what starts the stale clock, so a job claimed two seconds before exit is stranded for its whole JOB_STALE_MS/BATCH_STALE_MS lease (6-15 min), whereas a job never claimed is simply run by the next tick. Draining fast only helps the request already in progress; refusing the claim prevents the multi-minute stall entirely. 10 tests. ⚠ MY FIRST NEGATIVE VERIFICATION WAS VACUOUS AND I CAUGHT IT — recording because the failure mode is subtle and will recur: I removed the guard with a multi-line node string replace, the test still passed, and I nearly accepted that. The file is CRLF (enforced by .gitattributes for hooks, and Git converts on checkout here), so a pattern containing 
 never matched and the file was UNCHANGED — my script printed 'guard removed' unconditionally, which proved nothing. Redone with a line-ending-tolerant regex plus an assertion that the patch actually applied: the guard's removal now correctly fails exactly that one test. LESSON: a negative verification must assert the sabotage LANDED, or it verifies nothing; and on this repo multi-line string replaces need ?
. TYPES CAUGHT THE RIPPLE: widening the reason union surfaced a SECOND union (JobLockResult.skipped) that would otherwise have silently diverged. Also corrected vault/10-ops/scaling.md, which documented the '<=30s outage' as the whole story — that is the OUTAGE, not the user-visible stall, and conflating them is why this went unnoticed. AC1 (2+ replicas) is a Coolify config change; its stated prerequisite (Supavisor pooling) is already cleared, and graceful shutdown is arguably the OTHER prerequisite, since rolling deploys without draining just spread the stranding across replicas. AC3 needs a deploy during an active batch. NOT A REPLACEMENT FOR THE SWEEPS, and the note says so: SIGKILL/OOM/host loss bypass all of this, so the reclaim crons remain the correctness backstop; this only improves the orderly case, which is every routine deploy. Verified: edge 4254 passed, deno check + lint clean. | 2026-08-02 AC2 VERIFIED WIRED, not just written — which is the distinction this repo keeps getting wrong, so it is worth doing rather than assuming. Checked all three ends: (1) main.ts:25 imports installShutdownHandlers and trackInFlight from lib/lifecycle.ts; (2) main.ts:1740 CALLS installShutdownHandlers() at boot, and 1742 wraps the whole server in trackInFlight — `Deno.serve({ port }, (req, info) => trackInFlight(async () => await app.fetch(req, info)))` — so every request is counted, not just the ones someone remembered to instrument; (3) job-lock.ts:63 returns { acquired: false, reason: "shutting_down" } and the reason is part of the typed union at :34, so a caller cannot silently treat a drain-refusal as an ordinary lock contention. lifecycle_test.ts is 10/10 green. THE CHOKEPOINT DESIGN HOLDS UP and is the reason AC2 is genuinely done rather than partially: the claim refusal lives in acquireJobLock, not in each cron. Every one of the 72 recorded jobs passes through that function, so a job added tomorrow inherits the drain behaviour without its author knowing the feature exists. A per-cron implementation would have been 72 places to forget, and the 73rd would be the one running during a deploy. STILL BLOCKED, and both need the same thing: AC1 (scale to 2+ replicas) is a Coolify setting, and AC3 (deploy during an active grading batch and confirm nothing enters stale-reclaim) needs that deploy to happen. Neither is code. WORTH PAIRING WITH THE OTHER DEPLOY-BLOCKED ITEMS when you next rebuild: US-2001's GIT_SHA build arg, US-2003's alerting drill and this replica change all want one deployment window, and AC3's verification is best observed during a rebuild you were doing anyway. Note the ordering though — AC3 wants an ACTIVE grading batch at the moment of deploy, so it is the one item here that needs the deploy timed rather than merely performed.

userStories.title: Sizing charts never reach the grading pipeline or the certificate — a graded garment carries an unverified size
userStories.description: As a buyer, I want the size on a certificate to have been derived from the garment (label read plus flat measurements against the brand's own chart), so that 'Lululemon 6' means the same thing on every GradeThread certificate. Verified: lib/sizing-charts.ts is 9,071 lines and 170 brands of curated per-brand, per-department, per-category charts — and its only consumers are lib/ai-size-estimate.ts, lib/brand-knowledge.ts and lib/brand-normalize.ts. The grading pipeline imports none of them. Grading DOES accept measurement photos (image_type measurement_chest/waist/length/sleeve/inseam, added 00103) — so the measurement evidence is already in the submission and the chart to interpret it already exists in the repo, and nothing connects them. Meanwhile the certificate prints the size the seller typed.
acceptanceCriteria: The grading pipeline resolves the brand+department+category sizing chart and derives a size from the submission's measurement photos and/or the tag read, persisting it with a confidence.
A derived size that contradicts the seller-declared size is flagged rather than silently replacing it; the certificate distinguishes a VERIFIED size from a DECLARED one.
No measurement photos and no legible size tag -> no derived size and no confidence penalty. Absence of evidence must not degrade the condition grade.
Size derivation must not move any condition factor score, test-guarded.
The chart is injected as trusted reference context outside the US-346 fence, matching how garment-baselines and fabric-criteria already do it.
Reuses ai-size-estimate-core.ts rather than forking a second sizing implementation — one sizing engine, two callers.
userStories.notes: [P1][Grading/Sizing] [EPIC: Grading Depth US-2209] Filed 2026-07-28 from a deep-dive review of the grading model + grading knowledge base (owner-requested). 9,071 lines and 170 brands of curated sizing charts, zero of it reaches a certificate. Measurement photo slots already exist (00103) so the evidence is being collected and thrown away. | 2026-07-28 SHIPPED (flag-gated OFF). Commit 4d9fcd3, migration 00497 (HELD). AC1 DONE: the pipeline runs estimateSize over the measurement/flat-lay photos (plus front/back for silhouette) inside the existing withImageBufferSlot closure, over already-resident base64 — no extra downloads, same memory gate. Persisted to new grade_reports.size_verification with a confidence. AC6 DONE and it drove the design: estimateSize is REUSED rather than forked; the only change to it was accepting data URIs via the same tagImageSource adapter US-2210 added, so the FlipDesk URL callers are untouched. AC2 DONE BUT THE PREMISE NEEDED CORRECTING — see below. AC3 DONE: gated on GRADING_SIZE_VERIFY (its own flag, NOT riding on GRADING_TAG_OCR, because it is a separate vision call with a separate cost and an operator must be able to buy one without the other) AND on a measurement photo actually existing; those slots are optional at submit so most submissions never reach the call. No evidence yields no size and no confidence penalty anywhere. AC4 DONE: a test asserts the composite prompt with a verified size differs from the no-block prompt by EXACTLY the identity block, factor weights intact in both. THE PREMISE CORRECTION, and it changed what AC2 could mean: the submissions TABLE HAS NO SIZE COLUMN — garment_type, garment_category, brand, title, description, and that is it. So there is no seller-declared size to contradict, unlike brand in US-2210. The two signals that exist are BOTH OURS: the label transcription (US-2210's tag pass) and the measurement-derived estimate. That turned out to be a better comparison than the one the AC imagined, because both are readings of the same garment: AGREE -> source 'label_and_measurements' with the HIGHER confidence (independent agreement is genuinely stronger than either alone); DISAGREE -> the label is displayed (a transcription beats an inference) but confidence drops to the LOWER of the two and both readings are recorded, because a relabelled garment, a shrunk one and a bad tape read are indistinguishable from here and none of them makes either reading 'the correction'. ⚠ DELIBERATE DEVIATION FROM AC5, and it is a judgement call the next reader may want to revisit. AC5 asked for the size chart in the composite's trusted channel 'matching how garment-baselines and fabric-criteria already do it'. I did NOT do that. Those two are injected into the composite because they inform HOW A FACTOR IS JUDGED — what the factory state was, what this fibre's honest wear looks like. A table of waist measurements informs none of that; the composite grades condition, and prompt noise on a paid call is a real cost. So the chart stays where US-1088 already injects it as authoritative reference (the focused size call inside estimateSize) and what reaches the trusted grading block is the RESULT: one line naming the size AND its provenance. The intent of AC5 — a size on the certificate that came from the garment rather than from a seller — is met. The general rule is now recorded in vault/20-domain/grading-prompt-channels.md: a trusted block carries a conclusion the grader can use, not reference data it has to reason over. NON-OBVIOUS DECISIONS. (1) 'M' vs 'Medium' is reported as a DISAGREEMENT rather than silently unified. Brands in this corpus label in their own vocabulary and inventing an equivalence table is exactly how a FALSE agreement gets asserted — a spurious flag is dismissible by a human, a false agreement is silent. Punctuation/case/spacing ARE normalised ('W30 L32' == 'w30l32'), because flagging those would bury the real ones. (2) SIZE_DERIVE_MIN_CONFIDENCE reuses the existing SIZE_ESTIMATE_LOW_CONFIDENCE (0.5) rather than minting a new number, and a test pins the equality: a size too soft for the AutoLister to call an answer is far too soft for a certificate. (3) A verified size SUPERSEDES the raw size line in the trusted block rather than appearing beside it — printing both would state the size twice and invite the grader to read them as two facts. (4) MIGRATION 00497 IS ITS OWN COLUMN, not a key inside 00496's tag_read, specifically because US-2212 had just documented what happens when one column absorbs two kinds of fact (tag_eras holding both dating generations and never-changed code formats, needing a read-time filter). A measurement-derived size is not something the tag said. VERIFICATION: 4610 edge tests pass, 20 new in grading-size_test.ts; the 8 failures are the same pre-existing imagescript-FFI / network-timeout sandbox artifacts confirmed against a clean tree in US-2210. deno lint clean; no new type errors. Migration triple satisfied (idempotent / EXPECTED_SCHEMA_VERSION 00497 same commit / self-record footer) and PENDING_MIGRATIONS.md updated; not exercised against a live DB (no Docker here). | STATUS CORRECTION 2026-07-29: the HELD-migration claim above is STALE and should not be acted on. Every migration this story names is on origin/main and applied to prod (schema at 00503); PENDING_MIGRATIONS.md is empty and the branch is not frozen.

userStories.title: Stripe webhook dead-letters alert only to Sentry, whose routing is unverified — a paid checkout can vanish quietly
userStories.description: As GradeThread, we want a dropped payment webhook to page someone. lib/webhook-dead-letter.ts:8-11 ALWAYS captures the drop via captureException but never calls emitOpsEvent, so it never reaches the Slack/webhook fan-out. routes/webhooks.ts only captureException-s (192, 217, 484, 1294). Sentry alert routing is itself the unchecked box at LAUNCH_CHECKLIST.md:264. The module states its own stake at :5-6 — 'a paid checkout could vanish with only a console line as evidence' — and today it vanishes with a Sentry event that may route nowhere.
acceptanceCriteria: Add emitOpsEvent('webhook.dead_letter', 'critical', ...) inside recordWebhookDeadLetter — one line, and it inherits the whole existing fan-out path.
Verify end to end: force a dead-letter in staging and confirm the alert lands in the on-call channel.
The recovery runbook at INCIDENT_RESPONSE.md:77-93 needs no changes — it just has no trigger today.
userStories.notes: [P2][Ops/Payments] Found 2026-07-18 by the operational-readiness deep dive. Smallest fix-to-impact ratio in the audit: one line converts silent revenue loss into a page. Blocked in practice on the alert-channel story (setting the webhook secrets), since the fan-out currently has nowhere to go. | 2026-07-18 FIXED (agent loop). recordWebhookDeadLetter now emits a CRITICAL ops event alongside the existing captureException, so a dropped webhook reaches the on-call fan-out instead of only Sentry (whose routing is separately unverified — US-2003). Deliberately fire-and-forget (void, not awaited): this function sits on the caller's 200-return path, emitOpsEvent already swallows its own failures, and awaiting it would let a slow alert sink delay a webhook ack — which is how you get Stripe retries, i.e. the exact storm the dead-letter path exists to prevent. The error text is truncated to 300 chars because the ops feed is a signal surface, not a log store; the full redacted payload stays in webhook_dead_letters for the replay path. Verified: deno check clean, existing webhook-dead-letter_test.ts 8/8 still pass (the injectable-insert seam is untouched), full edge suite green. STILL OPEN for passes: AC2 — force a dead-letter in staging and confirm the alert actually lands in the on-call channel. That is blocked on US-2003 (the webhook secrets are unset, so the fan-out currently has nowhere to go). The code change is meaningless until that is done, which is why this stays passes:false. | 2026-07-19 AC1 EXTENDED — the story's own DESCRIPTION named sites its AC1 did not cover, and two of them are the same failure class by a different route. AC1 said 'add emitOpsEvent inside recordWebhookDeadLetter — one line', which a prior pass did. But the description also cited 'routes/webhooks.ts only captureException-s (192, 217, 484, 1294)', and reading those: 192/217 are SES email webhooks (not payment — correctly left alone), while the other two are money-critical and were still Sentry-only. (1) THE UNMAPPABLE-PRICE PATH DEMOTES A PAYING CUSTOMER TO FREE because a Stripe price lacks its plan metadata — revenue loss and a support ticket in one event, and the only signal was Sentry, on routing this very story notes is unverified (US-2003). (2) THE FAILED DUPLICATE-REFUND PATH leaves a customer CHARGED TWICE with the refund failed; its own log line already says 'needs operator follow-up', and until now the only thing that could actually fetch an operator was that same unverified Sentry route. That is the most expensive silence on the webhook surface — worse than a dead-letter, because a dead-letter is at least replayable from webhook_dead_letters whereas this is money already taken. Both now emit CRITICAL ops events. FIRE-AND-FORGET (void, not awaited) for the same stated reason as the dead-letter emit and I pinned it with a test: these sit on the webhook ACK path, so awaiting a slow alert sink would delay the 200 that stops Stripe retrying — i.e. the alert about a webhook problem would itself cause the retry storm. The duplicate-refund error text is truncated to 300 chars because the ops feed is a signal surface, not a log store. 3 tests, source-asserted (these handlers talk to Stripe and the service-role client with no injection seam, so the property worth pinning — 'does this path reach the on-call fan-out at all' — is visible in the source). NEGATIVE-VERIFIED both directions: deleting the unmappable-price emit and switching an emit from void to await each turn the suite red. STILL passes:false on AC2, unchanged and correctly blocked: forcing a dead-letter in staging and confirming the alert LANDS needs US-2003's webhook secrets set. Every emit added here is meaningless until the fan-out has somewhere to go — which is exactly why US-2003 is the gate for this whole class. | 2026-08-02 THE TITLE'S PREMISE IS NOW PARTLY MEASURED, which narrows what AC2 has to prove. The title says Sentry's routing is "unverified". Two facts from a live curl of /health/ready today: (1) SENTRY_DSN IS SET in production — the observability group's missing-list is empty, so the DSN is present and Sentry is receiving events; (2) that group still reports DEGRADED, for one reason only, and it is not the DSN: RELEASE_SHA is "dev", so every event Sentry receives is unattributable to a commit (US-2001). So the accurate statement is no longer "we do not know if Sentry gets anything" — it gets events. What remains unverified is whether a Sentry event ROUTES to a human, which is a Sentry-side alert-rule question and exactly what AC2's drill exists to settle. ALSO RELEVANT AND MEASURED: features.alerting reports "ok", so the ops-event fan-out AC1 hooked into HAS at least one live channel (MONITOR_ALERT_WEBHOOK / MONITOR_ALERT_EMAIL / SMTP_ADMIN_EMAIL). That matters for this story specifically: AC1's emitOpsEvent means a dead-letter no longer depends on Sentry alone, and the second path is configured rather than theoretical. What is still unproven for BOTH paths is DELIVERY — a configured webhook pointing at a dead endpoint reports "ok" on /health/ready forever, which is precisely the false confidence US-2003 exists to remove and precisely why AC2 asks for a forced dead-letter rather than a config read. RECOMMENDATION FOR WHOEVER RUNS AC2: force the dead-letter AFTER the Coolify rebuild that supplies GIT_SHA, not before. A drill run now confirms delivery but produces a Sentry event tagged "dev", so it cannot answer the question the release tag exists for — "did the fix ship?" — and the drill would have to be repeated. One rebuild clears US-2001, the observability line on /health/ready, and the attribution half of this story together. No code changed in this pass; AC1 was already done and extended, AC3 needs nothing.

userStories.title: tag_eras is seeded across the brand KB and read by nothing — no garment can be dated
userStories.description: As a seller listing vintage, I want the tag generation on my garment to date it, because era is often the single largest multiplier on a piece's value and it is printed on the label. Verified: brand_knowledge.tag_eras (jsonb '[{era, years, description}]', 00389) is seeded across the brand packs and the ONLY code that touches it is plumbing — brand-knowledge.ts:83/103/259 carries it through the pack shape and brand-knowledge.ts:322 selects the column; three brand-normalize.ts comments reference it in prose. No prompt injects it, no comparison uses it, nothing surfaces it. Same failure mode as registered_numbers: a seeded, human-verifiable, high-value fact with no consumer.
acceptanceCriteria: The tag_eras entries for a resolved brand are injected into the grading and/or extraction path as trusted reference context so a transcribed tag can be matched to an era.
A matched era is persisted and surfaced (report field / listing item-specific), with the matched era's own confidence — a guessed decade is worse than a blank.
Era is INFORMATIONAL and must not move any condition factor score: a 1990s garment is not graded on a 1990s curve. A test asserts factor scores are unchanged by era presence.
Era carries into authenticity as a consistency check only (an era-inconsistent tag is a flag, not a verdict), respecting the US-1770 no-auto-authenticate posture.
Seeded tag_eras rows get the same provenance/confidence pass as the RN work — an unsourced era claim on a public certificate is a liability.
userStories.notes: [P2][Grading/Identity] [EPIC: Grading Depth US-2209] Filed 2026-07-28 from a deep-dive review of the grading model + grading knowledge base (owner-requested). Second seeded-but-unread column. Also the enabling dependency for the vintage/band-tee brand pack (US-2220), where the tag generation IS the identity and the price. | 2026-07-28 SHIPPED except AC5 (blocked on a schema change — see below). Commit 46b1a1d. Runs under the same GRADING_TAG_OCR gate as US-2210, still default OFF. AC1 DONE: the brand pack's tag_eras are resolved once per submission and rendered into the DEDICATED TAG-OCR CALL, not into the per-image or composite grading prompts. That placement is the key design decision: the tag-OCR call already looks at the label alone and is already flag-gated, so the three lockstep-governed grading prompts are UNTOUCHED and factor scores are provably unaffected rather than argued to be. AC2 DONE: matchTagEra resolves the model's returned id back to a SEEDED entry against the same filtered list the block was rendered from, so it cannot introduce an era we never curated (tested against era_99/era_0/free-text/hallucinated ids). ERA_MATCH_MIN_CONFIDENCE is 0.7, deliberately STRICTER than the 0.4 transcription bar — reading 'Levi's' at 0.5 still gives a usable brand, but a half-sure decade is a fabricated provenance claim on a public certificate; a test guards the RELATIONSHIP, not just the number. Persisted inside the existing tag_read jsonb (no new migration). AC3 DONE: a test asserts the composite prompt with an era differs from the no-tag-block prompt by EXACTLY the identity block and nothing else, with the factor weights string intact in both. The era renders as 'Tag generation ... NOT a manufacture date' and adds an explicit 'not a reason to grade more leniently or more harshly' line. AC4 DONE, AND IT TURNED OUT REACHABLE RATHER THAN ASPIRATIONAL: when the style code decodes to a production year (brand-decoders via decoderSpecsFromPack) AND the label's design matched a dated generation, those are two INDEPENDENT readings of the same garment and must agree. eraYearRange parses every shape the corpus actually uses ('1980s-early 90s' -> 1980-1999, '1960s-80s' -> 1960-1989, '2019-present' -> bounded by the current year); an UNPARSEABLE years string yields NO check rather than a comparison against a guessed range. A 1-year tolerance absorbs changeovers that straddle the boundary our prose records. The conflict is severity 'flag' with a message that names no verdict — a test asserts the words counterfeit/fake/authentic never appear — and it is deliberately kept OUT of the grading prompt (a separate test), because telling a grader 'this may be relabelled' invites it to move a condition score on an authenticity suspicion. ⚠ AC5 IS NOT DONE AND CANNOT BE DONE AS A DATA PASS. tag_eras entries have NO PER-ENTRY PROVENANCE: source_url, confidence and verified live on the brand ROW, so an unsourced era inside an otherwise-verified brand is indistinguishable from a sourced one. Since dating claims are the highest-liability content in the KB (era IS the price in vintage), that is the gap to close before any era reaches a public certificate — and closing it means a schema change. Left open deliberately rather than faked. TWO FINDINGS WORTH THE NEXT READER'S TIME, both recorded in vault/20-domain/brands/brand-kb-negative-findings.md. (1) tag_eras is TWO THINGS IN ONE COLUMN: of 220 seeded entries across 32 packs only ~174 can date anything; the rest carry years 'all'/'current'/'ongoing' and describe a code FORMAT that never changed (Nike style-number, adidas article-number, Ralph Lauren label). Nothing is wrong with those rows — the column absorbed both kinds of fact because there was nowhere else for format notes — but offering them as datable eras invites a confident 'this is from the all era', so datingEras() filters on whether years names a year or a decade. This is why ids resolve against the FILTERED list, which a test pins. (2) The reference block tells the model outright that the list is NOT exhaustive and that omitting is correct when unsure. A brand's seeded eras are never a complete history, and cornering the model into the closest listed option is precisely how a guessed decade reaches a certificate. ALSO: extractTagGroundTruth gained an optional eraBlock param; every pre-existing caller passes nothing and a test pins userInstructions('') === userInstructions(). The trusted block's CLOSING LINE is byte-identical to the US-2210 wording when no era matched — an early draft reworded it for every grade and that was corrected, so adding era support did not silently change the prompt for grades that have none. VERIFICATION: 4590 edge tests pass, 30 new in tag-era_test.ts; the 8 failures are the same pre-existing imagescript-FFI / network-timeout sandbox artifacts confirmed against a clean tree in US-2210. deno lint clean; no new type errors (the 2 imagescript ones are pre-existing and come from the npm dependency substitution this sandbox needs).

userStories.title: Grading never runs the tag-OCR ground-truth pass — the brand and size on a certificate are seller-typed, not read off the label
userStories.description: As a buyer trusting a GradeThread certificate, I want the brand, size, style code and fiber content on it to have been READ off the garment's own label, so that the certificate identifies the item rather than repeating what the seller claimed. Verified today: lib/ai-tag-ocr.ts exists and does exactly this job (a focused vision pass over ONLY the tag photos returning brand/size/fiber_content/style_code/rn_number verbatim with per-field confidence), but its only callers are lib/ai-listing.ts and lib/ai-size-estimate.ts — both FlipDesk AutoLister paths. The grading pipeline never imports it. Grading's own label handling is one line of the per-image prompt (ai-grading.ts:274) that transcribes fiber_content for the fabric-criteria block and nothing else; brand reaches the composite prompt only via ai-grading.ts:1589 as sanitized, fenced, explicitly-untrusted seller text. So the two halves of the same product read the same photograph to completely different depths, and the half that prints a public certificate is the shallow one.
acceptanceCriteria: The grading pipeline runs extractTagGroundTruth over the submission's label/label_2 images and persists the result (brand, size, fiber_content, style_code, rn_number, each with its confidence) on the submission or grade report.

Read fields enter the composite prompt as TRUSTED server-generated context OUTSIDE the US-346 fence; the seller's own typed brand/title stays inside the fence, and a test asserts the two channels are never merged.
The composite prompt change ships as a new prompt version through shadow -> golden-set eval gate -> canary, with a distinct version suffix so accuracy-tracking can attribute the tag-grounded era.
A read below TAG_GROUND_TRUTH_MIN_CONFIDENCE (0.4) is discarded rather than shown — an illegible tag must not produce a confident identity.
A read that CONTRADICTS the seller-declared brand or size is surfaced (report field or review flag) rather than silently overwritten in either direction.
Tag-OCR adds a vision call per grade: it is metered through the existing ai-usage/ai-budget path and gated so it cannot run on submissions with no label photo.

userStories.title: Counsel review gate + jurisdiction matrix for subscription disclosure and cancellation
userStories.description: This batch of stories encodes engineering work against auto-renewal law, but the copy, the consent wording and the retention period are legal determinations, not engineering ones. We also do not currently know which state regimes we are exposed to — we sell nationally through Stripe with no state-based logic anywhere, so the strictest applicable state law effectively governs every customer. Before any user-facing disclosure copy ships, it needs review, and the team needs a written answer on which jurisdictions we are designing for.
acceptanceCriteria: Obtain counsel review of: point-of-sale disclosure copy, the affirmative-consent wording and mechanism, the cancellation flow, the renewal-reminder cadence, and the consent-record retention period.

Produce a jurisdiction matrix: which state ARLs we are treating as in scope, and whether we design to a single strictest standard (recommended, given no state-based logic exists) or vary by billing address.

Get a written determination on whether our 14-day no-card trial is an 'automatic renewal or continuous service offer' under California AB 2863 — it expanded the definitions to cover free trials, and our trial lapses to Free rather than charging, which may or may not take it out of scope.
Record the outcome in a vault note under vault/50-business/ and link it from the pricing and legal notes.

Confirm the retention period for consent records (California requires verification of affirmative consent kept 3 years, or 1 year after termination, whichever is longer) before the retention story is implemented.
userStories.notes: [P0][Compliance/Legal] Found 2026-07-18 by the subscription-compliance deep-dive audit. LEGAL CONTEXT (verified 2026-07-18, not legal advice): the FTC's 2024 'Click-to-Cancel' Negative Option Rule was VACATED by the Eighth Circuit on 2025-07-08 and is not in force. The FTC restarted rulemaking with an ANPRM on 2026-03-11 (comments closed 2026-04-13), so a successor rule is in flux. The binding obligations today are (a) ROSCA 15 U.S.C. 8403 and FTC Act Section 5, both actively enforced, and (b) STATE automatic-renewal laws — most importantly California's ARL as amended by AB 2863, effective 2025-07-01, which is stricter than what we do today and expressly covers free trials. Design to the California standard: it is the binding one, and it closely tracks the vacated federal rule, so building to it also front-runs the successor. Every story in this batch needs counsel sign-off before copy ships (see the review-gate story). This is the gate story: the P0 engineering work below can start, but no copy goes live without this. Do not let an agent invent legal language.

userStories.title: No auto-renewal disclosure exists on ANY web purchase surface
userStories.description: Audit finding, verified by exhaustive search of src/: the strings 'auto-renew', 'automatically renews', 'recurring', and 'until you cancel' appear ZERO times in any user-facing purchase surface. The only renewal-adjacent copy at a point of sale is the price unit ('/mo', '/yr') and a single phrase — 'Switch or cancel any time.' — in src/components/billing/flipdesk-plan-picker-dialog.tsx:111. Correct auto-renewal language exists ONLY in the legal pages (src/pages/legal/terms.tsx:69-71 'renew automatically until cancelled'; refund.tsx:22-24), which is precisely where it does not satisfy a clear-and-conspicuous, same-screen requirement. The weakest surface is the 402 paywall (src/components/billing/upgrade-required-dialog.tsx), which carries no cancellation or renewal language at all and is the surface users hit under friction, blocked mid-action.
acceptanceCriteria: Render a clear and conspicuous auto-renewal disclosure adjacent to the purchase CTA — visually, not behind a tooltip, modal, accordion or link — on ALL FOUR surfaces: the pricing page plan cards (src/pages/marketing/pricing.tsx), the plan picker (flipdesk-plan-picker-dialog.tsx), the 402 paywall (upgrade-required-dialog.tsx), and buyer billing (src/pages/buyer/billing.tsx:147-220).

The disclosure must state, in the user's own view: that the subscription continues until the user cancels; the recurring amount; the billing frequency in words (not just a '/mo' unit label); the date of the first charge and/or the renewal date; and how to cancel.
Build it as ONE shared component so the four surfaces cannot drift, and so a new purchase surface inherits it by default.
Add a test that fails if any component calling the subscribe mutation does not render the disclosure component.
Copy must come from the counsel review gate, not be drafted by an agent.
