userStories.title: Deepen brand-decoders cross-checks — the strongest deterministic signal we have
userStories.description: brand-decoders.ts is a data-driven regex decoder engine whose crossCheck produces DecodeInconsistency on impossible dates (date_in_future, date_before_brand at :236-245), fed into the prompt as trusted DECODER_CROSS_CHECKS outside the seller-input fence (ai-authenticity.ts:346-353). This is deterministic contradiction detection — it does not depend on model judgment, cannot be talked out of a finding, and is already built and underused. It is the highest-confidence authenticity signal available today and the one most worth extending. CORRECTION 2026-07-19 (after reading vault/20-domain/brands/brand-kb-decoder-bar.md, which the grading-engine skill instructs be read BEFORE adding any decoder): this story as originally filed invites the exact failure that note forbids. Decoders must clear tag-printed AND regular AND BRAND-UNIQUE IN FORMAT, plus a fourth question added 2026-07-19 — WHICH ENTITY does the identifier name? Reebok, PUMA, Chanel/Moncler/Balenciaga serials, the Canada Goose hologram and URBN OB###### are all deliberately decoder-less; they look like coverage gaps and are not. Decoder authority OUTRANKS the AI on conflict, so a false decoder does not merely add a wrong guess — it overrides a correct one. Expanding coverage by submission volume, as originally written, would mint false positives.
acceptanceCriteria: Treat CROSS-CHECKS and DECODERS as different risk classes. A cross-check detects a contradiction (impossible date, mismatched era) and cannot mis-attribute a brand — that is the safe expansion path and where effort should go. A decoder RECOVERS a brand from a code and can override a correct read.
Any new decoder must clear all three bar tests AND the which-entity question, with the reasoning recorded in the vault note alongside the existing table.
Do NOT seed a decoder for any code listed as a deliberate refusal — extend the refusal table instead if a new one is evaluated and rejected.

A parent-wide or shared identifier (URBN OB######, shared RN 66170) can never attribute a sibling brand. Any RN/CA cross-check must handle shared RNs explicitly rather than treating RN -> brand as one-to-one.
Codes that fail the bar get transcribed into tag_eras or authentication_tells, never wired to brand recovery.
A contradiction from a deterministic decoder must dominate model optimism — verify applyVerdictCap composition holds (caps compose as a min and never raise).
Surface which decoders fired in the operator view so a verdict is explainable.
userStories.notes: [P1][Authenticity/Signal][EPIC: Visual Authenticity] Found 2026-07-19 by the authenticity deep-dive audit. STRATEGY CONTEXT: Certilogo was the starting reference, but its model does not transfer — it verifies a brand-issued CLG code / QR on a security label sewn in at manufacture (its AI image recognition authenticates the TAG and detects cloned codes, not the garment's construction). GradeThread inspects garments it never manufactured, with no token. The transferable play is visual authentication of the garment itself, anchored on evidence we can actually capture. Note the scaffolding is ~80% built (ai-authenticity.ts is live in production) while the evidence base is ~5% — this epic closes that gap in order: contain what is already live, then raise evidence quality, then productize the claim. Deterministic signal is also the most defensible claim: 'the date code is impossible for this brand' is a fact, not an opinion. Prioritize this over model-side tuning. The safe, high-value work here is CROSS-CHECK expansion (contradiction detection), not decoder expansion (brand attribution) — the vault note is unambiguous that a false decoder is worse than no decoder. Read vault/20-domain/brands/{brand-kb-decoder-bar,brand-kb-alias-refusals,brand-kb-negative-findings}.md before touching this. | 2026-07-19 ⚠ THIS STORY'S FOUNDING PREMISE IS FALSE — READ BEFORE STARTING. The description states the cross-checks are 'fed into the prompt as trusted DECODER_CROSS_CHECKS outside the seller-input fence'. THEY ARE NOT. Traced end to end: buildTellsBlock (ai-authenticity.ts:386) accepts a crossChecks array and renders the DECODER_CROSS_CHECKS block, and assessAuthenticity reads it as `context.crossChecks ?? []` (:543) — but NOTHING IN THE CODEBASE EVER SUPPLIES IT. All four production callers (grading-pipeline.ts:1243, buyer-authenticity.ts:50, public-grading.ts:1106, authenticity-eval.ts:484) pass `{ tells }` only. So the array is always empty, the block never renders, and crossCheckDecodeResult — the only producer — has ZERO callers (found by audit-unwired-exports.mjs). THE CONSEQUENCE FOR THIS STORY: every AC is about DEEPENING a signal that is not connected. Adding decoders and cross-checks as written would extend a pure function whose output still reaches nothing, and the work would test green throughout — the deepened signal simply never reaches the model. WIRE IT FIRST, and note the plumbing already exists on the consuming side, so this is genuinely small: ai-extract.ts already computes decoderHits: DecodeResult[] (:946,:981) in production. The missing step is running crossCheckDecodeResult over those hits and passing the result as context.crossChecks. BUT IT IS NOT A ONE-LINER, and this is the part worth flagging: this ADDS DYNAMIC PER-ITEM CONTEXT TO AN AUTHENTICITY PROMPT, which the grading-engine skill requires be flag-gated and to SUFFIX prompt_version so accuracy tracking can attribute eras (the same rule that governs +baseline/+fabric/+visual). Shipping it unflagged would silently change verdicts under an unchanged version string and make every before/after accuracy comparison meaningless. AC6 (applyVerdictCap composition) also cannot be verified today, because a contradiction can never currently reach the model to dominate its optimism. RECOMMEND: split the wiring (+ flag + version suffix + eval) out as its own story ahead of this one; the decoder-bar discipline in AC2-AC5 is unaffected and still correct.

userStories.title: iOS silently omits the entire paid consumer grading path, including the 14-day dispute flow
userStories.description: As a consumer grading on iOS, I want the same journey the web offers. There are TWO independent grading pipelines in the edge: the consumer/certified path (routes/grade.ts:209 /submit, :751 /pay/:id, :837 /status/:id, :1117 /dispute) and the FlipDesk/reseller path (/api/flipdesk/grading/{validate,submit,submissions/:id}). Web implements BOTH (new-submission.tsx:647, bulk-submission.tsx:332, submission-detail.tsx:244). iOS implements ONLY the FlipDesk path — Grading/GradingService.swift:6,55 documents and calls validate -> submit -> GET /submissions/:id — and grepping iOS for grade/pay, grade/status and grade/dispute returns NOTHING. So iOS has no consumer certified-grading submission, no per-grade payment flow, and NO GRADE DISPUTE FLOW at all.
acceptanceCriteria: Decide explicitly whether the consumer grading path belongs on iOS. Nothing in IOS_PARITY_AUDIT.md or the Android plan mentions this omission either way, which is weak evidence it is accidental rather than a product decision — settle it in writing.
If it belongs: implement submit / pay / status / dispute on iOS against routes/grade.ts.

If it does not: document why, and confirm the dispute obligation is discharged some other way — a 14-day dispute window that only one client can exercise is a support and chargeback liability regardless of intent.
Any parity matrix must stop treating 'grading submission' as ONE row; scoring it that way marks iOS complete while the entire paid consumer path is missing.
userStories.notes: [P1][iOS/Parity] Found 2026-07-18 by the cross-platform parity deep dive. Two implementations of the core revenue journey is the highest-value drift surface in the repo, and the mobile client omits the paid half. The dispute gap is the sharpest edge: US-1340 tracks a 14-day dispute window as a real obligation, and a user who graded on iOS has no in-app route to exercise it.

userStories.title: iOS: bulk photo import is strictly serial though a bounded-concurrency helper already exists
userStories.description: Both PHPicker import paths — AutoListerReviewModel.swift:218-243 and PhotoIntakeView.swift:907-923 — are plain serial for loops awaiting per photo: result.loadImage() (I/O; for iCloud-backed photos a NETWORK round trip each), then PhotoCompressor.compressOffMain (CPU), then a detached DHash.compute (CPU, :238-240). Meanwhile PhotoCompressor.compressBatch(_:maxConcurrent:) (PhotoCompressor.swift:64-91) exists for exactly this — bounded concurrency, per-item autoreleasepool, order-preserving — and a grep of the whole ios/ tree shows its ONLY caller is Inventory/PhotosDropHandler.swift:20. Neither high-volume import path uses it.
acceptanceCriteria: Wrap the whole per-photo unit (load + compress + dHash) in the chunked withTaskGroup shape already used correctly three times in this codebase: PhotoCompressor.compressBatch, DisclosureStore.renderAll (Disclosure/DisclosureStore.swift:88-115) and ReconciliationService (:215-242).

Keep concurrency modest (3-4) so only a few full-resolution UIImages are resident — that memory property is why compressBatch was written, and parallelising without it trades a latency win for a jetsam risk.
Preserve input order via the enumerate-and-sort approach at DisclosureStore.swift:106.
userStories.notes:
[P2][iOS/Performance] Found 2026-07-18 by the iOS audit. The dominant cost is loadImage(), not compression: for iCloud-backed photos that is a serialized network fetch per photo, so a 200-photo import is 200 sequential round trips. Symptom: bulk import sits on the spinner for minutes rather than tens of seconds when photos are not local, and it widens the window for the 'still downloading from iCloud' partial-failure path the code already anticipates (:255-259). NOT FIXED HERE — Swift is unbuildable on Windows.

VERIFIED 2026-07-18 — REAL, still open, deliberately NOT fixed blind.

Confirmed at PhotoIntakeView.ingestLibraryPicks (:907): a plain `for result in results` loop awaiting result.loadImage() then compressOffMain per item. Strictly serial, so 200 iCloud-backed photos are 200 sequential network round trips.

Refinement to the story premise: the existing helper CANNOT be applied directly. PhotoCompressor.compressBatch takes [UIImage] — images already in memory — while the bottleneck is loadImage() upstream of it. What compressBatch does provide is the exact PATTERN to copy: a windowed `withTaskGroup(of: (Int, T).self)` writing into a pre-sized results array, which preserves picker order (the loop comment notes order matters for the tray) and bounds residency.

DESIGN CONSTRAINT worth recording, because the obvious implementation is wrong: do NOT load all images first and then call compressBatch. compressBatch own header explains why — it keeps only a few full-resolution UIImages resident so a large drop does not spike memory into a jetsam kill. Loading 200 full-res UIImages up front reintroduces exactly that risk. The correct shape is ONE windowed TaskGroup where each task does loadImage + compress together, so at most maxConcurrent full-res images exist at any moment.

Why not fixed here: this is ~25 lines of NEW concurrent Swift on the bulk-import path, with ordering and memory-residency invariants, and it cannot be compiled or tested on this Windows checkout. That is a different risk class from the one-word LazyHStack change — needs a macOS session.

userStories.title: No price-change notice or consent path on any platform
userStories.description: No code path notifies a user of a price increase before it takes effect. Stripe's price.updated and customer.subscription.updated-with-price-delta are not inspected (webhooks.ts:244-281). On Apple, the ASSN router (lib/appstore/notifications.ts:18-32) does not handle PRICE_INCREASE or DID_CHANGE_RENEWAL_PREF — Apple collects price-increase consent natively so this is not a rejection risk, but the server never learns a price change occurred, and an unconsented lapse arrives only as a generic EXPIRED. On Google Play, PRICE_CHANGE_CONFIRMED is explicitly a no-op (lib/google-play/rtdn.ts:11,107).
acceptanceCriteria: Notify subscribers in advance of any price increase, stating the old price, new price, effective date and how to cancel first.
Handle Apple PRICE_INCREASE and DID_CHANGE_RENEWAL_PREF so server state reflects platform-side changes.
Decide and document whether a price increase requires fresh affirmative consent on the web (it commonly does under state ARLs) and implement accordingly.
Do not implement a price change of any kind until this exists.
userStories.notes: [P2][Compliance/Billing] Found 2026-07-18 by the subscription-compliance deep-dive audit. LEGAL CONTEXT (verified 2026-07-18, not legal advice): the FTC's 2024 'Click-to-Cancel' Negative Option Rule was VACATED by the Eighth Circuit on 2025-07-08 and is not in force. The FTC restarted rulemaking with an ANPRM on 2026-03-11 (comments closed 2026-04-13), so a successor rule is in flux. The binding obligations today are (a) ROSCA 15 U.S.C. 8403 and FTC Act Section 5, both actively enforced, and (b) STATE automatic-renewal laws — most importantly California's ARL as amended by AB 2863, effective 2025-07-01, which is stricter than what we do today and expressly covers free trials. Design to the California standard: it is the binding one, and it closely tracks the vacated federal rule, so building to it also front-runs the successor. Every story in this batch needs counsel sign-off before copy ships (see the review-gate story). Currently latent — no price change has been attempted. It becomes a live exposure the moment pricing moves, which makes it cheap to fix now and expensive to fix under deadline. | 2026-07-19 AC2 DONE (mechanism — no counsel). Apple PRICE_INCREASE and DID_CHANGE_RENEWAL_PREF now reach server state. routeNotification gained a THIRD kind of verdict, record_only, distinct from both an entitlement action and 'ignore'. THAT DISTINCTION IS THE WHOLE POINT: Apple owns price-increase consent natively, so ACTING on these would be wrong — if the customer refuses, Apple lapses the subscription and we hear EXPIRED. But ignoring them meant that later EXPIRED was uninterpretable: indistinguishable from an ordinary cancellation, with no way to tell that a price change preceded it. Recording without acting is exactly the right posture, and it is the same 'known-ignored vs unexamined' distinction I built for the Stripe switch in US-2128 — the two surfaces had the identical defect. REUSED recordAppstoreEvent rather than hand-rolling the insert: it already namespaces stripe_event_id as appstore:<id> and swallows 23505, so an Apple retry cannot double-record. (My first attempt DID hand-roll it — the helper was 180 lines above and I had not looked. Worth noting because writing the second copy is always easier than finding the first.) 4 tests, including the two that matter: record_only must NOT be an entitlement action (not sub_active, not sub_expired, not revoke), and an unknown type must STILL fail closed to ignore — widening a router is exactly when a permissive default sneaks in. REMAINING, and correctly split: AC1 (notify subscribers in advance of an increase) needs the COPY, which is US-2114's gate — but note the DETECTION half is now free: US-2117's migration 00486 added pricing_plan_revisions, an append-only price history written BY TRIGGER, so 'a price changed' is already a queryable fact rather than something needing new plumbing. AC3 is explicitly a decision ('decide and document whether a price increase requires fresh affirmative consent on the web') and belongs to counsel. AC4 is a CONSTRAINT rather than work — do not ship a price change until AC1/AC3 exist — and is worth keeping visible: the pricing_plans trigger will now record any change, so an accidental one leaves evidence. Google Play PRICE_CHANGE_CONFIRMED is still a no-op (rtdn.ts) and is the same shape as the Apple fix if someone wants symmetry. Verified: edge 4310 passed, deno check + lint clean. | 2026-07-19 (cont.) AC2 EXTENDED TO GOOGLE PLAY — the symmetry I flagged last pass, and it turned out to be the SHARPER of the two platforms. Apple's PRICE_INCREASE is a notification that a price WILL change; Google's PRICE_CHANGE_CONFIRMED is the user ACCEPTING one. That makes it a consent artifact — exactly what subscription_agreements (US-2117) exists to hold — and dropping it meant the only server-side evidence of the acceptance was the eventual renewal amount, which is an INFERENCE rather than a record. classifyRtdn now returns record_only for type 8, and the reconciler writes an audit row via the existing recordEvent dep (idempotent on the event id) while touching no entitlement: Google owns the consent UI, so acting would pre-empt it, and the next renewal RTDN settles the amount. ADDED A DISTINCT OUTCOME VALUE rather than reusing 'ignored': both leave entitlement untouched, but one wrote an audit row and the other did not. Collapsing them would leave the RTDN log unable to answer 'did we ever learn the user accepted a price change?' — which is the entire point of the branch. TWO THINGS THE TYPE SYSTEM AND AN EXISTING TEST CAUGHT, both of them the system working: (1) adding the union variant broke the route glue's narrowing at `action.productType`, which is TypeScript correctly refusing to let a new action fall through unhandled; (2) an existing test asserted type 8 → ignore and went RED, correctly — it was encoding the old behaviour, and it was right to fail rather than let the change pass silently. Updated it to state WHY 8 left that group, so the next reader sees the reasoning rather than an unexplained gap in [9,10,11]. PROCESS NOTE: this took four attempts because bash ate template literals and regex escapes in inline node -e scripts (the fifth such incident today). Anything containing backticks or regex now goes through the Edit tool, not a shell string. Verified: edge 4312 passed, deno check + lint clean.

userStories.title: Two divergent cancellation paths — the stale portal route bypasses the reviewed flow
userStories.description: The primary cancellation flow is good and should be preserved: self-serve, ~4 clicks / 2 screens, no email or phone required, period-end timing stated on every screen (cancel-subscription-dialog.tsx:106,178,219), a required acknowledgement checkbox, clearly-labelled escape buttons, and an 'Undo cancel' banner afterwards (billing.tsx:373-395). It has one retention interstitial with two off-ramps ('Pause instead' / 'Switch to cheaper plan'), which is defensible but is the part most worth a second look. The defect is a SECOND path: selecting the Free tile in the plan picker routes to the Stripe billing portal instead (flipdesk-plan-picker-dialog.tsx:393-406), with a stale comment 'until US-216's cancel flow ships' — US-216 has shipped. That path bypasses the reviewed dialog and shows different, portal-native copy.
acceptanceCriteria: Route the Free-tile selection through the reviewed cancellation dialog; remove the stale portal path and its comment.
Audit for any other route to cancellation and ensure all converge on one reviewed flow.
Have the review gate assess the retention interstitial against 'simple mechanism' expectations — in particular whether two deflection off-ramps before the confirm step is defensible.
Confirm cancellation is available in the same medium as signup for every purchase path (web-purchased cancels on web; IAP correctly defers to the platform via .manageSubscriptionsSheet).
userStories.notes: [P2][Compliance/Web] Found 2026-07-18 by the subscription-compliance deep-dive audit. LEGAL CONTEXT (verified 2026-07-18, not legal advice): the FTC's 2024 'Click-to-Cancel' Negative Option Rule was VACATED by the Eighth Circuit on 2025-07-08 and is not in force. The FTC restarted rulemaking with an ANPRM on 2026-03-11 (comments closed 2026-04-13), so a successor rule is in flux. The binding obligations today are (a) ROSCA 15 U.S.C. 8403 and FTC Act Section 5, both actively enforced, and (b) STATE automatic-renewal laws — most importantly California's ARL as amended by AB 2863, effective 2025-07-01, which is stricter than what we do today and expressly covers free trials. Design to the California standard: it is the binding one, and it closely tracks the vacated federal rule, so building to it also front-runs the successor. Every story in this batch needs counsel sign-off before copy ships (see the review-gate story). California AB 2863 requires cancellation through the same medium used for the original transaction. Web is fine; the divergent path is the risk, not the flow itself. | 2026-07-19 AC1 + AC2 DONE (no counsel needed — this half is a code defect, not copy). AC1: selecting the Free tile in the plan picker now routes to the REVIEWED cancellation dialog instead of opening the Stripe billing portal. The portal path skipped everything the reviewed flow was designed for: the period-end statement on every screen, the required acknowledgement checkbox, the reason capture, and the undo banner. A divergent second route is how an audited flow stops being the one users actually hit. THE DESIGN POINT: it is a CALLBACK (onRequestCancel), not a self-rendered dialog, because CancelSubscriptionDialog ALREADY opens this picker as its 'switch to a cheaper plan' off-ramp — rendering the cancel dialog inside the picker would have made the two mutually recursive. The parent owns the flow; the picker only reports intent. When the prop is omitted (i.e. the picker was opened FROM the cancel dialog) the Free tile simply closes the picker, returning the user to the cancel flow they are already in rather than stacking a second copy of it. AC2 AUDITED: after the fix, every remaining portal.mutate() call site is legitimate and NOT cancellation — the plan picker's own non-cancel branch (same-tier interval change) and past-due-banner's 'update payment method'. Using the portal is fine; routing a CANCELLATION through it is not, because cancellation is the flow carrying the review requirements. 4 guard tests pin that distinction explicitly, including one asserting past-due-banner may keep its portal call, so a future reader does not 'fix' it by mistake. The strongest assertion is ordering: the isCancelToFree branch must come BEFORE portal.mutate() AND must return — a guard that merely EXISTS while falling through would leave the bug intact while looking fixed. NEGATIVE-VERIFIED by deleting the guard: that test goes red. STILL OPEN: AC3 (have the review gate assess whether TWO deflection off-ramps before the confirm step is defensible under 'simple mechanism' expectations) is explicitly a US-2114 counsel-review item, not an engineering call — the story itself routes it there. AC4 (cancellation available in the same medium as signup) is stated in the story as already satisfied — web-purchased cancels on web, IAP correctly defers to the platform via .manageSubscriptionsSheet — and I did not re-derive it. Verified: tsc clean, lint 0 errors, web 2293 passed. | 2026-08-03 AC4 VERIFIED — and it was NOT satisfied. No migration. The note said AC4 was 'stated in the story as already satisfied', i.e. taken on the audit's word and never checked. Checking it found a real defect on the server. THE WEB AND iOS HALVES DID HOLD: src/pages/billing.tsx computes isAppstoreManaged and hides every Stripe subscription CTA behind it, showing 'Manage this plan in the GradeThread iOS app' instead; iOS presents .manageSubscriptionsSheet in PaywallView and PlanSection and never calls the web cancel endpoint. THE SERVER HALF DID NOT. appstoreSubscriptionBlocksStripe guarded the SUBSCRIBE and CHANGE-PLAN endpoints and not CANCEL. An App Store subscriber has no flipdesk_subscription_id, so POST /flipdesk/cancel fell straight through to 'No subscription to cancel' — a 400 telling a paying customer they have nothing while Apple carried on billing them monthly. Someone who believes that message reasonably concludes they are not subscribed, and the next thing they hear is a renewal receipt. That is worse than an error: it is a confident wrong answer on a billing question. HIDING A BUTTON IS NOT ENFORCEMENT, which is why the UI half passing did not make AC4 true. The endpoint is reachable from any client holding a token, and the iOS app talks to the same API. FIXED: cancel now returns the same 409 + `action` contract the purchase paths already use (manage_in_app / manage_in_play), which the clients already branch on. Apple and Google both REQUIRE cancellation on-platform, so the honest answer is not an error at all — it is where to go. ORDERING IS THE DEFECT, NOT PRESENCE, and the guard says so: both checks can exist and the wrong one still win, because an in-app subscriber has no Stripe subscription id. A case pins that the medium check runs BEFORE the no-subscription check. 6 new cases in cancel-medium-parity_test.ts: the precedence helpers still recognise active/trialing/past_due on both stores AND still return false for Stripe (or web cancellation breaks for the people it is for), the cancel route refuses and names where to go, the ordering, the purchase paths keep their own guards (cancel and purchase have to agree about who is in-app managed — this story is about them drifting apart once), the billing page still hides the CTAs, and iOS still defers to the platform sheet without calling the web endpoint. ⚠ MY OWN GUARD MATCHED ITS OWN COMMENT, fourth time this session: the ordering case searched for the string 'No subscription to cancel', which the comment above the fix QUOTES to explain the bug — and that comment sits before the guard, so the scan reported the ordering as still broken. Comments are stripped now. NEGATIVE-VERIFIED FIVE WAYS: the cancel guard removed, the guard moved after the no-subscription check, the refusal losing its action, a trialing in-app subscriber no longer recognised, and the billing page showing Stripe CTAs. Each reddened. (One mutation initially reported a false pass because .replace hit the SUBSCRIBE handler's occurrence first — re-run scoped to the cancel handler, where it reddens correctly.) REMAINING: AC3 only — whether TWO deflection off-ramps before the confirm step is defensible under 'simple mechanism' expectations. That is explicitly a US-2114 counsel item, not an engineering call. VERIFIED: full edge suite 5400 passed / 0 failed, deno check + lint clean across 1345 files.

userStories.title: Refund policy contradicts the vault: an undisclosed 14-day money-back guarantee
userStories.description: vault/50-business/pricing.md:204-205 states 'Subscriptions: 14-day money-back guarantee on the first subscription invoice only.' No such guarantee appears on either public legal page — src/pages/legal/terms.tsx:80-82 and src/pages/legal/refund.tsx:45-47 both state subscription fees are non-refundable once a billing period has begun. Either the vault is stale, or we are operating a guarantee we do not disclose (or declining one we promised internally). Support and billing decisions are presumably being made against one of these.
acceptanceCriteria: Determine which is authoritative and reconcile — update the vault note or the public policy, in the same commit per the vault same-commit rule.
If the guarantee is real, disclose it at the point of sale, where it is also a conversion asset.
Review the ToS/refund pages alongside the new disclosure copy so the point-of-sale statements and the legal pages agree.
Check the EU/UK right-of-withdrawal waiver (refund.tsx section 4) and chargeback clause (section 5) with counsel while the pages are open.
userStories.notes: [P2][Compliance/Legal-docs] Found 2026-07-18 by the subscription-compliance deep-dive audit. LEGAL CONTEXT (verified 2026-07-18, not legal advice): the FTC's 2024 'Click-to-Cancel' Negative Option Rule was VACATED by the Eighth Circuit on 2025-07-08 and is not in force. The FTC restarted rulemaking with an ANPRM on 2026-03-11 (comments closed 2026-04-13), so a successor rule is in flux. The binding obligations today are (a) ROSCA 15 U.S.C. 8403 and FTC Act Section 5, both actively enforced, and (b) STATE automatic-renewal laws — most importantly California's ARL as amended by AB 2863, effective 2025-07-01, which is stricter than what we do today and expressly covers free trials. Design to the California standard: it is the binding one, and it closely tracks the vacated federal rule, so building to it also front-runs the successor. Every story in this batch needs counsel sign-off before copy ships (see the review-gate story). Cheap to resolve and it removes an internal/external inconsistency that would look bad in any enforcement or dispute context. | PARTIAL 2026-08-02 — AC1 RESOLVED by the owner; AC2 does not apply; AC3/AC4 still need counsel. AC1: the vault was wrong and the public pages are authoritative. I put the evidence to the owner rather than guessing, and they chose delete-the-claim. THE EVIDENCE, gathered before asking so the question was cheap: no 14-day money-back guarantee exists anywhere in the codebase — not in constants, not in the Stripe setup, not in the webhook handlers. Refunds are MANUAL admin actions through admin-billing.ts with an MFA step-up. Both public pages say the opposite of the vault (refund.tsx section 3 and terms.tsx: subscription fees non-refundable once a billing period has begun, except where required by law or expressly granted in writing). What DOES exist is a 14-day free TRIAL, which is real, advertised on the landing page and in the plan picker, and is a completely different thing. Two features sharing a number is the most likely origin of a policy nobody agreed to. WHY THIS MATTERED IN A DIRECTION, and it is the part worth keeping: an internal note promising a refund the public pages deny is a promise support might honour case by case. That produces an UNDISCLOSED policy applied inconsistently, which is worse than either answer on its own — worse than not offering it, and worse than offering it openly. AC2 does not apply: there is no guarantee to disclose at the point of sale. The vault section is rewritten to state the three real rules (subscriptions non-refundable, credit packs non-refundable once a grade is generated but credits never expire, billing errors refunded within 60 days), each pointing at the page or constant that owns it, with a callout recording what the claim was and why it was wrong. refund.tsx and terms.tsx are added to the note's code_refs so a change to either now drifts the note. A SECOND CONTRADICTION FOUND AND DELIBERATELY NOT FIXED: terms.tsx says "Unused grading credits DO NOT ROLL OVER and are not refundable". That conflates two different things. Purchased credit packs never expire — constants.ts:384, migration 00037 and 00415 all say so explicitly. The MONTHLY PLAN ALLOWANCE (users.grades_used_this_month) does reset each cycle and genuinely does not roll over. The word "credits" is used for both, so the sentence is true of one and false of the other. It UNDERSTATES what a paying customer gets, so it costs conversion rather than creating legal exposure — but it is still a false statement in the Terms. I did not edit it: AC4 puts these pages under counsel review, and rewriting Terms copy ahead of that trades one unreviewed statement for another. Recorded in the vault note under its own heading so it is not lost, and carried on this story. NOTE ON MY OWN FIRST READING: I initially thought refund.tsx contradicted the vault on credit expiry too. It does not — "credits do not expire INTO A CASH BALANCE" is about cash redemption, and I had read a truncated line. Checked the full sentence before acting. STILL OPEN: AC3 (reconcile the point-of-sale copy with the legal pages — nothing to reconcile now that there is no guarantee, but the credits sentence above is in scope) and AC4 (the EU/UK right-of-withdrawal waiver in refund.tsx section 4 and the chargeback clause in section 5, both needing counsel).

userStories.title: Generalize the iOS tag-quality gate to web and to every macro slot
userStories.description: iOS already has the right pattern: TagPhotoQuality.swift:24-47 enforces a 700px floor plus on-device OCR requiring at least 4 characters before accepting a tag photo. Web has no tag-quality gate at all, and neither platform applies a quality gate to any other macro slot. A blurry or too-distant macro shot currently reaches the model looking exactly like a good one.
acceptanceCriteria: Port the tag-quality gate to web.
Apply a quality gate to every authenticity macro slot, with per-slot thresholds.
Reject or warn in-capture with actionable guidance ('move closer', 'hold steady') rather than failing silently after upload.
Feed the measured quality into authenticity confidence rather than treating accepted/rejected as binary.
userStories.notes: [P2][Authenticity/Capture][EPIC: Visual Authenticity] Found 2026-07-19 by the authenticity deep-dive audit. STRATEGY CONTEXT: Certilogo was the starting reference, but its model does not transfer — it verifies a brand-issued CLG code / QR on a security label sewn in at manufacture (its AI image recognition authenticates the TAG and detects cloned codes, not the garment's construction). GradeThread inspects garments it never manufactured, with no token. The transferable play is visual authentication of the garment itself, anchored on evidence we can actually capture. Note the scaffolding is ~80% built (ai-authenticity.ts is live in production) while the evidence base is ~5% — this epic closes that gap in order: contain what is already live, then raise evidence quality, then productize the claim. The pattern exists and is proven on iOS — this is generalization, not invention. | 2026-07-31 AC1+AC2+AC3 DONE; AC4 recorded as deferred, not half-built. New src/lib/macro-photo-quality.ts is the web port: per-slot long-edge floors + a sharpness floor, pure assessment separated from the browser measurement so the logic is testable without a canvas. THE ONE THING NOT PORTED, deliberately: the iOS on-device OCR check. The browser has no built-in recognizer and bundling Tesseract's ~2MB wasm on every page load to replicate a check whose PURPOSE is 'is there enough detail here to read' is the wrong trade -- normalized Laplacian variance answers that directly instead of by proxy, costs a few hundred bytes, and catches what OCR was standing in for (blur, shake, glare, too far). AC2 is real per-slot thresholds, not one number renamed: 700px keeps the iOS tag baseline; serial/marking get 900 because a struck code is physically smaller than tag print and resolves less at the same pixel count; surface/corner/sole get 800. Full-garment slots are deliberately EXCLUDED -- photo-standards.ts already governs those at eBay's 500px floor, and the two gates answer different questions ('will eBay accept it' vs 'can the model read it'). WIRED INTO BOTH CAPTURE SURFACES, which mattered more than it looks: the submission flow only has tag/label/detail slots, so wiring it alone would have left the authenticity slots (serial, marking, surface, corner, sole) ungated -- those live in the FlipDesk photo-uploader. Submission renders an amber per-slot line; the uploader raises a warning toast post-upload. Both assess the COMPRESSED bytes rather than the camera original, because compressImage caps at 2400/1600px and the model only ever sees what was stored. LENIENT IN BOTH DIRECTIONS, matching iOS: warns and offers a retake, never blocks, and every uncertain input (unknown dimension, decode failure, NaN) fails OPEN -- a gate that blocks on its own inability to measure blames the seller for our bug, and a false 'retake this' is exactly what trains sellers to ignore the nudge. 27 tests asserting BOTH halves (fires on bad, silent on good, passes exactly AT the floor), plus the metric's own property -- zero on a flat image, large on a hard-edged one, and strictly lower on a blurred copy of the same image, which is what matters rather than any absolute number. AC4 DEFERRED WITH THE GROUNDWORK IN PLACE: the assessment already carries a continuous 0..1 `score` on both pass and fail precisely so authenticity confidence can read a measure instead of a pass/fail bit, but delivering it to the grading pass means persisting it per photo -- a schema change, and the held-migration rule means a migration commit cannot be pushed without the operator applying the SQL first. Verified: tsc -b clean, lint 0 errors, 2898 tests pass, build green.

userStories.title: Guided macro capture — framing, distance and lighting for authenticity shots
userStories.description: There is no guided capture for authenticity evidence: no framing overlay, no distance guide, no lighting instruction. iOS uses .builtInWideAngleCamera with no zoom or focus tuning (CameraSession.swift:238), so macro shots depend entirely on the seller's instinct. Authentication tells are only legible at consistent framing and lighting, and inconsistent capture is itself a source of false positives.
acceptanceCriteria: Add per-slot capture guidance: what to photograph, how close, and how to light it, with a framing overlay.
Investigate closer-focus camera configuration on iOS for macro slots.
Provide worked examples of a good vs unusable macro shot for each slot type.
Measure whether guidance actually improves delivered pixel density and gate the rollout on that.
userStories.notes: [P2][Authenticity/Capture][EPIC: Visual Authenticity] Found 2026-07-19 by the authenticity deep-dive audit. STRATEGY CONTEXT: Certilogo was the starting reference, but its model does not transfer — it verifies a brand-issued CLG code / QR on a security label sewn in at manufacture (its AI image recognition authenticates the TAG and detects cloned codes, not the garment's construction). GradeThread inspects garments it never manufactured, with no token. The transferable play is visual authentication of the garment itself, anchored on evidence we can actually capture. Note the scaffolding is ~80% built (ai-authenticity.ts is live in production) while the evidence base is ~5% — this epic closes that gap in order: contain what is already live, then raise evidence quality, then productize the claim. Depends on the macro slots existing first. | 2026-07-31 AC1 DONE (web). New src/lib/macro-capture-guidance.ts: a distance line, a lighting line and a framing tightness per macro slot. The existing photo-profiles hints said WHAT to shoot and nothing about distance or light, which is where macro shots actually fail. LIGHTING ADVICE IS SLOT-SPECIFIC ON PURPOSE, and this is the substantive part: the failure modes are OPPOSITE. A struck serial is visible only by its shadow and needs single-side low-angle light; a glossy care label needs even indirect light or the print blows out. One reusable 'use good light' sentence would have been easier and would not have changed a single photo -- a test asserts the lighting lines are not all identical, because boilerplate would pass every other assertion in the file. Surfaced on BOTH web capture surfaces: the camera dialog gets a dashed framing box over the live preview plus the two lines beneath it (new optional photoType prop), and the FlipDesk uploader -- where the authenticity slots live and there is no camera dialog -- composes them into its per-slot tooltip rather than inventing a new affordance. THE OVERLAY IS SIZED TO BE SATISFIABLE, which is the reviewable judgement: a guide box you can fill and still be told 'move closer' is worse than no box, so the fill fractions are chosen against the US-2136 floors at the US-2135 caps, and a test walks every slot asserting that filling the box delivers more pixels than that slot's own floor -- so raising a floor without revisiting the overlay fails in CI rather than in a seller's hands. The box is decorative only; the capture is still the full frame, so it constrains composition and never the saved pixels. THE COVERAGE TEST IS WHY THIS PAIRS WITH US-2136: every slot the quality gate can reject now has guidance for getting it right, because a gate without guidance is just blame. STILL OPEN: AC2 (closer-focus camera configuration) is iOS and cannot be built in this environment; AC3 (worked good-vs-unusable examples per slot) needs real example imagery, which is design work rather than code; AC4 (gate the rollout on measured pixel-density improvement) needs the per-photo measurement persisted first, which is US-2135 AC3 and blocked on a migration. Verified: tsc -b clean, lint 0 errors, 2912 tests pass, build green.

userStories.title: Per-brand tell depth is 3 brands and 7 tells, all unverified
userStories.description: CANONICAL_TELLS covers exactly three brands (louisvuitton, coach, gucci) with 7 tells total across categories date_code/stamp/hardware/serial/font — every one marked 'seed:brand-authentication-tells (unverified — review in admin)' at confidence 0.5-0.65, against a taxonomy of 11 categories that includes stitching, construction and material. The separate seeded brand_knowledge.authentication_tells rows are legacy {tell, detail} shape, coerced on read to category 'other' with NO redFlag field (brand-authenticity.ts:88-92), so they contribute almost nothing to the contradiction logic that drives the verdict. admin-brand-knowledge.ts is a working curation surface with validateTellsForWrite and is the right place to do this. EXTENDED 2026-07-19: the KB is also ONE-SIDED. Every field models what a GENUINE example looks like — authentication_tells, tag_eras, country_patterns, registered_numbers — and there is no counterfeit-pattern modelling at all: no known fake markers, no superfake characteristics, no record of a specific counterfeit production tell. authentication_tells is a single column marked 'informational' doing double duty for both directions. Combined with seeded content that says 'NEVER auto-authenticate', the KB currently argues against the product it feeds.
acceptanceCriteria: Migrate legacy {tell, detail} rows into the structured shape so they can carry a category and a redFlag and actually affect the verdict.
Expand verified tells to the brands with real submission volume; mark provenance and confidence per tell.
Establish a review workflow so a tell moves from unverified to verified deliberately, with a named source.
Gate: a brand with no verified tells should widen limitations and lower confidence rather than producing a confident verdict from generic reasoning.

Model counterfeit-side knowledge distinctly from genuine-side tells — a known fake marker is a different kind of fact from 'what a real one looks like', and collapsing them into one informational column is why neither drives the verdict.
Reconcile the seeded 'NEVER auto-authenticate' guidance with the shipped product posture (see US-2133) rather than leaving the KB and the product in contradiction.
userStories.notes: [P2][Authenticity/Signal][EPIC: Visual Authenticity] Found 2026-07-19 by the authenticity deep-dive audit. STRATEGY CONTEXT: Certilogo was the starting reference, but its model does not transfer — it verifies a brand-issued CLG code / QR on a security label sewn in at manufacture (its AI image recognition authenticates the TAG and detects cloned codes, not the garment's construction). GradeThread inspects garments it never manufactured, with no token. The transferable play is visual authentication of the garment itself, anchored on evidence we can actually capture. Expert-dependent. (2) Most of the 599 are not authentication tells — they are brand-identification, sizing and comping rules ('American Eagle runs LARGE', 'Anthropologie also SELLS other brands', 'PINK IS NOT VICTORIA'S SECRET — comp it separately'). So AC1 is a SEPARATION job first: split identification knowledge out of authentication_tells, then categorize only what actually authenticates. userStories.title: Legal ToS/privacy versions are hardcoded in both clients while the server derives them from the DB — and iOS has no re-acceptance gate
userStories.description: As GradeThread, we want consent records to name the version the user actually saw. The edge derives current legal versions DYNAMICALLY from DB rows (lib/legal-versions.ts:66, consumed at routes/legal.ts:73,105,162). Both clients HARDCODE them: ios/GradeThread/Auth/AuthStore.swift:19-20 (legalTosVersion / legalPrivacyVersion = '2026-04-01') and src/lib/constants.ts:1491-1494 (LEGAL_VERSIONS). The only sync mechanism is a code comment (AuthStore.swift:17-18, 'Keep IN SYNC with the web ... and the edge mirror') with no automated guard. Worse, iOS has NO re-acceptance gate at all: web has src/components/auth/legal-gate.tsx; iOS never calls /api/legal (0 matches).
acceptanceCriteria: Clients must READ the current version from the server rather than hardcoding it, or a build-time guard must fail when the constants disagree with the DB-backed source.
Implement a re-acceptance gate on iOS equivalent to legal-gate.tsx.
Add a test/guard covering the three-way agreement (edge DB, web constants, iOS constants) — a comment is not a mechanism.
userStories.notes: [P1][Compliance/Legal] Found 2026-07-18 by the cross-platform parity deep dive. The failure mode is silent and legally material: the moment an operator publishes a new ToS row via admin-legal.ts, web and iOS signups keep recording 2026-04-01 — users are attested to a version they were never shown, and iOS users are never re-prompted at all. That is a defensible-consent failure, and exactly what an enterprise or legal review looks for. | 2026-07-18 SCOPED DOWN + GUARD ADDED (agent loop). ⚠ THIS STORY OVERSTATED THE RISK and the correction matters more than the fix. It claims users are 'attested to a version they were never shown'. For the WEB that is not what happens: legal-gate.tsx does NOT trust the hardcoded constant — it asks /api/legal/status (its own comment says so at :29) — and /api/legal/accept stamps the SERVER's current versions (legal.ts:103-106), never a client-supplied value. So after a FORCING republish the system SELF-CORRECTS: the gate fires and an immutable legal_acceptances row is written with the real version. The genuine residual hole is narrower and does NOT self-correct: on a MINOR republish (requires_reacceptance:false) requiredSince deliberately does not advance, so the gate correctly stays quiet — while handle_new_user (00142:79) still records the CLIENT-SUPPLIED constant into users.tos_accepted_version. The new user was shown the live document (/terms serves current) but their record names an older version, and nothing later corrects it. Moderate, not the defensible-consent failure described. FIXED WHAT IS FIXABLE HERE: added src/lib/__tests__/legal-versions-lockstep.test.ts pinning the baseline across all THREE projects that hold it — web LEGAL_VERSIONS, edge FALLBACK_TOS/PRIVACY_VERSION, and iOS AuthStore.legalTosVersion/legalPrivacyVersion — plus a shape check so a placeholder value cannot silently disable the gate. NEGATIVE-VERIFIED from every direction: drifting the web constant fails 2 assertions, drifting the iOS constant fails 1. That iOS assertion is the valuable one — Swift cannot be compiled on a Windows checkout, so a source-level check is the ONLY cross-project verification available for it. STILL passing:false on the two real ACs: (1) the durable fix is for the server to stamp the version at signup rather than trusting client metadata — that is a migration to handle_new_user and I did not want to stack a third held one; (2) iOS still has NO re-acceptance gate at all (grep for api/legal across ios/ returns nothing), which remains the largest genuine gap in this story and needs a macOS session. [2026-07-19 AC3 DONE + AC1 GUARD HALF. AC2 NEEDS macOS — story stays open] AC3 was the whole point of the story (a comment is not a mechanism) and is now real: src/test/legal-version-parity.test.ts asserts the THREE-WAY agreement between the edge fallbacks (FALLBACK_TOS_VERSION / FALLBACK_PRIVACY_VERSION), web LEGAL_VERSIONS, and the iOS AuthStore.swift static lets, by parsing each source. Negative-verified by bumping the iOS constant to 2026-09-01 — the guard fails naming all three values. AC1: took the guard option the AC explicitly allows rather than making clients read /api/legal at runtime. A build-time comparison against the live DB is not possible (no DB at build), and the edge FALLBACK constants are the DB-backed sources checked-in form, so this pins what CAN be pinned. Making the clients dynamic remains the stronger fix and is still open. Also asserted the versions are ISO dates: the edge ORDERS versions to decide whether re-acceptance is required, so a free-form string would break that comparison silently. And the parse-succeeded guard is explicit, because comparing null to null would have passed vacuously — it caught a real bug immediately when a heredoc ate the backslashes in my regex and both parsers returned null. AC2 NOT DONE and deliberately not faked: iOS has no re-acceptance gate (never calls /api/legal) while web has legal-gate.tsx. I cannot build or test Swift on Windows, and writing a compliance gate blind is precisely the wrong place for that. A test asserts the gap STILL EXISTS so it flips the moment someone implements it, rather than the story looking complete because the parity guard is green. AuthStore.swift now documents the gap in place. Seventh prose-matching guard failure this session: my new Swift comment names /api/legal, which the absence assertion matched. Comments are stripped now. | 2026-07-19 ⚠ STALE HELD-MIGRATION CLAIM — do not act on it. The migration(s) this note calls HELD (00142) are all on origin/main, verified individually with git log origin/main against each file rather than inferred from the linter's summary. The standing rule makes this decisive: a commit containing a migration is NOT pushed until the operator has applied the SQL, so a migration present on origin/main was pushed, which means its hold was already released. PENDING_MIGRATIONS.md agrees — every entry through 00490 (the highest migration in the tree) is marked APPLIED and confirmed by the user, so nothing is genuinely pending. WHY THIS MATTERS ENOUGH TO CORRECT: a stale hold tells the next reader the branch is frozen when it is not, which either invites a pointless prod session or — worse — makes them hold back an unrelated push that was always safe. Correction APPENDED rather than edited into the original sentence, because these notes are append-only and the history of what was believed when is itself worth keeping.

userStories.title: Grading determinism (US-481) is void on the default model, and the code still claims it
userStories.description: ai-config.ts:157-179 documents that grading ALWAYS uses a low temperature, defaulting to 0 (fully greedy decoding), because a certified score backs a public 'standardized' value prop. But gradingSamplingParams() returns output_config.effort — not temperature — for effort-based models, and the default grading model (DEFAULTS.model = claude-sonnet-5) is effort-based. So getGradingTemperature() is never called on the shipping path, GRADING_MAX_TEMPERATURE and the whole clamping apparatus are dead code, and grading runs at the model's own non-greedy decoding. A regrade of the same photos can return a different score with no explanation.
acceptanceCriteria: DECIDE the product position: is a regrade of identical photos allowed to return a different score? That is a trust question, not an engineering one.
If determinism is still the promise: add a self-consistency check (grade twice, compare, flag divergence) or pin a decoding mode that guarantees it.

If it is NOT the promise: correct the ai-config.ts comment block, which currently asserts a property the code does not have, and disclose run-to-run variance wherever the 'standardized grade' claim is made.
Either way the comment must stop describing temperature clamping as though it governs grading.
userStories.notes: [P1][Grading/Trust] Found 2026-07-18 by the grading-engine deep dive. This is NOT a code bug — effort-based models do not accept temperature, so the US-1033 migration was a correct API fix. The defect is that it silently removed a DOCUMENTED GUARANTEE and nobody updated the guarantee. Code that claims a property it no longer has is the most dangerous state for a trust product, because everyone downstream reasons from the claim rather than the behaviour. I deliberately did not 'fix' it: the right answer is a product decision — restore determinism (costly, possibly not available on this model family) or stop promising it (cheap, but it changes what a certificate means). [2026-07-19 PARTIAL — AC3(a)+AC4 DONE, AC1/AC2/AC3(b) BLOCKED ON A PRODUCT DECISION] Verified the technical claim in full: getDefaultModel()=claude-sonnet-5 is effort-based, so gradingSamplingParams() returns output_config.effort and NO temperature; getGradingTemperature()/GRADING_MAX_TEMPERATURE are dead on the shipping path. userStories.notes: [P2][Content] Found 2026-07-18 by the SEO/marketing deep-dive audit. userStories.title: Reviewer tells never flow back into brand knowledge — the loop is half-built
userStories.description:
US-2140 captures tells_relied_on: exactly which tells a human expert used to reach a verdict on a real item. That is the highest-value authenticity data the system can generate, and nothing aggregates it. It flows into the golden set as a single eval case and stops there — it never reaches brand_knowledge.authentication_tells or CANONICAL_TELLS, which are what ground future assessments.

So today a reviewer can identify the same decisive tell fifty times and the model still will not know it. Closing this converts every human review into permanent, reusable brand knowledge instead of one test case.
acceptanceCriteria: Aggregate tells_relied_on per brand and surface candidates in the admin brand-knowledge curation surface (admin-brand-knowledge.ts already exists with validateTellsForWrite).
PROPOSE, never auto-promote: a tell entering the KB changes future verdicts, so it needs the same deliberate review a seeded tell gets. Frequency is evidence, not authority.
Carry provenance — which reviews supported the tell, and how often it was decisive vs merely noted.
Respect the vault's brand rules before writing anything: read vault/20-domain/brands/ (the decoder bar, the alias refusals, the negative findings) — several absences there are deliberate.

Migrate the legacy {tell, detail} rows into the structured shape as part of this, or aggregated tells will land in a field that contributes nothing to the verdict (brand-authenticity.ts:88-92 coerces them to category 'other' with no redFlag).
userStories.notes: [P2][Authenticity/Knowledge][EPIC: Visual Authenticity] Found 2026-07-19 reviewing the authenticity module for gaps after the epic's backend landed. Cheap and compounding — it wires two systems that already exist. Overlaps US-2139 (tell depth); do them together, since this is the mechanism that makes US-2139 self-sustaining rather than a one-off curation push. PARTIAL 2026-07-19: lib/tell-candidates.ts + GET /api/admin/grading/authenticity/tell-candidates. Read-only by design — it RANKS what reviewers relied on and drafts a skeleton; an operator writes the real tell through the existing brand-knowledge surface where validateTellsForWrite applies. Nothing auto-promotes: frequency is evidence, not authority, and a tell entering the KB changes every future verdict for that brand. Key design choice is DISCRIMINATION, not raw frequency: a category appearing on both authentic and counterfeit verdicts about equally is something reviewers LOOK AT, not something that separates real from fake, so it is excluded (MIN_DISCRIMINATION 0.7) — seeding it would add noise to every verdict. Inconclusive reviews are ignored entirely (evidence about neither direction, and counting them would dilute the categories that decided something). Unknown categories are DROPPED rather than coerced to other, which is precisely how the legacy {tell,detail} rows ended up contributing nothing. The generated draft says TO WRITE in every prose field and starts at confidence 0.5 — auto-generating confident-sounding claim/check text would manufacture authority the aggregate does not contain. Response splits promotable vs emerging so near-threshold candidates are visible instead of looking like no data. 4384 edge tests pass (+8). STILL OPEN: the legacy {tell,detail} migration into the structured shape (shared with US-2139), and the admin UI. BUGFIX 2026-07-19 (self-audit): brand_key was derived as brandKey(rawBrand) in three places I wrote, skipping alias resolution. The canonical path is brandKey(canonicalizeBrand(raw)) — as getEffectiveTellsForBrand does — so a seller writing "Levi Strauss" keyed as levistrauss while the KB row is levis, and "Blue Bell" (the pre-1986 parent mark that IS a Wrangler) keyed as bluebell. The two never join, and the failure is INVISIBLE: a lookup that finds nothing looks exactly like a brand we have no knowledge of. Consequences were real in all three: golden-set cases filed under keys nothing reads (so per-brand coverage, which is what blocks activation, read thinner than reality); tell candidates an operator would promote into a key nothing reads; and per-brand accuracy splitting one brand across its spellings, diluting exactly the per-brand regression it exists to detect. Fixed with a single exported brandKeyForRaw() in brand-normalize.ts (one derivation, not three copies), callers now DROP an unresolvable brand rather than bucketing it under "", and four regression tests pin the alias behaviour. FOLLOW-UP 2026-07-19 (self-audit): tells_relied_on was accepted as any string array on write while the aggregator DROPS anything that is not a known AuthTellCategory — so a reviewer could record free-text tells, see a 201, and have the signal silently vanish at aggregation. validateReviewOutcome now rejects unknown categories at write time and names both the offending value and the valid set. BUGFIX 2026-07-19 (self-audit): all three authenticity aggregate queries had unsafe caps. A limit with no ORDER BY is not a cap, it is an arbitrary sample — Postgres may return any 5000 rows, so recent-vs-baseline drift would be computed over a set that changes between calls. Worse, the tell-candidates query limited ONLY when a brand filter was supplied, leaving the LARGER unfiltered read unbounded. All three now order newest-first before limiting (so a capped read keeps the recent window intact — the part drift and clustering are actually about), share one AUTHENTICITY_AGGREGATE_CAP, and log when the cap bites. Same silent-truncation class as the certificate sitemap that quietly stopped at its first API page: a truncated aggregate reads as complete. UI 2026-07-19: /admin/authenticity console shipped (src/pages/admin/authenticity.tsx), route + nav registered. Gate status is the FIRST thing on the page rather than three clicks deep, because an ungated prompt is currently serving real users including a public endpoint. Accuracy NEVER renders a single number — the two error directions sit side by side and are labelled by WHO they harm (buyer got a fake we vouched for / seller had a genuine item flagged, which nobody reimburses), because a combined figure stays flat while a version trades one for the other. | SCOPED 2026-07-30, AC5 NOT ATTEMPTED — deliberately, because the obvious version of it is a regression. Measured the corpus: 179 legacy payload arrays holding 599 individual {tell,detail} entries across the 37 *_brand_knowledge.sql seeds; structured payloads = 0. Two findings that change what AC5 is. (1) A BULK CATEGORIZATION WOULD SILENTLY REMOVE A PAID DISCLOSURE. authenticity-coverage.ts:53 isActionableTell returns true when category !== 'other' OR redFlag is set, so assigning categories alone flips every one of those 179 packs from 'inert' to 'actionable' — which lifts coverageConfidenceCap from COVERAGE_CAP_INERT 0.75 to 1.0 and empties the limitations string the PURCHASED add-on owes its buyer (US-2219 shipped that cap precisely because these rows cannot move a verdict). Not one new verified fact would have been added. That is a user-visible regression on a paid product, dressed as a data migration. (2) MOST OF THE 599 ARE NOT AUTHENTICATION TELLS AT ALL — the column is doing double duty as general brand knowledge. Real examples from the seeds: 'American Eagle runs LARGE', 'Anthropologie also SELLS other brands', 'PINK IS NOT VICTORIA'S SECRET — comp it separately', 'AERIE IS AMERICAN EAGLE — and the tag does not say so'. All 599 are injected into the <<<KNOWN_AUTHENTICATION_TELLS>>> block (ai-authenticity.ts:409-422) under the instruction 'check the item against EACH and report a finding per tell', capped at MAX_TELLS 60 per brand — so sizing and comping rules both generate noise findings and can crowd out real tells. The reshape is therefore a SEPARATION problem first (identification vs authentication knowledge) and a categorization problem second; doing the second without the first is what makes it harmful. AC5 is the SAME work as US-2139 AC1, and authenticity-coverage.ts:20 already names US-2139 as its owner ('Re-shaping the legacy rows is US-2139's job'). Recommend deleting AC5 from this story as a duplicate and carrying it only on US-2139, where the counterfeit-side modelling (US-2139 AC5) that a real redFlag needs also lives. Already guarded, so nobody can do this silently: authenticity-coverage_test.ts:201 asserts structured payloads == 0 and tells the next author to update the floor rather than delete the test. AC1-AC4 remain shipped per the earlier PARTIAL/BUGFIX/UI segments. Nothing changed in code this pass.

userStories.title: The grading standard has qualitative criteria but no measurable tolerances
userStories.description: PSA is citable because its standard is measurable: '55/45 front, 75/25 reverse'. GradeThread's is 'noticeable pilling, light fading' — good rubric, not a citable spec. Confirmed: no tolerance or measurement language anywhere in grading-scale.ts or grade-standard.ts. Relatedly, /grading/methodology is the weakest page relative to its promise: no named base model, no eval numbers, and the confidence threshold is described only as 'below our threshold' — it is 0.75 and it is documented in CLAUDE.md.
acceptanceCriteria: Add measurable tolerances where the factor genuinely admits them (pilling density, fade delta-E, hole/tear dimensions in mm, seam separation length, stain area).
State the 0.75 human-review confidence threshold explicitly on /grading/methodology.
State what can be said about the model and evaluation without leaking prompt IP.

userStories.notes: [P2][GEO/Authority] Found 2026-07-18 by the SEO/marketing deep-dive audit. This is the explicit PSA-playbook gap in the strategy doc's own mapping table, and it is the difference between 'a rubric' and 'the standard'. Adds no new URLs. [2026-07-19 PARTIAL — AC2+AC4 DONE, AC1 SUBSTANTIALLY DONE, AC3+AC5 OPEN] KEY FINDING: the premise was half wrong. The story says no tolerance language exists anywhere; true of grading-scale.ts/grade-standard.ts, but defect-weighting.ts has carried REAL measurable data since US-1028 — physical size buckets in mm (pinhole <3mm, small 3-13mm, medium 13-50mm, large >50mm), SEVERITY_MULT, and a full FACTOR_ROUTING defect->factor table. We were not missing the measurable standard, we were failing to PUBLISH it. Nothing had to be invented. Done: AC2 the 0.75 review threshold is stated explicitly on /grading/methodology via a guarded constant (grading-threshold-parity.test.ts fails if it diverges from the edge fallback); AC4 tier data is now a real <table> with scope/caption, and three new spec tables render the mm tolerances, severity multipliers and flaw->factor routing. New src/lib/grading-standard.ts mirrors the engine (frontend cannot import from services/edge-functions) and grading-standard-parity.test.ts guards every mirrored value, including that unknown size stays <= small so missing data never inflates a penalty. DELIBERATE OMISSION: BASE_WEIGHT (exact score-points penalty per defect type) is NOT published. Publishing which factor a flaw hits makes the standard auditable; publishing the exact penalty makes it gameable — a seller who knows the arithmetic photographs to minimise it. A test asserts it stays out. Reversing that is a product call. STILL OPEN: AC1 residue — pilling density and fade delta-E have NO engine equivalent and were deliberately not invented; adding them means defining new measurement in the engine first. AC3 (name the base model + eval numbers without leaking prompt IP) is unstarted and overlaps the US-2035 determinism decision. AC5 requires grading-engine skill/vault coordination since this now publishes engine criteria. | 2026-07-19 AC5 DONE. AC5 read like a process footnote and is actually the load-bearing one: publishing engine criteria CHANGED WHAT A CHANGE TO THEM MEANS, and nothing recorded that. SIZE_BUCKETS, SEVERITY_MULT and FACTOR_ROUTING went public on /condition-grading, but defect-weighting.ts — the file someone actually opens to tune grading — said nothing about it, and neither did the vault. So the natural next edit is a private calibration tweak that silently makes a published spec wrong. Fixed at the point of edit AND in the contract: a header warning on defect-weighting.ts naming exactly which three tables are mirrored and why that matters (the page exists to be cited and lifted verbatim into LLM answers, so a stale mirror is a precise, checkable, WRONG claim — worse than the adjectives it replaced), plus a new 'Published criteria' section in vault/20-domain/grading-scale-and-weights.md with defect-weighting.ts and grading-standard.ts added to code_refs so the CI drift guard now watches them. THE NON-OBVIOUS FACT, and I VERIFIED IT RATHER THAN ASSUMING: the parity guard lives in the WEB project, so `deno test` alone does NOT catch an engine-side change. Proved it by moving SEVERITY_MULT.minor 0.5 -> 0.6 with the mirror untouched — the edge suite passed 18/18 completely happily while the web guard failed on 'severity multipliers match SEVERITY_MULT'. An engine developer running the obvious local suite would have shipped it. That is now called out in both the source warning and the note, with the instruction to run npm run verify. Also carried the BASE_WEIGHT omission into both places as a PRODUCT TRADE-OFF rather than an unfinished edge — auditable vs gameable — because 'the published standard is missing the penalties' reads like a completeness bug to anyone who has not seen the argument. STILL OPEN: AC1 residue (pilling density, fade delta-E have no engine equivalent; adding them means defining new measurement in the engine first, not writing prose) and AC3 (naming the base model + eval numbers), which remains blocked behind the US-2035 determinism product decision. Verified: 2472 web + 4437 edge tests pass, deno check + lint clean, vault:lint clean at 100 notes.

userStories.title: No product/pricing/UI A/B testing — PostHog flags are never read client-side
userStories.description: There is a sophisticated server-side flag engine with deterministic FNV-1a bucketing, rollout percentages and plan targeting (lib/feature-flags.ts:114-166), plus four experiment engines (lib/experiments-governor.ts:19) — but they cover email subject lines, drip timing and AI prompts only. PostHog is initialized yet only capture() is ever called (src/lib/analytics.ts:237-239); feature flags are never read, there is no client useFeatureFlag hook and no exposure event. So paywall copy, pricing presentation and onboarding cannot currently be tested. All the primitives exist — this is a connector, not a framework build.
acceptanceCriteria: Add a client useFeatureFlag hook backed by PostHog, with an exposure event so results are analyzable.
Respect the existing consent gating — no flag evaluation before consent.
Prove it with one real experiment on a conversion surface (paywall copy or pricing layout).
Document how server-side flags and client-side experiments relate, so the two systems do not drift.
userStories.notes: [P2][Growth/Experimentation] Found 2026-07-18 by the SEO/marketing deep-dive audit. Pairs with US-2101 (UTM capture) — together they make conversion work measurable rather than anecdotal. | 2026-07-19 AC1+AC2+AC4 DONE; AC3 (one real experiment) DELIBERATELY LEFT OPEN. The connector exists: src/lib/client-experiments.ts (logic, testable without React) + src/hooks/use-feature-flag.ts (subscription plumbing), returning {variant, ready}. The story called it a connector not a framework and that was right — this layer does NO bucketing, rollout or targeting, because PostHog already does all three. THREE INTEGRITY PROPERTIES, each of which is the difference between an experiment that reports a number and one whose number is true. (1) CONSENT IS STRUCTURAL, NOT CHECKED: flags are read off window.posthog, which analytics.ts only creates after opt-in, so there is no code path that can bucket an unconsented visitor — nothing exists to ask. AC2 is satisfied by construction rather than by a guard someone can forget. (2) NO MID-SESSION FLIPS: a resolved variant is LOCKED for the page session. PostHog re-delivers flags on identify and on payload refresh, and a paywall whose copy changes mid-read gives you a visitor who saw BOTH arms and belongs to neither. (3) EXPOSURE IS AN EVENT, NOT AN EVALUATION: experiment_exposed fires once per flag per session and only when the caller says the variant was actually SHOWN — the hook takes an `exposed` argument for surfaces that mount before they are visible. Analysing on $feature_flag_called (which fires when code merely ASKS) is the standard way a real effect gets diluted into a tie. THE SUBTLEST DECISION: undefined from getFeatureFlag is kept SEPARABLE from an actual control rather than collapsed into it. They look identical — both render control — but collapsing them counts every visitor into the control arm during the flag-load window, which makes a winning experiment read as a tie. That is why the return is {variant, ready} and not just a string. 13 tests. NEGATIVE-VERIFIED all three properties by simulating the careless edit: dropping the lock reddens 2, dropping the exposure resolution-guard reddens 1, collapsing undefined into control reddens 3; restoring returns to green. AC4 DONE as vault/40-growth/experimentation.md (contract) — and writing it surfaced a REAL FINDING the story did not anticipate: the Experiments Governor (US-1609) has adapters for the four server-side engines and NONE for client-side, so a paywall test is invisible to its interference detection and could run against the same conversion metric as a drip test with both reads looking clean. Recorded as a warning callout with the manual check to do meanwhile. Also noted: the consent category model has no vault note, which is a gap. AC3 NOT DONE ON PURPOSE: there is no web paywall component (paywall is iOS/Android), so the named surface is the pricing page, and choosing what to test there means authoring alternative pricing copy/layout — a product and design decision, not a code one. The mechanism is ready and wiring a chosen variant is now a small edit. Verified: 2462 web tests pass, tsc -b clean, vault:lint clean (3 drift warnings pre-existing from earlier commits today, not from this work).

userStories.notes: [2026-07-02 admin backend audit, findings #1–#3] NOT verifiable from this host (no prod DB/Coolify access) — agent loop must SKIP this story (treat like DEFERRED); it is tracked here so the ops work isn't lost. Companion code story: cron registry drift guard. | 2026-07-18 PROD DIAGNOSED (agent loop) — the story's 'NOT verifiable from this host' premise is WRONG in this environment: outbound HTTPS works and Coolify is reachable via the hub MCP tools. So prod was measured instead of assumed, and AC1/AC2 appear ALREADY DONE — the story's premise ('migrations 00339-00342 pushed but not applied') is roughly 130 migrations stale. THE ARGUMENT: the deployed edge is built from origin/main, whose EXPECTED_SCHEMA_VERSION is 00474 (00474_push_subscriptions is the highest migration on origin/main). In production a confirmed-behind comparison calls onFatal -> Deno.exit(1) AFTER the ~40s grace window (schema-version.ts:170-180) — the container refuses to start. https://functions.gradethread.com/health returns 200 with env:production, and authenticated- free public endpoints reading real tables all return live data (/api/grading/public/transparency returns real volume+quality figures; condition-index 200; the certificates endpoint 200). A running production edge therefore implies the DB is at 00474 or AHEAD, i.e. 00332-00474 are applied. Corroborating: the live cert page renders 'Certificate No. GT-7Y3BCAF', proving grade_reports.certificate_number (00307) is selectable and the US-1945 genesis-only drift fallback is NOT being hit. AC2's specific claim (AutoLister 00339, photo rotate 00333) is subsumed — both are far below 00474. ⚠ ONE RESIDUAL UNCERTAINTY, stated rather than hidden: the version read goes through the supabaseAdmin.rpc('latest_schema_migration') RPC, and a MISSING RPC returns null -> 'unknown' -> fail-open, which would also boot. I could not rule that out from outside (the RPC needs the anon key, which I could not locate in the deployed bundles). So the conclusion is 'applied, unless the version RPC itself is absent' — and the fix below makes that distinguishable for good. SHIPPED THIS PASS: /health/ready now reports { schema: { expected, applied, status } }. Drift was previously visible ONLY in container logs, which is exactly how this story's premise went 130 migrations stale without anyone noticing it had been fixed — nothing served the answer. Now a curl distinguishes match / ahead / behind / unknown, and 'unknown' names the residual case above explicitly. Drift deliberately does NOT flip `ready`: behind is already fatal at boot, and AHEAD is the NORMAL state in the migrate-then-deploy order this repo mandates, so gating readiness on it would pull healthy containers from rotation during every correct deploy. 5 new tests in health_test.ts (incl. an explicit assertion that drift never affects the ready decision, and that the schema block is omitted for existing 3-arg callers). Full edge suite 4099 passed / 0 failed. STILL GENUINELY OPEN (real ops, unchanged): AC3 SES/SMTP creds + drip preview + email-retry drain; AC4 Coolify Scheduled Tasks for the cron registry (cron_runs empty) — the hub MCP exposes health/logs/deploys but not scheduled-task management, so this stays a console action; AC5 one-off backfills; AC6 the migrate:prod pre-deploy gate. RECOMMEND: re-scope this story to AC3-AC6 and drop AC1/AC2, or verify AC1 in one command after the next deploy — curl https://functions.gradethread.com/health/ready and read .schema.applied. | 2026-07-18 LAUNCH_CHECKLIST ENV NAMES VERIFIED — clean, no action. Cross-checked every env-var-shaped token in LAUNCH_CHECKLIST.md (67 of them) against a 31 MB corpus of all repo source, config and .env.example files: ALL 67 are real names that something actually reads. The four that first looked orphaned (ACCESS_KEY_ID, SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, DEV_ID, VERIFICATION_TOKEN) are a slash-shorthand in the table — 'SES_AWS_REGION/ACCESS_KEY_ID/SECRET_ACCESS_KEY' and 'EBAY_APP_ID/CERT_ID/DEV_ID/VERIFICATION_TOKEN' — and the expanded forms all exist (SES_AWS_* in lib/email-transport.ts, EBAY_CERT_ID and EBAY_DEV_ID in lib/ebay-client.ts, EBAY_VERIFICATION_TOKEN in lib/ebay-notification-subscriptions.ts). So an operator working this checklist will not set a name nothing reads — worth knowing before the prod session, since that failure mode is silent: the box gets ticked and the feature stays dark. NO GUARD ADDED, deliberately. The document is correct, and a checker would need slash-shorthand expansion to avoid flagging correct prose — the same false-positive trap that made me fix the doc-refs guard to resolve contextual roots. Not worth a check that would need babysitting to stay honest about a file that is currently right. ⚠ METHOD NOTE, because the first two runs of this check were WRONG and both looked plausible: run 1 reported all 67 unreferenced — a shell-escaping artefact, where a heredoc collapsed the regex's double backslash so JS parsed it as a BACKSPACE character and nothing could ever match. It was only obviously false because ANTHROPIC_API_KEY being unread is impossible. Run 2 reported 4, which were the shorthand above. Only run 3 was true. Any script containing regex escapes should be written with the editor, not embedded in a shell heredoc.
