userStories.title: iOS: SyncEngine can prune the entire local database when the session lookup fails
userStories.description: ios/GradeThread/Persistence/SyncEngine.swift:367 does `let selfId = try? await ...auth.session.user.id`, swallowing the failure. At :430 that means the .eq('user_id', ...) filter is dropped, :438 treats the resulting zero rows as a complete result, and SyncMergeActor.reconcileDeletes:564 then prunes the entire local mirror. A transient session read failure wipes the user's offline data.
acceptanceCriteria: A failed session lookup aborts the sync rather than proceeding unfiltered.
reconcileDeletes refuses to prune when the fetch was not provably complete and scoped.
Test: a session-lookup failure leaves local data intact.
Check crash/analytics for users whose local item count dropped to zero.
userStories.notes: [P0][iOS/Sync] [Audit 2026-07-30 module/platform sweep] Reported by an audit agent; the cited line was not independently re-verified in this session — confirm before fixing. Data loss on the customer's device. Highest-severity mobile finding. | 2026-08-04 VERIFIED against the code, and the failure path is real — with one narrowing that changes who it hits. THE CHAIN HOLDS EXACTLY AS FILED: SyncEngine.swift:367 is 'let selfId = try? await SupabaseShared.client.auth.session.user.id.uuidString', which swallows a throw into nil; :368 is 'let ownerId = WorkspaceScope.activeOwnerId ?? selfId'; :386-388 pass that ownerId into fetchServerIds for inventory_items, sales and flipdesk_expenses; and fetchServerIds:430 applies the tenant filter only under 'if let scopeUserId'. Nil scope means the query runs UNFILTERED. If it then returns zero rows, :438's short-page rule ('a short page means we've read every surviving id') treats an EMPTY set as a COMPLETE set, and reconcileDeletes prunes the local mirror against it. THE NARROWING, and it is the reason this has not been reported by users at scale: BOTH sources have to be nil. A user inside a workspace has WorkspaceScope.activeOwnerId set, so the filter still applies and the bug cannot fire. It fires for a solo seller on their personal scope whose session read transiently fails — which is the ordinary configuration, so this is not exotic. WHAT IS ALREADY DEFENDED, worth knowing so the fix is not duplicated: fetchServerIds returns nil (skip pruning) on any thrown error and on hitting maxRowsPerPass with rows remaining; :398 bails when ALL five fetches failed; :404 re-checks the scope epoch so a workspace switch mid-scan cannot prune the new tenant; protectedIds and protectedItemIds shield queued creates and pending edits. Every one of those guards handles a DIFFERENT failure. None of them covers 'authenticated as nobody, legitimately got zero rows' — an empty non-nil set passes the :398 guard cleanly. SMALLEST CORRECT FIX is AC1: make an unresolvable owner id abort the reconcile, since an unscoped id-scan is never something this function wants. AC2 is the belt-and-braces version and is also worth having. | PARTIAL 2026-08-06 — AC1, AC2 and AC3 are DONE in code; AC4 is an operator read of crash/analytics and cannot be done from here. THE ROOT FIX (AC1), at ios/GradeThread/Persistence/SyncEngine.swift: reconcileDeletesIfDue() and pullRemote() both used to do 'let ownerId = WorkspaceScope.activeOwnerId ?? selfId' and carry on when BOTH were nil. Both now go through a new pure static SyncEngine.resolveScopeOwnerId(workspaceOwnerId:sessionUserId:) and ABORT when it returns nil — the reconcile returns before any id-scan (and before lastReconcileAt is stamped, so the throttle is not burned and the very next pass retries), the pull returns .failure(SyncScopeError.unresolvedTenantScope) so it surfaces on the existing banner / lastPullError path instead of looking like an empty account. THE RESOLVER'S CONTRACT IS THE INTERESTING PART and is why it is a named function rather than an inline '??': a nil sessionUserId abandons the pass EVEN WHEN A WORKSPACE IS SELECTED. The story's narrowing said the bug needs both sources nil, which is true of the crash chain, but the underlying condition is that the session read failing means the requests go out UNAUTHENTICATED — so a workspace id would scope a query that returns nothing anyway. Scoping an unauthenticated read is not safer than not scoping it. A BLANK id is also treated as absent, because .eq('user_id','') matches nothing and produces the same empty set by a different route. AC2 IS DONE TWICE, DELIBERATELY, at two different altitudes. (a) Type level: fetchServerIds(table:scopeUserId:String?) became fetchServerIds(table:scope:ReadScope) with cases .owner(String) and .parentRLS. One nil used to mean two unrelated things — 'listings/item_photos have no user_id column' and 'the owner id did not resolve' — and only one of those is safe. Now a caller holding no id has nothing valid to pass; the dangerous state is unrepresentable rather than merely guarded. (b) Destructive site: SyncMergeActor.reconcileDeletes gains a NON-OPTIONAL leading scopeOwnerId: String and refuses to prune (breadcrumb, no deletes) when it is blank. That repeats the check where the deletes actually happen, so any future caller inherits the floor. AC3: 4 new XCTest cases in ios/GradeThreadTests/SyncTests.swift. The load-bearing one is test_reconcileDeletes_unresolvedScopeLeavesEveryTableIntact — every id set EMPTY (i.e. 'the server has nothing') plus a blank scope must leave items, sales and listings all intact; its control test_reconcileDeletes_resolvedScopeStillPrunesOnEmptySets asserts the SAME empty sets DO prune under a resolved scope, so the guard is proven to reject the unscoped case specifically rather than to have disabled reconciliation. Plus two on the resolver: failed-session-with-workspace returns nil, and workspace-then-self precedence with blank-falls-through. The five pre-existing reconcileDeletes call sites in that file were updated for the new parameter. VERIFICATION LIMITS, stated plainly: Swift cannot be built or tested on this Linux host (no toolchain), so these changes are NOT compile-verified here — iOS CI on macOS runners is the gate. What WAS run locally: python3 ios/Scripts/no-ungated-print.py passes, and a grep for name collisions on ReadScope / SyncScopeError / nonBlank / resolveScopeOwnerId across all of ios/ found none. NOT CHANGED, and worth knowing: paginatedFetch keeps its scopeUserId: String? because the disputes fetch legitimately passes selfId and the pull path is not the destructive one; the pull guard above means ownerId is non-nil everywhere it is used. REMAINING: AC4 only — check crash/analytics for users whose local item count dropped to zero. That is an operator read of Sentry/PostHog, not a code change; the new breadcrumbs ('Sync reconcile aborted: tenant scope unresolved' and 'Sync reconcile refused: prune requested under an unresolved tenant scope') give it something to correlate against going forward.

userStories.title: iOS: PhotoUploadService is built without a modelContainer, so pending mutations are silently dropped
userStories.description: ios/GradeThread/Upload/AppDelegate.swift:21 constructs PhotoUploadService(store:) with no modelContainer:. PhotoUploadService.swift:781 enqueuePendingMutation opens with `guard let container = modelContainer else { return }`. Every mutation queued through that instance is discarded with no error.
acceptanceCriteria: AppDelegate passes the modelContainer.
The guard logs or throws rather than returning silently, so a future miswiring is loud.
Test asserting a queued mutation is persisted.
userStories.notes: [P1][iOS/Upload] [Audit 2026-07-30 module/platform sweep] Reported by an audit agent; the cited line was not independently re-verified in this session — confirm before fixing. | 2026-08-04 VERIFIED, and one detail in the story is understated: the container CANNOT be injected later. PhotoUploadService.swift:41 declares 'private let modelContainer: ModelContainer?' — a let, immutable after init — with ':109 modelContainer: ModelContainer? = nil' as a defaulted init parameter. AppDelegate.swift:21 is 'lazy var photoUploadService = PhotoUploadService(store: photoUploadStore)' and grep across all of ios/ finds no other assignment: the only other reference to the instance is AppDelegate:123 calling handleBackgroundEvents. So the app's one PhotoUploadService is permanently nil-container. A TRAP FOR WHOEVER FIXES IT: the AppDelegate comment three lines below says 'Initialized lazily so the ModelContainer the service uses can be injected after the App scene constructs it' — that sentence is attached to backgroundRefresh (a separate property), not to photoUploadService, and reading it as a promise about the upload service is how this stayed unnoticed. Making the container injectable means changing the let, or constructing the service later. THE BLAST RADIUS IS THREE GUARDS, not one — :740, :763 and :781 all 'guard let container = modelContainer else { return }' (the third returns []). So it is not only enqueuePendingMutation that no-ops; the read path at :763 returns an empty list too, which means a failed upload is neither queued nor visible. AC2 matters as much as AC1 here: three silent returns is how a wiring mistake survives. | PARTIAL 2026-08-06 — all three ACs are implemented; NOT compile-verified (no Swift toolchain on this Linux host), so iOS CI on the macOS runners is the gate. AC1 DONE, but NOT by 'AppDelegate passes the modelContainer' as written — the story's own note explains why that sentence has no implementation: the container lived on GradeThreadApp as a STORED property, and a stored property cannot be handed to another stored property (appDelegate) during init, which is precisely how photoUploadService ended up container-less. THE FIX INVERTS THE OWNERSHIP: ModelStoreProvider.load() now runs in AppDelegate (a stored 'let storeOutcome'), and GradeThreadApp reads it back through a COMPUTED 'private var storeOutcome { appDelegate.storeOutcome }' — computed properties can reference self, stored ones cannot, and that asymmetry is the whole trick. AppDelegate.photoUploadService is then 'PhotoUploadService(store: photoUploadStore, modelContainer: storeOutcome.container)'. load() is pure and touches nothing on UIApplication, so moving it from App-init to delegate-init changes the owner and not the behaviour; the didResetStore / isInMemoryFallback notice path in App.swift reads through the same computed property and is unchanged. Deliberately NOT the alternative: an attachModelContainer(_:) called from the root .task, mirroring BackgroundRefreshService. That would have worked but leaves the same class of bug alive — an unattached instance still compiles. AC2 DONE BY DELETION, which is stronger than what the AC asked for. The AC wanted the three guards to log instead of returning silently; instead 'private let modelContainer: ModelContainer?' became non-optional and the init parameter lost its '= nil' default, so all three 'guard let container = modelContainer else { return }' sites (deletePendingUploadMutation, pendingUploadFilenames, enqueuePendingMutation) are GONE and the miswiring is now a compile error. A loud runtime log still ships the bug; a required parameter cannot be forgotten. This is why AC2 'matters as much as AC1' — the note was right, and the compiler is the loudest available channel. AC3 DONE, two new XCTest cases in ios/GradeThreadTests/PhotoUploadTests.swift, covering BOTH directions of the container because the story's blast-radius note is the important part. (1) test_queuedUploadMutation_isPersistedInTheServicesOwnContainer — the write half: a failed link leaves a durable .uploadPhoto replay row in the container the service was CONSTRUCTED with. (2) test_staleTempSweep_keepsFileAQueuedUploadStillNeeds — the read half, which NO test covered and which is why a missing container was worse than 'the retry is lost': pendingUploadFilenames() returned [] behind its guard, so cleanupStaleTempFiles saw nothing referenced and would delete the staged JPEG the queued upload replays from, converting a recoverable failure into missingLocalFile. The test writes a referenced and an unreferenced staged JPEG of the same age and asserts the referenced one SURVIVES while the orphan is swept, so it fails in the exact way the old wiring did. Both use a unique sessionIdentifier so no test claims the production background session, and the sweep test cleans up its files in a defer. ALSO CHANGED: test_cancelAll_resetsStoreDeterministicallyAfterCancellation was the one construction site that omitted the container — the same omission the app made — and now passes makeContainer(); the makeTask helper takes an optional localFileURL because PhotoUploadTask.localFileURL is a 'let' and could not be mutated after construction. VERIFIED LOCALLY: python3 ios/Scripts/no-ungated-print.py passes; grep confirms PhotoUploadService has exactly two construction sites in the whole repo (AppDelegate + the tests), so no ShareExtension or widget caller was left behind by the signature change.

userStories.title: Android: expense dates walk back one day on every edit-sync cycle
userStories.description: android/app/src/main/java/com/gradethread/app/money/ExpenseRepository.kt:128 sends ExpenseDraft.isoDate(entity.spentOn), which re-derives YYYY-MM-DD from a UTC-midnight epoch using ZoneId.systemDefault() (ExpenseDraft.kt:72). userStories.notes: [P1][Android/Money] [Audit 2026-07-30 module/platform sweep] Reported by an audit agent; the cited line was not independently re-verified in this session — confirm before fixing. Already solved on iOS — port, do not redesign. | 2026-08-04 VERIFIED, including the part that makes it embarrassing: the bug is DESCRIBED IN ITS OWN DOC COMMENT and was still shipped. ExpenseDraft.kt:69-71 says outright that re-deriving 'moves an evening expense to the next day east of Greenwich and to the previous day west of it', and :72-73 is exactly that — 'fun isoDate(epochMs: Long, zone: ZoneId = ZoneId.systemDefault()) = Instant.ofEpochMilli(epochMs).atZone(zone).toLocalDate().toString()'. ExpenseRepository.kt:129 calls it inside wireBody. CONFIRMED IT COVERS EDITS, which is the whole premise: wireBody has ONE caller, line 61, on a path that computes 'val id = draft.id ?: UUID.randomUUID()...' with the comment 'An edit keeps its id so the upsert replaces rather than duplicates' and then does client.from(TABLE).upsert(body). One code path for insert and edit, so every re-save re-derives, and the drift compounds per edit rather than settling. So AC3's 'across several edit cycles' is the right test shape. NOTE FOR AC2: iOS solved this at ExpenseStore.swift:34-43 — port that, and check whether the Android ExpenseEntity should carry the calendar date as a string rather than an epoch at all, since as long as the local column is epoch-millis the conversion has to happen somewhere and can be got wrong again.

userStories.title: Android: the local database is reopened per call site and deleted on any open failure
userStories.description: android/.../sync/db/GradeThreadDb.kt:77 — DatabaseProvider.open is not memoized, and line 88 runs context.deleteDatabase(dbName) on any step-1 failure. Four call sites open it: UploadWorker.kt:74, UploadWorker.kt:125, capture/CaptureScreen.kt:76, plus the Hilt singleton. A transient open failure destroys the user's offline data.
acceptanceCriteria: One memoized instance, injected, not opened per call site.
deleteDatabase is reserved for a genuine, identified corruption case and is not the catch-all for any open failure.
Test: a simulated transient open failure does not delete the database.
userStories.notes: [P1][Android/Sync] [Audit 2026-07-30 module/platform sweep] Reported by an audit agent; the cited line was not independently re-verified in this session — confirm before fixing. Same class as the iOS SyncEngine finding — silent local data loss. | 2026-08-04 VERIFIED — both ACs hold, but the story's summary is harsher than the code and the correction matters for scoping. THERE IS A RECOVERY LADDER, not a blind delete. DatabaseProvider.open runs three steps: (1) build + force 'db.openHelper.readableDatabase' to make Room's deferred open happen NOW, outcome NORMAL; (2) on ANY step-1 failure, context.deleteDatabase(dbName) + rebuild, outcome RESET; (3) on failure of that, an in-memory database, outcome EPHEMERAL, so it never crashes on data. There is also an outcomeFlow StateFlow feeding a user-facing 'local data was reset' banner. So the user is at least TOLD. THE DEFECT IS STILL REAL and is precisely AC2: step 2 is reached by any step-1 throw — a locked file, a transient I/O error, low storage, a migration hiccup — not only by genuine corruption, and runCatching discards the exception so nothing distinguishes them. AC1 ALSO HOLDS: open() is not memoized, and there are three non-Hilt call sites re-invoking it — CaptureScreen.kt:79 inside a remember, and UploadWorker.kt:74 and :125 — alongside the DatabaseModule.kt:34 Hilt singleton whose own comment (:22) says it is a singleton BECAUSE open runs the recovery. So the singleton's rationale is documented and then bypassed three times, and each bypass is an independent chance to hit the destructive branch. SUGGESTED SHAPE: inject the Hilt-provided instance at all three sites, and gate deleteDatabase on an identified corruption signal (SQLiteDatabaseCorruptException / SQLiteDatabaseLockedException distinction) rather than on Throwable.

userStories.notes: [P2][Android/Inventory] [Audit 2026-07-30 module/platform sweep] Reported by an audit agent; the cited line was not independently re-verified in this session — confirm before fixing. | 2026-08-04 VERIFIED, both halves. AC1/AC2: ItemCanvasViewModel.kt's save onSuccess block copies state with saving=false, original=_state.value.draft and savedAtLeastOnce=true — it never clears hasLocalChanges. The flag is set to true at :319 and the ONLY place it is cleared is sync/MutationReplayer.kt:131 (and :142 for sales), on the offline-queue replay path. userStories.title: Impersonation is unbounded, unmarked, non-revocable, and allows account deletion as the user
userStories.description: admin-impersonation.ts:43-132 gets the entry right: super_admin only (:44), users:role scope (:38), fresh step-up (:49), self and privileged targets refused (:54, :68-73), start audited (:116). Everything after the token is minted is open. No time limit — generateLink type magiclink (:90) yields a normal Supabase session for the target, access token plus long-lived refresh token, in the admin's browser, with no cap anywhere. No revocation on stop — src/lib/impersonation.ts:126-129 only redeems the resume token and never calls auth.admin.signOut(targetId), so a copied refresh token outlives the session. No marker — there is no impersonated_by claim and no server-side active-impersonation row, so every request made while impersonating is indistinguishable from the real user's. And destructive actions are fully available: POST /api/account/delete's only server-side control is the confirm string (account.ts:390); the password re-auth at :625-631 is client-side only. A super_admin can impersonate a disputing customer, cancel their subscription and delete their account, and every downstream record shows the customer did it.
acceptanceCriteria: A hard maximum impersonation duration, enforced server-side.
Stopping impersonation revokes the target's sessions.

The impersonated session carries a server-visible marker, and destructive routes (account delete, subscription cancel, marketplace disconnect, grading spend) refuse or require additional authorization while it is set.
The account-delete password re-auth moves server-side.
PRIVILEGED_ROLES (:40) is {admin, super_admin} so a reviewer can be impersonated — decide whether that is intended.
admin-impersonation.ts:137 writes target_id straight from the request body with no check against the start record, so the stop audit row is client-controlled. Fix.
Confirm the GoTrue OTP TTL in prod — it sets the real lifetime of the impersonation and resume tokens.
userStories.notes: [P0][Admin/Security] [Audit 2026-07-30 module/platform sweep] Reported by an audit agent; the cited line was not independently re-verified in this session — confirm before fixing. A target's own MFA does not protect them: a magiclink redemption yields an aal1 session. | PARTIAL 2026-08-03 — AC1-AC6 DONE. AC7 is an operator check on prod and stays open. EVERY CLAIM VERIFIED. The entry really is well guarded and the story says so; everything after the token was minted really was open. Confirmed line by line: no cap anywhere, /stop only redeemed the admin's resume token, no marker of any kind, and the stop audit row read target_id straight from the request body. AC1 DONE. NEW admin_impersonation_sessions (00521) plus lib/impersonation-session.ts. Cap is 30 minutes, ENFORCED ON READ rather than by a scheduled sweep — the window between a cap passing and a job noticing is exactly when a forgotten session is most dangerous. And a start that cannot be RECORDED does not happen: a failed insert returns 500 and mints nothing, because a session with no row is precisely the unbounded, unmarked, unrevocable one this story removes. AC2 DONE. /stop revokes the target's sessions through GoTrue's admin logout with scope global. supabase-js cannot do this — auth.admin.signOut wants a JWT, which is the one thing the server does not have — and 'global' is the only scope that reaches a refresh token already copied out of the browser. The result is RETURNED rather than swallowed: an un-revoked stop means the target's tokens are still live and the operator needs to know now. AC3 DONE. The marker is a database row, not a token claim, deliberately: a claim is equally invisible to any route that does not parse it and cannot be revoked once minted. isImpersonated FAILS CLOSED — a lookup error returns true, so a database blip refuses the destructive action. Being wrong that way costs a real user one retry; being wrong the other way is unrecoverable. Guarded by ENUMERATION at eight sites (account delete, buyer + flipdesk subscription cancel, billing portal, and all five marketplace disconnects) rather than by a blanket middleware, which would have to enumerate what is destructive anyway and would silently permit anything it did not know about — the same failure shape US-2354 removed from the scope guard. AC4 DONE. The delete password re-auth moves into the edge, against GoTrue's password grant, and fails CLOSED: an unreachable auth service means the password cannot be proved, and 'cannot prove' must not read as 'proved' on the one endpoint that permanently destroys an account. It deliberately does NOT use the service-role client, which would mint a session — a successful check must prove the password and produce nothing reusable. The browser's local check is REMOVED rather than kept alongside: two places deciding the same thing is how one drifts, and the browser's answer was never the one that mattered. OAuth accounts are exempt on both sides; demanding a password that does not exist is not a control. AC5 DECIDED: reviewer joins PRIVILEGED_ROLES. The set means 'roles whose account carries authority a super_admin should not be able to borrow', not 'roles above a line in the ladder'. A reviewer holds grading:review — they adjust issued grades, which are the product, and RLS grants them human_reviews through is_reviewer_or_admin(). Impersonating one produces a grade adjustment audited to the reviewer rather than to the admin who made it: the same non-repudiation loss the admin exclusion exists to prevent. AC6 DONE: the stop record comes from the START row. The old shape let an admin impersonate one person and log having stopped impersonating another, which is worse than no row because it reads as evidence. A stop with no live session is still audited, with no_active_session set — a double-click and a probe both look like that, and both are worth seeing. PROVEN ON A REAL DATABASE: corpus applied to a throwaway stack, then the target cannot SELECT the row, cannot UPDATE it to end their own impersonation record (0 rows), and the record survives deleting BOTH parties with the emails intact. That last one matters — the record of an impersonation is not the impersonator's to erase. TWO GUARDS CAUGHT MY NEW CODE, both correctly. rls-guard demanded the new table be classified in SERVICE_ROLE_ONLY (deny-all in both directions: a readable table leaks operator activity to the person being impersonated, a writable one lets them end the RECORD while the session continues). no-bare-fetch caught both new outbound calls having no deadline — the GoTrue logout runs while an admin waits on /stop, and the password check is the last thing between a request and a permanent deletion. Both go through fetchWithTimeout now. COLUMN NAMING, worth recording: actor_id / target_id rather than actor_user_id / target_user_id, because rls-guard discovers tenant tables by the literal string user_id and this is an operator table that must have no policy at all. Added to the service-role-tables note as a worked example — the existing rule covers ONE owner column and says to call it owner_user_id, which does not help when there are two. A MISTAKE THAT KEEPS RECURRING, so it is written down: my first AC4 assertion searched for the word signInWithPassword and fired on my own comment explaining what the old local check used to do. Second time this session a guard has accused its own prose. It matches a CALL now. NEW services/edge-functions/src/tests/impersonation-bounds_test.ts, 10 cases. NEGATIVE-VERIFIED THREE WAYS (stop reading the body again, isImpersonated failing open, the guard dropped from one marketplace route), each restored. Vault: NEW vault/20-domain/impersonation.md carries the contract. REMAINING: AC7 — confirm the GoTrue OTP TTL in prod. It sets the real lifetime of the minted impersonation and resume tokens, so it is a SECOND clock running alongside the 30-minute cap: the cap bounds what the server honours, the TTL bounds how long the link stays redeemable. Both should be known. VERIFIED: deno check clean, deno lint clean across 1317 files, edge suite 5206 passed / 0 failed, web 3225 passed / 0 failed, tsc -b clean, eslint 0 errors, build green through the 216-route prerender, vault-lint 135 notes clean. | 2026-08-03 FOLLOW-UP on AC5. The decision landed but its REFUSAL MESSAGE did not: adding reviewer to PRIVILEGED_ROLES left the 403 saying "Impersonating an admin or super-admin is not allowed", so a refused reviewer was told about a rule that was not the one applied. That is not cosmetic — the next operator reads a message that disagrees with the code, concludes the check is broken, and goes hunting a bug that is not there. The message now names all three roles and says WHY (their actions audit to them, not to you), and the new test asserts it against PRIVILEGED_ROLES itself rather than a fixed string, so the two cannot drift apart again. AND THE GUARD WAS SATISFIED BY ITS OWN PROSE — a new variant of the recurring trap. My first version checked the raw source slice, which includes the explanatory comment above the message, and that comment names every role: reverting to the stale message left the case GREEN, passing on prose about the very bug it was written to catch. Only the negative verification found it; the assertion read as correct. It strips comments now. Previous instances of this family accused their own prose; this one was SATISFIED by it, which is the more dangerous direction because nothing fails. AC7 remains and is an OPERATOR/CONFIG check, not a database one: the GoTrue OTP TTL is an env var on the self-hosted auth container (GOTRUE_MAILER_OTP_EXP), so it cannot be added to prod-diagnostics.sql. It matters because it is a SECOND clock — the 30-minute cap bounds what the server honours, the TTL bounds how long the minted link stays redeemable, and the longer of the two is the real exposure. VERIFIED: deno check clean, deno lint clean across 1338 files, full edge suite 5332 passed / 0 failed.

userStories.title: The admin scope drift-guard cannot catch an unguarded mutation, and one already shipped
userStories.description: admin-scope-coverage_test.ts:50 computes hasGuard as src.includes('requireScope('), so a single occurrence anywhere in the file satisfies mode 'mutations'. Router mode correctly asserts the use('*') shape (:81-83), but admin-users.ts, admin-bulk.ts, admin-scopes.ts and admin-guarantee-pool.ts are all mutations mode, so a new unguarded .post() in any of them passes CI. This has already happened: admin-bulk.ts:199 POST /resolve has no requireScope at all and adminBulkRoutes has no router-wide guard (:38). It resolves up to 200 arbitrary emails to {id, email, full_name, suspended} — a user-enumeration and email-confirmation oracle available to any admin regardless of scope.
acceptanceCriteria: The guard parses per-route rather than doing a whole-file substring match.
admin-bulk.ts:199 gets a scope.
A deliberate no-scope route must be explicitly registered as exempt with a reason, not silently pass.

Note the wider context: the default admin role holds 8 of 9 scopes (rbac-scopes.ts:123-132) and the test actively pins it that way, so scope enforcement is a no-op for a default admin and only becomes a real control once an operator narrows a role. Decide whether that default is right.
userStories.notes: [P1][Admin/Security] [Audit 2026-07-30 module/platform sweep] Reported by an audit agent; the cited line was not independently re-verified in this session — confirm before fixing. | 2026-08-02 EVERY CLAIM VERIFIED, including the one that matters most — the unguarded route really is there. THE GUARD: admin-scope-coverage_test.ts computes const hasGuard = src.includes("requireScope(") — a whole-FILE substring, exactly as reported. For mode "router" it additionally asserts the use("*") shape, so that mode is sound; for mode "mutations" a single requireScope anywhere in the file satisfies it. THE ROUTE THAT ALREADY SLIPPED THROUGH: admin-bulk.ts declares adminBulkRoutes = new Hono<AdminEnv>() with no router-wide use("*"), and its four POSTs are /credits with requireScope("billing:write"), /suspend with requireScope("moderation:write"), /regrade with requireScope("grading:review") — and /resolve with NOTHING. The file passes CI because the other three routes contain the substring. Confirmed what /resolve returns: it accepts up to MAX_TARGETS = 200 entries and answers with {id, email, full_name, suspended} per match, resolved by id OR by email. So it is precisely a user-enumeration and email-confirmation oracle, available to any admin regardless of scope. AC4's CONTEXT CONFIRMED AND EXACT: SCOPE_KEYS lists nine scopes (billing:write, grading:review, moderation:write, content:publish, users:role, ops:write, marketplace:write, support:write, growth:write) and DEFAULT_ROLE_SCOPES.admin lists eight — every one except users:role. So the story's "8 of 9" is right to the key, and the consequence is worth stating plainly: for a DEFAULT admin, every requireScope call in the codebase except users:role is a no-op. Scope enforcement only becomes a real control after an operator narrows a role, and nothing in the product prompts them to. That makes AC4 the highest-leverage AC here — fixing the guard and adding a scope to /resolve hardens a boundary that, for the default configuration, still admits everyone. IMPLEMENTATION NOTE for AC1: "parse per-route" is more than a regex tweak, because the two shapes are different — a router-wide use("*", requireScope(...)) protects everything after it, while a per-route guard sits as the second argument of .get/.post/.patch/.delete. A parser has to recognise both or it will report false positives on every correctly-guarded router-mode file. The nearest existing model in this repo is the enumeration style used by admin-direct-write-guard.test.ts and items-full-bounded-reads.test.ts: enumerate every route with its guard, and require an explicit DECLARED entry with a reason for any that has none — which is also exactly what AC3 asks for. Note both of those guards were reworked on 2026-08-02 under US-2383 (memoized scan + SCAN_TIMEOUT_MS); copy the fixed shape, not the old one, or the new guard becomes the next flake. | 2026-08-02 AC1 AND AC3 SHIPPED. AC2 DELIBERATELY NOT DONE, and the story's framing of it is WRONG — correcting that is the most important part of this note. THE CORRECTION: the story says POST /resolve slipping through is something that "has already happened", implying an accidental omission the weak guard failed to catch. It was not accidental. lib/admin-scope-map.ts's entry for admin-bulk.ts has always carried the rationale "Each bulk op maps to its owning scope: /credits → billing:write, /suspend → moderation:write, /regrade → grading:review. POST /resolve is a read-only target lookup (no scope; US-1562)." So the exemption was a considered, written decision recorded in the very registry the guard reads. The guard's weakness is real and worth fixing; the claim that it let an accident through is not. That distinction matters because AC2 as written ("admin-bulk.ts:199 gets a scope") is a request to REVERSE a prior decision, not to fix a defect — and doing that silently, from a story that mis-describes how the route got there, is how a considered choice gets undone by someone who never saw the argument. AC1 DONE: "mutations" mode is no longer a whole-file src.includes("requireScope(") check. A new ROUTE_REG parses each mutating registration with a 300-char window (so middleware on a following line still counts) and every one must carry its own requireScope. MEASURED before building it: across all four mutations-mode routers — admin-guarantee-pool, admin-users, admin-scopes, admin-bulk — there are 10 mutating routes and exactly ONE without a scope, POST /resolve. So the change reddens nothing except the known case, which is why it could land as an enforcement rather than a migration. AC3 DONE: NEW ADMIN_ROUTE_SCOPE_EXEMPTIONS in admin-scope-map.ts — file + method + path + a mandatory written reason, enforced at 80 characters so "legacy" cannot be the whole justification. /resolve is registered there with the US-1562 argument stated in full AND the counter-argument from this story stated next to it (the response confirms whether an address has an account, so an admin narrowed to no scopes can still enumerate users; reversing it needs a new read scope, since all three bulk ops would want it). The decision is now data a reviewer can argue with instead of prose inside a rationale string. THE EXEMPTION LIST CANNOT ROT: two further tests make it shrink-only — an entry whose route no longer exists fails, and an entry whose route has SINCE been guarded fails and tells you to delete it, so the allowlist can never be what is permitting a route that the guard would now pass on its own. A third test feeds the parser a known sample (guarded, unguarded, and a multi-line registration) and asserts what it sees, because a regex that silently matches nothing would make the whole guard pass vacuously — the same failure as the substring check, one level down. NEGATIVE-VERIFIED, not assumed: a probe route added to admin-users.ts made the guard fail naming POST /__probe_unguarded, and repointing /resolve's exemption at a non-existent path made the staleness test fail with the right message. Both probes reverted, tree confirmed clean. VERIFIED: full edge suite 5042 passed / 0 failed, deno lint clean across 1287 files, deno check clean. AC4 REMAINS OPEN and is still the highest-leverage item: nine scopes exist and the default admin holds eight, so for a default admin every requireScope except users:role is a no-op. Hardening route coverage does not change that; deciding whether the default is right does.

userStories.title: Buyer plan gating: all 13 gate flags are now accounted for — only the free-tier usage count (AC4) is left
userStories.description: lib/buyer-entitlements.ts:221 defines requireBuyerFeature, the 402 upgrade-required guard, and nothing calls it. Its helper buyerFeatureEnabled is used only by it and by tests. So no buyer route enforces plan gating except buyer-authenticity.ts:24, which does its own inline check. buyer-wants.ts — the demand board, a Connoisseur-tier feature — has no gate at all. Every buyer paid feature is available on the free tier.
acceptanceCriteria: Inventory which buyer routes are supposed to be tier-gated, and against which tier.
requireBuyerFeature is applied to each of them.
A test asserts every tier-gated buyer route returns 402 for a free-tier user.
Measure how many free-tier buyers have been using paid features before deciding whether to grandfather them.
userStories.notes:
[P1][Buyer/Billing] [Audit 2026-07-30 module/platform sweep] Reported by an audit agent; the cited line was not independently re-verified in this session — confirm before fixing. The dead-code sweep called this its top finding. Revenue leak, not just dead code. | 2026-08-02 VERIFIED, and quantified. requireBuyerFeature is defined at lib/buyer-entitlements.ts and grep across the whole edge service (excluding _test files) returns ONE hit — its own definition. Zero callers, exactly as reported. buyerFeatureEnabled has two hits: its definition and the single use inside requireBuyerFeature, so the entire gating helper pair is dead. THE SIZE OF THE GAP: BuyerGateFlags in lib/buyer-plans.ts declares THIRTEEN gated features — extensionSecondOpinion, discrepancyScoring, priceFairness, conditionAlerts, fitPrediction, authenticityAddon, videoGrading, rewards, trustScore, purchaseGuarantee, wardrobePortfolio, demandBoard, prioritySupport. Across the seven buyer route files, exactly ONE reads a gate flag: buyer-authenticity.ts checks ent.gateFlags.authenticityAddon inline. buyer-closet.ts, buyer-purchases.ts, buyer-rewards.ts, buyer-trust.ts and buyer-wants.ts contain no gate reference at all (buyer-profile.ts's only hit is the word "entitlements" in a comment). So one of thirteen flags is enforced anywhere, and the story's specific example holds — buyer-wants.ts, the demand board, has no gate. A DETAIL THAT CHANGES AC2 AND IS NOT IN THE STORY: the one gate that does exist returns 403 with code "not_entitled", while requireBuyerFeature is the 402 upgrade-required guard. They are not interchangeable. Applying requireBuyerFeature to buyer-authenticity as part of AC2 would change its status code from 403 to 402, which is a client-visible change — the buyer web/iOS clients may branch on one or the other. Either check the clients first, or leave authenticity on 403 and say why. Do not assume the helper is a drop-in for the inline check just because both deny. SEQUENCING NOTE on AC4: it asks how many free-tier buyers have been using paid features before deciding whether to grandfather. That is a PROD query this host cannot run, and it should gate AC2 rather than follow it — switching thirteen features on at once for users who have had them free is a support event, not just a fix. Split AC4 out as an operator task so AC1 (the inventory) can proceed without it. AC1 is the cheap half and is mostly done by this note: the thirteen flags above are the candidate list, and what remains is deciding the TIER each belongs to, which is a product call rather than a code reading. | PARTIAL 2026-08-03 — AC1, AC2 and AC3 DONE. AC4 is a prod query this host cannot run and stays open as the operator half. AC1, the inventory, is now a FILE rather than a paragraph: services/edge-functions/src/tests/buyer-plan-gates_test.ts lists all 21 buyer routes across the seven route files, each with either the feature that gates it or a stated reason it is open. AC2: TWO ROUTES WERE GENUINELY UNPROTECTED and are now gated. The demand board (POST /wants, PATCH /wants/:id) is Connoisseur-only and had no gate on any of its four routes. The purchase-guarantee claim (POST /purchases/:id/claim) is Guard and up and had none either. Both now call requireBuyerFeature and RETURN its refusal. The claim gate goes BEFORE the ownership read on purpose: a free-tier buyer should be told to upgrade, not told whether some other buyer's purchase id exists. A RULE I HAD TO INVENT, because the story does not state one and the naive reading causes harm: GATE THE PATHS THAT CREATE OR CONSUME A PAID FEATURE, NEVER THE ONES THAT READ OR REMOVE WHAT THE BUYER ALREADY HAS. Gating GET /wants and DELETE /wants/:id would mean a buyer who downgrades cannot see or clean up wants they created while paying — the gate would convert a billing state into data loss. Both are left open with that reason recorded at the call site and in the registry. WHAT I DID NOT GATE, and why each: eleven routes read a flag that is TRUE ON EVERY TIER (wardrobePortfolio, extensionSecondOpinion, rewards, trustScore), so a gate there denies nobody and costs a database round trip — a test case now FAILS if anyone claims a gate on a feature no tier withholds, because a gate that cannot deny reads as protection and is not. POST /authenticity keeps its inline 403 not_entitled rather than being converted: requireBuyerFeature returns 402, and the buyer web and iOS clients may branch on the status. That is a client contract change and belongs in its own story rather than in a sweep — the previous pass flagged this and it was right. AC3: the story asks for a live 402 assertion for a free-tier user. That needs an authenticated request against a seeded buyer, i.e. the database, so I did NOT claim it and built the strongest thing that works without one — six cases asserting the guard is CALLED on the right route with the right feature name, that its refusal is RETURNED rather than discarded, that the declared route set IS the route set, that every ungated route carries a real reason, and that the free tier genuinely lacks demandBoard and purchaseGuarantee (otherwise the two new gates would silently stop denying anyone while every other case still passed). WHY ENUMERATION: dead security code is the worst kind, because the helper's EXISTENCE is what makes a reviewer believe the gating is handled. Nothing about reading buyer-wants.ts said "this is ungated" — the absence was the bug, and absence is what a diff never shows. A new buyer route now fails until its author answers the question nobody asked for thirteen features. NEGATIVE-VERIFIED FOUR WAYS: removed the demand-board gate (reddened naming the route and flag), kept the call but discarded its Response (reddened on the return), added an undeclared /probe route (reddened as an unlisted route), and re-declared the claim gate against the rewards flag (reddened as a gate that denies nobody). Each restored. A MISTAKE WORTH RECORDING: my first route regex was a bare .get( / .post(, which also matched c.get("userId") in every handler and reported a phantom route per file. Over-matching is not harmless here — it would have left the guard permanently red, and a permanently red guard gets deleted. It is anchored to the Routes receiver now and says so. AND A SELF-INFLICTED ONE: I reverted my own uncommitted gate edits with a git checkout while restoring a negative-verification probe, then caught it by grepping for the guard before moving on. VERIFIED: deno check clean, deno lint clean across 1310 files, full edge suite 5166 passed / 0 failed, tenant-isolation 17/0. REMAINING: AC4 (how many free-tier buyers have been using the demand board and the guarantee claim, to decide grandfathering) is a prod query — it belongs with the other operator diagnostics in scripts/prod-diagnostics.sql. Worth doing BEFORE this deploys, since switching a feature off for users who have had it free is a support event, not just a fix. | 2026-08-03: this story's last open AC is now answerable by scripts/prod-diagnostics.sql, which the operator runs in ONE psql session alongside the other blocked stories. Read-only, verified by executing against a real database with ON_ERROR_STOP=1 — so it cannot fail the operator's session on a wrong column name, which is the failure mode that makes someone distrust the whole file. §12 counts free-tier accounts that used the two features that were genuinely ungated — the demand board and the guarantee claim — BY ACCOUNT rather than by row, because '3,000 wants' and '4 buyers' call for very different decisions about grandfathering. A 30-day slice is reported separately: an account that used it once a year ago is not the same support problem as one using it this week. | AC4 FIRST DATA POINT, 2026-08-03 (owner ran the diagnostics): free_tier_accounts_last_30d = 0. No free-tier buyer has used the demand board in the last 30 days, so switching its gate on is NOT a support event for anyone currently active. That is the half of AC4 that decides urgency. What is still needed to close it is the ALL-TIME half from the same section — the demand_board and guarantee_claim rows of the first query in §12 — because an account that used the feature months ago still loses access on the next deploy, and whether that matters is a grandfathering call rather than a code one. | PROD ANSWER 2026-08-03 (owner ran scripts/prod-diagnostics-console.sql). §12's 30-day slice returned 0. Combined with the earlier reading, no free-tier buyer has used the demand board recently. Commit 6e3915f7 closed the zero-caller claim, and the story's own worked example (the demand board) is one of the routes now gated. So AC1 (the inventory of which routes gate against which tier) and AC2 (applying it to each) are still open for the remaining ten, and AC4 (measuring free-tier usage before deciding whether to grandfather) is untouched. Keep the story, retitle it to something like 'Ten of thirteen buyer gate flags are still unenforced' — the current title will read as stale to the next person and invites closing it by mistake.

| 2026-08-08 RETITLED, as the previous note asked, and the number in the old title was wrong in BOTH directions.

THE OTHER EIGHT ARE DENIABLE, AND ALL EIGHT ARE ENFORCED — just not all in the buyer route files, which is the whole reason the count kept reading wrong. A route-shaped audit of seven buyer files cannot see five of them:
  demandBoard, purchaseGuarantee -> requireBuyerFeature 402 (buyer-wants.ts x2, buyer-purchases.ts)
  authenticityAddon -> inline 403 not_entitled (buyer-authenticity.ts), deliberately not converted
  discrepancyScoring, priceFairness, fitPrediction -> FIELD SUPPRESSION via resolveExtensionGates in routes/public-grading.ts:1107-1122 and :1818 — the extension scan returns, with the paid fields nulled

  prioritySupport -> NO runtime path by design; lib/plan-gate.ts:52 states it is an SLA/routing attribute

THE SHAPES DIFFER AND ALL OF THEM ARE RIGHT. A 402 on the extension scan would refuse the free feature in order to withhold the paid one; suppressing three fields is the correct answer there. Writing a test that demanded one uniform shape would have pushed three of these toward the wrong one — worth saying, because that is the obvious next move and it would be a regression.

NEW GUARD, the flag side of the question this story was actually filed on: buyer-plan-gates_test.ts already enumerated all 21 ROUTES, which answers "is this route gated?" and cannot answer "is this paid feature enforced anywhere?". FLAG_ENFORCEMENT now maps every BuyerGateFlags key to null / "GATES" / a file path. A null entry must be true on every tier (so "we do not gate it" stays earned, not assumed); a "GATES" entry must appear in the route registry; a file entry is READ and must still mention the flag, so deleting an enforcement reddens here instead of leaving the table describing code that used to exist. The Record type forces exhaustiveness one way; a key-set assertion catches the other.

userStories.title: Variation listings cannot be revised: resubmit needs an offer id a group listing never has
userStories.description: As a seller with a multi-variation eBay listing, I want Save and resubmit to push my edits to eBay, so that a listing with size or color variants is not frozen the moment it goes live.
acceptanceCriteria: POST /api/flipdesk/ebay/listings/:id/revise on a listing whose listings.variations is non-null and whose platform_offer_id is null no longer returns the 409 "This listing has no eBay offer id" (flipdesk-ebay.ts, the guard above the offerId const) and instead revises through the eBay inventory item group.

The revise resolves its strategy group-FIRST, the same way the end path does via resolveEndStrategy (flipdesk-ebay.ts:8836), and keys the group on the PINNED listings.inventory_sku rather than the current inventory_items.sku, so a SKU rename cannot orphan the live group.

The group branch updates every variant inventory item and then calls createOrReplaceInventoryItemGroup and publishOfferByInventoryItemGroup (both already exported from services/edge-functions/src/lib/ebay-client.ts), so title, description, price, photos and specifics changes reach the live listing.

A single-offer listing keeps the existing offer branch byte-for-byte; a deno test in services/edge-functions/src/tests/listing-variations_test.ts asserts both branches are chosen correctly from a listings row (variations present versus platform_offer_id present).

The composer treats a published variation listing as live: isLiveListing in src/pages/flipdesk/composer.tsx stops requiring platform_offer_id when listings.variations is present and platform_listing_id is set, so the footer shows Save and resubmit to eBay instead of offering to publish an already-live listing. A vitest guard pins that gate.

Tenant scoping is unchanged: the revise route still reaches the listing through an owner-verified parent row (US-268), and services/edge-functions/src/tests/tenant-isolation_test.ts gains a case covering the group-revise branch.

Verified after deploy against a real multi-variation listing, not by reading code: the publish path never writes platform_offer_id for a group (the variation listingPayload in flipdesk-ebay.ts omits it), so unit tests alone cannot prove the round trip.
userStories.notes: PARTIAL 2026-08-03 — AC2, AC4 and AC5 DONE, plus a truthful refusal in place of misleading advice. AC1, AC3, AC6 and AC7 remain, and the reason is scoped rather than vague. VERIFIED THE WHOLE CHAIN FIRST. The revise route really does begin with `if (!row.listing.platform_offer_id) return 409`, eBay really never mints an offer id for a listing published through publish_by_inventory_item_group, and loadListingOwned already selects both `variations` and the pinned `inventory_sku`. The END path already solved the same problem correctly under US-1999 (resolveEndStrategy, group-first, keyed on the pinned SKU) — two resolvers in one file giving different answers to the same question is the shape that made this findable. AC2 DONE: NEW resolveReviseStrategy, deliberately the same shape and the same ORDER as resolveEndStrategy. Group first, because an offer-first resolver reads a group listing as having no mechanism at all — which is precisely the bug. Keyed on the PINNED listings.inventory_sku, since the inventory_item_group was created under the base SKU at publish and a later rename would aim the revise at a group that does not exist. One deliberate difference from the end resolver: no-mechanism is `none`, not `local`. Ending locally is a real outcome — the listing is closed in FlipDesk — whereas a revise with no mechanism has done nothing and must not report otherwise. A test pins both the agreement and that single divergence. AC5 DONE, AND IT WAS THE WORSE HALF OF THE BUG. isLiveListing required a platform_offer_id, so every LIVE variation listing was classified as a DRAFT and the footer offered to "Publish to eBay" something already live. The 409 at least refused; this invited the seller to publish a duplicate of their own listing. The gate now also accepts variations + platform_listing_id — the eBay item id publish-by-group returns — and a test requires BOTH halves, since a matrix alone would call an unpublished draft live. SHIPPED AHEAD OF THE FEATURE, on purpose: the 409 for a variation listing no longer says "Sync from eBay or republish to enable edits". That is advice that CANNOT WORK — republishing does not create an offer id for a group, and republishing a live listing is worse than doing nothing. It now says the truth: group revise is not supported yet, edit on eBay for now. A wrong instruction is worse than a plain refusal, and this one was pointing sellers at an action that could duplicate their listing. AC4 DONE: seven cases appended to listing-variations_test.ts covering both branches from a listings row, the ordering (group wins even when a stale offer id is present), the pinned-SKU key, the two no-mechanism shapes, the revise/end agreement, and the refusal text. NEGATIVE-VERIFIED: the resolver flipped to offer-first (reddened on the ordering case) and the composer's variation branch reduced to the matrix alone (reddened on the both-halves case). WHAT REMAINS AND WHY I DID NOT DO IT. AC1/AC3 are the group-revise branch itself: update every variant inventory item, then createOrReplaceInventoryItemGroup and publishOfferByInventoryItemGroup. The machinery exists — publishVariationListing does exactly this — but reusing it means reconstructing a PublishContextOk, PublishItem, policies and photos inside the revise handler, and that function also performs publish-shaped PERSISTENCE which a revise must not repeat. It is a substantial change to the most sensitive file in the service, on the path every seller's Save-and-resubmit uses, and AC7 states plainly that unit tests cannot prove the round trip because the publish path never writes platform_offer_id for a group. Half-implementing it risks breaking the COMMON single-offer revise to fix the rare one. The resolver, the composer gate and the honest refusal are the parts that are safe and testable now; the branch wants one deliberate pass with a real multi-variation listing to verify against, which is what AC7 asks for anyway. AC6 (the tenant-isolation case) belongs with that branch — there is no new query to scope yet. VERIFIED: deno check clean, deno lint clean across 1323 files, edge suite 5245 passed / 0 failed, web 260 files / 3236 tests 0 failed, tsc -b clean, eslint 0 errors, build green through the 216-route prerender.

userStories.title: A denied function call from anon or authenticated SEGFAULTS Postgres and restarts the whole database
userStories.description: As GradeThread, we want a permission-denied RPC to return an error instead of crashing the database, so that anyone holding the public anon key cannot restart production at will.
acceptanceCriteria: Establish whether the PROD Postgres image reproduces it. On the local Supabase image (PG 17.6) it reproduces every time; prod is a separate self-hosted image and this has NOT been tested there, deliberately, because the test is a denial of service against production. The safe check is to read the image tag and the supautils.hint_roles setting, not to call a denied RPC.

If prod reproduces: mitigate BEFORE anything else. Clearing supautils.hint_roles (it exists only to append a GRANT hint to the error message) or upgrading the image are the two candidates; whichever is chosen, prove it with a denied call against a staging copy of the same image.

A regression check that survives an image upgrade: a throwaway-stack test that revokes EXECUTE on a scratch function, calls it as anon, and asserts a clean 'permission denied for function' error with the connection still alive.

supabase/migrations/00527_revoke_public_function_execute.sql.BLOCKED is renamed back to .sql, EXPECTED_SCHEMA_VERSION bumped to 00527 in the same commit, and US-2282 closed — the SQL is already written and verified, it is only blocked on this.

The 5 functions already revoked from anon before this was known (refund_grade 00048, credit_ledger_reconciliation 00093, release_job_lock + try_acquire_job_lock 00094, reserve_snap/refund_snap 00099, reconcile_payout_link 00117, equity_snapshot_owners) are enumerated in the notes as the CURRENTLY reachable crash entry points, since they are what an attacker could use today.
userStories.notes: [P0][Security/DB] Found 2026-08-04 by accident while verifying US-2282 on a throwaway stack, and it is the reason US-2282 is not shipping. ISOLATED, not guessed — four probes on the local Supabase image (PostgreSQL 17.6, shared_preload_libraries includes supautils): (1) a trivial scratch function with EXECUTE revoked, called as anon => SIGNAL 11 SEGMENTATION FAULT, 'terminating any other active server processes', full database recovery; (2) same as authenticated => same crash; (3) same as a custom role NOT listed in supautils.hint_roles => clean 'ERROR: permission denied for function', connection alive; (4) a denied TABLE read as anon => clean error PLUS the supautils hint 'Grant the required privileges to the current role with: GRANT SELECT ON public.applied_migrations TO anon;'. supautils.hint_roles is set to exactly 'anon, authenticated, service_role', which is exactly the set that crashes. So the crash is in the supautils hint path for FUNCTION permission denials specifically; the table path is fine. ALREADY REACHABLE TODAY, WITHOUT ANY NEW MIGRATION: public.refund_grade(uuid) has been revoked from anon since 00048/00093, and calling it as anon crashes the database the same way — verified, not inferred. PostgREST exposes it as an RPC, so the input needed is the public anon key and one HTTP call. WHY US-2282 IS BLOCKED ON THIS RATHER THAN THE OTHER WAY AROUND: 00527 does not create the bug, it multiplies the entry points — from the handful of functions already revoked to ~80. Applying it into an unpatched image would hand an attacker eighty ways to restart the database instead of eight. The SQL is written, verified on a fresh stack, and parked at supabase/migrations/00527_revoke_public_function_execute.sql.BLOCKED; the .BLOCKED suffix is what keeps apply-prod-migrations.sh (which globs *.sql) from applying it. NOT TESTED AGAINST PROD ON PURPOSE. The test IS the denial of service, so running it would be the attack. The safe next step is to read the prod image tag and 'show supautils.hint_roles' over psql — both read-only — and compare against the local image. If prod's image differs enough not to reproduce, this closes as a local-only artifact and US-2282 unblocks immediately. | 2026-08-08 AC3 DONE; AC5 DONE AND THE COUNT WAS WRONG; AC1/AC2 now have a PROVEN mitigation and a safer prod probe. Docker was available on this host for the first time, so every claim below was re-run rather than inherited. REPRODUCED on public.ecr.aws/supabase/postgres:17.6.1.106 with all 552 migrations applied: a scratch function with EXECUTE revoked, called as anon, gives 'server closed the connection' and the server log shows 'terminated by signal 11: Segmentation fault' -> 'terminating any other active server processes' -> 'automatic recovery in progress'. ALSO reproduced with public.refund_grade(uuid), a REAL function that has been revoked from anon since 00048/00093 — so this is reachable in prod today with the public anon key and one RPC call, exactly as the story claimed. MITIGATION PROVEN (this is new): setting supautils.hint_roles = '' in /etc/postgresql-custom/supautils.conf and restarting Postgres turns the same call into a clean 'ERROR: permission denied for function' with the connection alive. Verified by flipping the config both ways twice. CRITICAL CONSTRAINT FOR WHOEVER APPLIES IT: this CANNOT be done from SQL or from a migration — supautils rejects 'ALTER SYSTEM SET supautils.hint_roles' with 'permission denied to set parameter' even as the postgres superuser. It is a postgresql.conf change on the host (Coolify), i.e. an operator action, and no migration in this repo can substitute for it. AC5 CORRECTED: the story listed ~8 reachable entry points; the real number is 14, enumerated from the live schema rather than by hand (select ... where not has_function_privilege('anon', oid, 'EXECUTE') over the 160 public functions): admin_adjust_credits, bump_cache_signal, credit_ledger_reconciliation, delete_account, get_cache_signal, latest_schema_migration, reconcile_payout_link, record_registered_number_sighting, record_style_code_observation, refund_grade, release_job_lock, reserve_guarantee_pool_drawdown, revoke_grade_credits, try_acquire_job_lock. AC3 SHIPPED: scripts/db-denied-rpc-crash-check.mjs, wired into verify.mjs --db and db-migrations.yml. It is ADVISORY (continue-on-error), NOT a gate, and that is a deliberate call recorded in both files: the stock image is vulnerable today, so gating would turn every migration PR red on arrival, and this repo already has the lesson that a permanently red guard gets switched off (US-1927 notes). Flipping it to a hard gate is step ONE of the mitigation, not a follow-up. VERIFIED BOTH DIRECTIONS with the final code: RED on the stock image (all three assertions fire), GREEN with hint_roles cleared. Three self-inflicted defects were found and fixed while building it, all the same class as bugs this repo has shipped before — an assertion on pg_postmaster_start_time() that CANNOT EVER FIRE (a backend SIGSEGV is handled by crash recovery; the postmaster never restarts), and twice using execFileSync where the text being asserted on is on STDERR (both the 'permission denied' string and the Postgres server log), which silently compared against an empty string. AC1 — A SAFE PROBE THAT WAS MISSED, worth trying before anything invasive: US-1927's 2026-07-18 note records that calling latest_schema_migration() against PROD as anon returned 42501 permission denied rather than a crash. latest_schema_migration is on the list of 14 above, so IF that observation was a real prod call it is evidence prod does NOT reproduce — and it cost nothing. Treat it as a lead, not proof: it is second-hand, and it is not certain the 42501 came from Postgres rather than from PostgREST's own check. Re-running that one read-only call is the cheapest next step and is not an attack. EVIDENCE POINTING THE OTHER WAY: vault/10-ops/backups.md:161 records the 2026-06-12 restore drill against 'the same Supabase image as prod' pinned at 17.6.1.106 — the exact image that crashes here. Nothing in the repo pins the prod tag, so that drill log is the only signal, and it suggests prod DOES reproduce. These two point opposite ways; resolve with the read-only check the story already specifies (read the image tag and 'show supautils.hint_roles' over psql). KEPT passes:false: AC1 (prod image determination) and AC2 (apply the mitigation) are operator actions on the Coolify host that cannot be done or validated from here, and AC4 (unblock 00527 / US-2282) must stay blocked until AC2 is done — applying it into an unpatched image would take the entry points from 14 to ~80.
