userStories.title: Offsite backups are uploaded unencrypted — R2 credentials alone yield a full plaintext database dump
userStories.description: As GradeThread, we want every backup artifact encrypted with a key we hold before it leaves the host, so that compromise of the Cloudflare R2 bucket or its rclone credentials does not expose the entire production database and every uploaded garment photo.
acceptanceCriteria: scripts/ops/backup-postgres.sh encrypts the pg_dump artifact with a key held by GradeThread (age or gpg) BEFORE the 'rclone copy' at line 55, so the object landing in r2:gradethread-backups/pg is ciphertext. R2's own server-side encryption does not satisfy this AC — the threat model is a leaked R2 credential, which server-side encryption is transparent to.

The .sha256 sidecar (backup-postgres.sh:50) is computed over the ENCRYPTED artifact, so the existing 'dump plus its .sha256 in the last 24h' offsite check from vault/10-ops/backups.md:50 still verifies what is actually stored.

scripts/ops/backup-storage.sh either encrypts the storage mirror or the runbook explicitly records the decision not to, with the reason — an rclone sync of the raw storage volume today exposes every submission image, including grading label photos, to anyone with the R2 credential.

scripts/ops/restore-postgres.sh and restore-drill.sh decrypt before pg_restore, and a restore drill against an ENCRYPTED artifact passes and is recorded in the drill table at vault/10-ops/backups.md:162 — an encryption change that breaks restore is worse than no encryption.

The backup encryption key is added to vault/10-ops/key-rotation.md's rotation table with a stated procedure, and the procedure covers the window where old ciphertext in the 30-day-retention bucket was written under the previous key.
vault/10-ops/backups.md documents that losing the backup key means losing every backup, and names where the key is stored (a reference, never the value).
userStories.notes: 2026-08-08 ALL SIX ACs BUILT AND VERIFIED END TO END; kept passes:false because the mechanism is done and PRODUCTION HAS NOT MOVED — the keypair does not exist yet and the updated scripts are not on the DB host. Docker plus an age implementation were both available here, so nothing below is reasoned-about; every claim was run. MECHANISM (AC1): backup-postgres.sh encrypts the dump with age to BACKUP_AGE_RECIPIENT before rclone copy. PUBLIC-key on purpose — the DB host holds only the recipient half, so it can encrypt but not decrypt, and rooting the database box does not also hand over the offsite archive. It FAILS CLOSED: with RCLONE_REMOTE set and no recipient it exits 1 having called rclone ZERO times (verified with a stub rclone on PATH that logs its argv). Happy path verified the same way: the only two objects handed to rclone are .dump.age and .dump.age.sha256, never the plaintext .dump. AC2: the sha256 is computed over the CIPHERTEXT, which is what the bucket actually holds. FOUND AND FIXED A PRE-EXISTING BUG WHILE DOING IT, and it would have bitten during a real recovery: sha256sum \"\" wrote the sidecar with the ABSOLUTE staging path (/backups/pg/...), and restore-postgres.sh verifies with sha256sum -c, which resolves whatever path the sidecar records. On a scratch host that path does not exist, so verification failed with 'No such file or directory' — i.e. the checksum could never have passed on any genuine offsite restore, only on the machine that wrote it. Both branches now cd first and record a BARE FILENAME. Proved by backing up to one directory, copying the artifact to another (what an offsite fetch does), and restoring successfully from there. AC3 (storage): the age-per-file approach does NOT fit an incremental rclone sync of thousands of objects — pre-encrypting per run breaks rclone's diffing. The mechanism is rclone's own CRYPT REMOTE (client-side, per object, sync still works), which is config-side, so what the script can enforce is refusal: backup-storage.sh reads 'rclone config show <remote>' and exits unless type = crypt, overridable only by an explicit STORAGE_BACKUP_ALLOW_PLAINTEXT=1. Checked against the config rather than the remote's NAME, because a remote called 'r2crypt' that is not of type crypt would otherwise read as safe. AC4 (the one the story warns about most — 'an encryption change that breaks restore is worse than no encryption'): restore-postgres.sh detects a .age input, verifies the checksum BEFORE decrypting (checking the stored object, not a derived one), decrypts to a mktemp file chmod 600 created empty before any plaintext is written, and shreds it via an EXIT trap — verified 0 leftover temp files after a run. restore-drill.sh now performs the encrypt/sha/verify/decrypt round-trip on EVERY run under an EPHEMERAL keypair, so the drill never touches the real key and a drill can no longer silently measure a procedure prod does not use (opt out only via DRILL_SKIP_ENCRYPTION=1). Drill PASS recorded in vault/10-ops/backups.md: migration 00559, 5 users, 20 submissions, 375 RLS policies all matched, dump 1s restore 5s. NOTE ON DRILL QUALITY: the first run passed with every row count at ZERO, which makes each 'OK' vacuous — a data-restore failure would have passed too. Seeded real rows and re-ran; the recorded numbers are from that run. NEGATIVE-VERIFIED, all four directions: no recipient => refuses and uploads nothing; no identity => refuses to restore; a single flipped byte in the ciphertext => checksum FAILS before decryption is attempted; and the drill asserts the .age artifact is NOT still a readable pg_dump (a passthrough bug would otherwise leave everything green while backups shipped in the clear). DOCS (AC5, AC6): key-rotation.md gains both keys in the rotation table plus a full section — the asymmetry that makes this key unlike every other one is that losing it is SILENT (backups keep running, /health stays green, the bucket keeps filling; you find out at the only moment it matters), and the 30-day-retention window means deleting the old identity on rotation day destroys most of the recovery range, so both identities are kept until the lifecycle rule has aged out the last object under the old one. backups.md gains an Encryption section saying plainly that losing the key loses every backup with no escrow and no support path, requiring two independent durable homes neither of which is the machine being backed up, and naming Infisical as the home for the identity (a reference, never a value) while noting it is NOT an app env var and no deployment surface reads it. Also corrected the offsite-freshness check there: the objects to look for are now .dump.age / .dump.age.sha256, and a bare .dump in the bucket means an OLD script is still deployed and the nightly is shipping plaintext. encryption-at-rest.md is the security-questionnaire page and carries these scripts in its code_refs, so it was updated in the same change per the vault same-commit rule — its store table and gap paragraph now say 'mechanism yes, production not yet' and explicitly tell the reader NOT to upgrade the customer-facing answer until the key exists on the host. vault:lint --strict green, all four ops scripts pass bash -n. REMAINING (operator, on the Contabo/Coolify DB host — this is the whole gap): (1) age-keygen the pair, put the identity in Infisical plus one offline copy, put the public recipient in /etc/cron.d/gradethread-backups; (2) rclone config a crypt remote and repoint the storage cron at it; (3) deploy the updated scripts to /opt/gradethread. Step-by-step is in the MANUAL callout in vault/10-ops/backups.md. Until all three are done prod backups remain plaintext, which is why this stays open. WORTH KNOWING: age has no Windows package, but rage (the Rust build, format-compatible) does — 'scoop install rage', then AGE_BIN=rage. Every script takes AGE_BIN, which is how the drill ran on this host.

userStories.title: Postal addresses and phone numbers are stored as plaintext columns while OAuth tokens next to them are AES-GCM encrypted
userStories.description: As a reseller, I want my home or business street address stored encrypted the same way my marketplace tokens are, so that a single leaked database dump or a SQL-injection read does not hand an attacker a mailing list of resellers with valuable inventory at those addresses.
acceptanceCriteria: public.users.ship_from_address (jsonb, added by 00325_user_business_shipping_profile.sql) and public.users.business_phone are stored as AES-256-GCM ciphertext produced by services/edge-functions/src/lib/crypto-aes.ts encryptToken(), with the owning user id passed as the aad option so a ciphertext copied onto another user's row fails to decrypt (US-268 tenant binding, same pattern as the marketplace token columns).

public.measure_card_requests street fields (ship_name, address_line1, address_line2, city, postal_code — added by 00351_measure_card_requests.sql) are encrypted the same way, keyed to owner_user_id. state and country stay plaintext so the fulfillment export can still filter and sort by region without decrypting every row.

A migration ships the US-1108 triple: idempotent SQL (safe to re-run on any prior state), EXPECTED_SCHEMA_VERSION bumped in services/edge-functions/src/lib/schema-version.ts in the SAME commit, and the self-record footer inserting its version into public.applied_migrations.

The migration backfills existing plaintext rows to ciphertext, and the read path tolerates both during the rollout — a row that does not parse as v1:/v2: is returned as-is rather than throwing, so a partial backfill cannot 500 the Settings page.

Every edge route that reads or writes these columns decrypts/encrypts at the boundary and stays tenant-scoped per US-268, with a case added to services/edge-functions/src/tests/tenant-isolation_test.ts.

The eBay ship-from location prefill (US-1442's original consumer) still populates correctly end to end after the change — verified against the flipdesk-ebay.ts path that consumes ship_from_address, not just by unit test.
A test asserts that decrypting a ship_from_address ciphertext with a DIFFERENT user id as aad throws, proving the tenant binding is real.
userStories.notes: 2026-08-08 AC2 DONE, AC4 and AC7 DONE for it, and AC1 IS BLOCKED ON A PREREQUISITE THE STORY DOES NOT NAME. The prerequisite is the most important thing in this note, because AC1 reads like a one-file change and is not. AC1 IS NOT REACHABLE YET, and it is a fact about the write path rather than a preference. src/pages/settings.tsx:306 writes users.business_phone and users.ship_from_address DIRECTLY from the browser with supabase-js under RLS, and 00526_users_self_update_allowlist.sql (restated in 00550) explicitly allowlists both columns. They are READ the same way in three places: settings.tsx:141-143, flipdesk/marketplaces.tsx:202 and lib/account-export.ts:54. EDGE_ENCRYPTION_KEY is an edge-only secret and must stay one, so encrypting those two columns first requires moving that write and all three reads behind an edge route. Doing the crypto without that would lock a seller out of their own Settings page and would break the account export. iOS and Android touch neither column (grepped both trees, zero hits), so the migration surface is web-only - which makes the prerequisite tractable, just not free. AC3's migration is ALSO wrong for AC1 as written: ship_from_address is jsonb, so storing an envelope string means a type change, not just a value change. AC2 SHIPPED, and measure_card_requests is the more sensitive of the two anyway - it holds a full street address, not a ship-from region. It has none of AC1's problem: deny-all RLS (rls-guard_test.ts:181), written by exactly ONE edge route (flipdesk-measure.ts POST /card-request) and read by exactly ONE (admin-measure-cards.ts listRequests, feeding the fulfilment CSV). Both sides already run where the key lives. NEW services/edge-functions/src/lib/measure-card-pii.ts encrypts ship_name, address_line1, address_line2, city and postal_code with encryptToken() and the OWNER'S USER ID AS AAD. state and country stay plaintext exactly as AC2 asks, and a test asserts the two lists cannot overlap - the export filters and sorts by region, and an equality on an encrypted column cannot use an index or match at all. AC7 IS THE CASE WORTH READING. Encrypting a column is easy to do in a way that helps nobody: one key, no binding, and anyone who can write a row can copy another tenant's ciphertext onto it and read the plaintext back through the normal decrypt path. AES-GCM covers additionalData with the auth tag, so A's address fails to decrypt under B's id. That is the US-268 property expressed in cryptography instead of in an .eq() someone has to remember, and it is asserted rather than assumed. THE WRITE ENCRYPTS BEFORE THE INSERT, not after it. An insert-then-update would leave the address readable in the WAL and in any replica that saw the first version, which is most of what a stolen-dump scenario actually covers. A key misconfiguration answers 503 rather than falling back to plaintext. THE READ USES THE ROW'S OWNER, never a caller-supplied id, and decrypts PER ROW: one un-backfilled or unreadable row must not take out the operator's whole fulfilment queue, so a failure blanks that address and logs the id. A blank that says so beats a plausible-looking wrong address on a mailing label. AC4 - TOLERANCE PLUS A BACKFILL, and the backfill is a SCRIPT because it cannot be a migration. pgcrypto offers AES in CBC/ECB only: no GCM, therefore no auth tag, therefore no AAD - a SQL backfill would produce ciphertext the edge cannot read carrying none of the security this story is about. NEW scripts/backfill-measure-card-pii.ts is DRY-RUN BY DEFAULT (--apply to write), refuses to start without EDGE_ENCRYPTION_KEY (encrypting under the wrong key would make every address silently unreadable while still LOOKING encrypted), and scopes its update by owner_user_id as well as id so a mis-derived id cannot write one seller's owner-bound ciphertext onto another's row, where it would be permanently undecryptable. Re-running it is a no-op: already-encrypted values pass through, so an interrupted run resumes with no bookkeeping. Double-wrapping would be UNRECOVERABLE, since the inner envelope's AAD is invisible from the outside, and a test pins that. MY OWN TEST HAD A BLIND SPOT AND THE SABOTAGE FOUND IT. The route-text check forbade `city:` in the insert, so an accidental SHORTHAND `city,` - which writes the same plaintext and overrides the spread - stayed green. It now checks both forms per column, which has to be per-column rather than 'no shorthand allowed', because `state,` and `country,` are legitimately shorthand there. 10 cases in NEW src/tests/measure-card-pii_test.ts. NEGATIVE-VERIFIED FIVE WAYS: the AAD dropped from both sides (the cross-tenant case fires), postal_code removed from the encrypted set, the insert overriding a column in shorthand form, the same in explicit form, and the admin export decrypting with a caller-supplied id. Each reddened with its own message; all files restored and re-run green. REMAINING: AC1 (needs the settings write + three reads moved behind the edge first), AC3 (no migration was needed for AC2 - the columns are already text and ciphertext fits; AC1's jsonb column is what would need one), AC5's tenant-isolation case, AC6 (the eBay ship-from prefill end-to-end, which consumes users.ship_from_address and is therefore downstream of AC1). VERIFIED: deno lint clean across 1426 files, deno check clean including the backfill script, full edge suite 5999 passed / 0 failed / 170 ignored.

userStories.title: End-to-end mobile/PWA story: snap → grade → list, offline beyond intake
userStories.description: As a mobile user, I want to capture a garment, grade it, and start a listing from my phone — with the PWA install offered wherever I am and offline support beyond just the intake form — so the mobile experience is a real workflow, not a FlipDesk-only afterthought.
acceptanceCriteria: The PWA install affordance (pwa-install-banner.tsx) is offered outside FlipDesk too (e.g. on snap.tsx / dashboard on mobile) with copy that fits the context
snap.tsx connects into the pipeline: a captured item can flow snap -> grade -> create FlipDesk item, instead of being an isolated 'what's it worth' page
Offline support (currently use-offline-intake.ts for intake only) extends to viewing submission status and certificates while offline; the service worker caches those routes
The mobile capture path reuses the upload validation/EXIF-strip rules (US-276); build + eslint clean
userStories.notes: [P3][Cohesion/Mobile] DEFERRED 2026-06-08 — needs real device/PWA QA, and the audit was partly stale. AC2 ALREADY EXISTS: snap.tsx already has a 'List it with FlipDesk' CTA (-> /dashboard/flipdesk) alongside 'Get a certified grade' (-> /dashboard/submissions/new), so it's not isolated from the pipeline. The rest is genuinely PWA/service-worker/offline work that can't be verified headless: (AC1) pwa-install-banner.tsx is mounted only in flipdesk/intake.tsx and calls ensureServiceWorker() — the SW is DELIBERATELY scoped to FlipDesk intake (vite.config 'service worker not auto-injected app-wide'; only the banner + use-offline-intake register it), so surfacing the install affordance app-wide changes SW registration scope and offline behavior and must be QA'd on a real device + as an installed PWA; (AC3) caching submission-status/certificate routes for offline is a Workbox/SW change whose correctness (cache invalidation, stale auth) only shows on a device. RECOMMENDATION: do this as a focused mobile/PWA session with an actual phone + installed-PWA testing — generalize the banner copy + mount point with intentional SW-scope changes, add Workbox runtimeCaching for the read-only submission/cert routes, and (optionally) a snap-photo -> FlipDesk-intake handoff that prefills the captured image (reusing US-276 validateImageUpload/stripImageMetadata). NOT shipping blind. Depends on [[US-736]]. | REOPENED 2026-08-08 (US-1996 AC3). This row was passes:true with an unresolved DEFERRED in its own notes, and the deferral is STILL NOT SATISFIED — AC1 (app-wide install affordance) and AC3 (offline submission-status/certificate caching) never shipped and cannot be verified without a real phone and an installed PWA. AC2 was already true when the deferral was written (snap.tsx has the FlipDesk CTA) and AC4 rides along with whatever AC1/AC3 touch. US-1996 AC3 offered two outs, reopen or record why the deferral is satisfied; only one of them is true here, so this moves back to the ACTIVE backlog rather than staying archived behind a passing flag. Deliberately NOT closed by transferring the work to a new story id: a successor would have left this row reading passes:true, which is the exact claim the guard exists to catch, and would have spent an id to avoid saying the work is unfinished. prd-lint stops flagging it because passes is now false, which is the honest reason rather than an appended closing token.

userStories.title: Third-party data subjects (claim buyers, consignors) have no erasure path — their PII is reachable only by deleting the seller's account
userStories.description: Account erasure (US-2005) is complete for the ACCOUNT HOLDER. Two tables hold identifying data about people who are NOT the account holder and who may never have had an account: guarantee_claims carries claimant_email (NOT NULL), claimant_name and order_reference for the BUYER who filed a claim (00197_buyer_guarantee_claims.sql:48); consignors carries name, contact_email and contact_phone for the CONSIGNOR who gave a seller items to sell (00107_consignors.sql:16-19). Both rows are FK-cascaded to the SELLER (guarantee_claims.seller_user_id, consignors.user_id, both ON DELETE CASCADE), so both are erased if and only if that seller deletes their account. The buyer and the consignor have no lever: no account to delete, no endpoint to call, and nothing in routes/account.ts reaches a subject who is not the caller. The inventory guard in account-email-purge_test.ts correctly skips both, because it asks whether the ACCOUNT HOLDER data survives — which it does not. The gap is that erasure is modelled as an account action, and a data-subject request is not the same thing.
acceptanceCriteria: Decide the intake first: whether a non-account-holder request is handled by an operator runbook against the DB or by a self-serve verified-email flow. A self-serve endpoint that erases rows on an unverified email claim is a deletion oracle — anyone could wipe another person's claim — so if it is self-serve, the verification step IS the story, not the delete.

A named procedure exists for erasing a buyer from guarantee_claims and a consignor from consignors, covering every column that identifies them (claimant_email + claimant_name + order_reference; name + contact_email + contact_phone), not just the address.

Decide per table whether the row is deleted or anonymized, and record the reason. A guarantee claim is an audit record of a payout decision, so anonymizing may be right where deleting is not — the same call email_consent_audit already got in US-2005.

The inventory guard learns the distinction. Today a new table holding third-party PII passes it, because the guard only asks whether the ACCOUNT HOLDER data survives. It should either cover third-party columns too or say in its failure message that it does not, so a green guard is not read as full coverage.
A test asserts the third-party purge leaves other subjects' claim/consignor rows intact — over-reach here destroys a payout audit trail and another person's record.
userStories.notes: [P2][Compliance/GDPR] Filed 2026-08-08 from US-2005, whose description named guarantee_claims but whose ACs only covered the account holder. NOT the same gap US-2005 fixed and not a regression of it: the account-holder path is complete and guarded. This is about a subject with rights and no account. Lower severity than US-2005 was — the data is admin-only behind the service-role edge, the volume is small, and no endpoint exposes it — but the obligation does not scale with volume. Worth pairing with US-2434 (the backfill): both are operator-run data tasks against prod and would share one runbook. | 2026-08-08 AC2, AC3, AC4 and AC5 DONE. AC1 stays OPEN because it is an intake decision, and the reason it can stay open is that the procedure is the SAME either way - an operator runbook and a verified-email self-serve flow both end in exactly these writes. NEW services/edge-functions/src/lib/third-party-pii-purge.ts is the procedure and deliberately contains NO ROUTE. AC1's own argument is why: an endpoint that erases on an unverified email claim is a deletion oracle - anyone could POST a stranger's address and destroy the audit record of a payout decision made against them. So if self-serve is chosen, the verification step is the work, and this module is what it calls afterwards. RECOMMENDATION for whoever decides: operator runbook, because the volume is small and the verification build is not. THE SCHEMA MADE US-2005's TWO MODES UNUSABLE, and that is the finding worth carrying forward rather than a preference. EMAIL_PURGE_PLAN has delete and anonymize-by-nulling. Neither works here: guarantee_claims.claimant_email is NOT NULL, so nulling raises 23502 and leaves the address exactly where it was; consignors.name is NOT NULL *and* carries UNIQUE(user_id, name) from 00107, so redacting two of one seller's consignors to the same constant raises 23505 on the second and that person keeps their real name while the run reports partial success. So there are THREE operations: null a nullable column, overwrite a NOT NULL one with a constant, and overwrite a NOT NULL + UNIQUE one with a constant made unique by the row's own id. The last is why the purge runs per row instead of as one filtered UPDATE. AC3 DECIDED - ANONYMIZE BOTH, DELETE NEITHER, and both reasons are about someone OTHER than the subject. guarantee_claims is the audit record of a money decision and two tables cascade from it - claim_accuracy_signals (00302), which feeds grading calibration, and guarantee_remedies (00319), which records a refund that actually happened; deleting the claim destroys the evidence that we paid, which is the seller's to rely on and not the subject's to erase. Same call email_consent_audit got in US-2005. consignors is the seller's own business record - split percentages, and inventory_items.consignor_id points at it ON DELETE SET NULL by deliberate design in 00107 so sale history survives; deleting the row detaches another party's records to serve a third party. A MATCHING DETAIL THE STORY DID NOT ANTICIPATE: consignors is matched by ROW ID, not by address. contact_email is nullable, so a consignor recorded by name alone has no address to key on and an email-keyed purge would never reach them - which is this story's own failure mode one level down. A test asserts the two kinds cannot run each other's plan, because a mismatched pair matches nothing and would report a clean run over data it never touched. RESIDUAL NAMED RATHER THAN OMITTED. guarantee_claims.reason, guarantee_claims.evidence_urls and consignors.notes are buyer/seller-authored free text that MAY carry an identifier, and the plan does not touch them. AC2 names three columns per table and these are outside it, and redacting them is not free: reason is NOT NULL and IS the claim, so blanking it turns a payout audit record into a row saying money moved for no stated cause. RESIDUAL_FREE_TEXT pins the list and a test asserts every skipped column appears in it, so the explanation cannot drift away from the behaviour. Whether a subject request should also scrub these is an OWNER call about how much audit substance an erasure may destroy - it is not a code gap for the next reader to close. AC4 DONE, and the framing changed. The inventory guard was not wrong - it skips any table that cascades from public.users, which is correct for the question it asks ('does the ACCOUNT HOLDER's address survive their own deletion?'). It is wrong only as a claim of full coverage. The skip line now says so at the exact `continue` where a third-party subject leaves the guard's field of view, and a NEW case asserts that guarantee_claims and consignors are handled by THIRD_PARTY_PURGE_PLAN. Named literally rather than rediscovered from the schema, because a re-derivation could drift to zero tables and pass while covering nothing. AC5 DONE - three subjects seeded on one seller, purge one, and the other two rows are asserted unchanged column by column. The tempting wrong implementation is to scope by seller_user_id, since that is how the row is normally owned; the test names that case. 9 cases in NEW src/tests/third-party-pii-purge_test.ts plus the AC4 case in account-email-purge_test.ts. One of them reads the whole migration corpus and asserts every column the plan writes actually exists, because a wrong column name answers PostgREST 42703, gets logged, and the run reports as a purge - it would look exactly like success. That case guards itself on corpus size so it cannot pass by loading nothing. NEGATIVE-VERIFIED FOUR WAYS: order_reference dropped from the plan (an identifier survives), the consignor tombstone made non-unique (both redact to the same string), the claim purge rescoped to seller_user_id (over-reach), and consignors removed from the plan (the blind-spot case fires with its full message). Each reddened on its own case; module restored and re-run green. REMAINING: AC1's intake choice, and then a caller - an operator tool or a verified flow. VERIFIED: deno lint clean across 1423 files, deno check clean, full edge suite 5989 passed / 0 failed.

userStories.title: Email-keyed PII retained for accounts deleted BEFORE the US-2005 purge shipped is still queryable
userStories.description: US-2005 added an email-keyed purge to the deletion path, so erasure is complete from that point on. It is not retroactive. Every account deleted before it shipped left its address — and in email_deliveries the full rendered html of every email we sent it — in the seven tables EMAIL_PURGE_PLAN now covers. Those users asked to be forgotten and were told {deleted:true}. The deletion log written by routes/account.ts records who was deleted and when, so the population is identifiable rather than hypothetical, which is what makes this actionable rather than a shrug.
acceptanceCriteria: Establish the population from the deletion log rather than guessing: which deletions predate the purge, and whether their addresses are still present in any planned table. Report the count BEFORE deleting anything — a backfill whose blast radius was never measured is how a cleanup becomes an incident.

Re-run the SAME plan, not a hand-written script. purgeEmailKeyedPii(address, io) already encodes which table is deleted and which anonymized; a parallel script would drift from it, which is the exact thing US-2005 spent its effort avoiding.
The run is idempotent and logged per address, so an interrupted pass resumes without re-deriving what it already did.
Record the outcome where a regulator-facing answer would be looked up, not only in this story: how many subjects, which tables, and the date the backlog reached zero.
userStories.notes: [P2][Compliance/GDPR][OPERATOR] Filed 2026-08-08 from US-2005, which fixed the path forward and explicitly left this as a prod data task. CANNOT be done from a dev checkout: it needs the production database. The code half already exists — purgeEmailKeyedPii takes an address and an IO seam, so the operator half is a script that enumerates addresses and calls it. Pairs with US-2433; both are operator-run data tasks and would share one runbook.

userStories.title: `npm run verify` failed for anyone with the local Supabase stack running — eslint was linting generated stack files
userStories.description: FIXED 2026-08-08 in the same pass that found it; filed so the fix is discoverable and so the class is on record. `supabase start` writes a generated, minified edge-runtime bundle to supabase/.temp/start-secrets/. That directory was not gitignored (only the single file supabase/.temp/cli-latest was, listed FOUR times) and was not in eslint's ignore list, so `npm run lint` — and therefore `npm run verify` — reported 189 errors in code nobody wrote. CI never sees it, because the web lane does not run `supabase start`. The people it broke are exactly the ones following CLAUDE.md: the tenant-isolation and money-cert suites both require the full local stack, so anyone who ran those and then ran verify got a wall of errors in minified output and no indication it was not their change.
acceptanceCriteria: DONE: .gitignore ignores supabase/.temp/ as a DIRECTORY, replacing four copies of a line that covered one file inside it.
DONE: eslint.config.js ignores supabase/.temp/** with the reason written at the ignore.

OPEN: supabase/.temp/cli-latest is TRACKED in git and also gitignored, which is why it shows as modified in every working tree that has ever booted the local stack. Ignoring a tracked file does nothing. It should be `git rm --cached`-ed, but that changes what is committed and is the owner's call, not a side effect of a lint fix.

OPEN: decide whether verify should FAIL when it lints a path that is gitignored. This bug was invisible until someone happened to run verify with the stack up; a check that the lint target set and the git-tracked set agree would have caught it on the first run.
userStories.notes: [P3][DX/CI] Found 2026-08-08 while running `npm run verify` to check a session's accumulated work, with the local Supabase stack up for the migration testing. The first two ACs were fixed on the spot; after the fix `node scripts/verify.mjs --web` is 11/11 checks and `--edge` is 4/4. THE THIRD AC IS THE INTERESTING ONE. A file that is both TRACKED and GITIGNORED is a state git gives no warning about: the ignore silently does nothing, and the file keeps appearing as modified forever. supabase/.temp/cli-latest has been in that state long enough that four separate ignore lines were added for it, each presumably by someone who saw it dirty and assumed it just needed ignoring. That is the tell — a rule added four times is a rule that never worked. | Done 2026-08-08. AC4 SHIPPED as scripts/check-tracked-ignored.mjs, wired into verify.mjs (web lane, BEFORE eslint so the cause is named before the wall of symptoms) and into ci.yml, so a --no-verify push cannot shed it. It runs one git call — `git ls-files --cached --ignored --exclude-standard` — and fails on any path not in its KNOWN baseline, and equally on a KNOWN entry that has LEFT the state, so the list can only shrink (the KNOWN_UNREACHABLE_CRONS pattern from cron-registry-drift_test.ts). Both directions negative-verified. THE STORY UNDERSTATED THE PROBLEM BY 33x. AC3 describes supabase/.temp/cli-latest as the tracked-and-gitignored file; measured, there are 32, and they are not one class but three, with three different correct fixes — which is exactly why the guard reports and refuses to guess: (1) services/edge-functions/deno.lock — THE IGNORE WAS THE BUG, NOT THE TRACKING, and this one I fixed outright because it changes nothing about what is committed. It was line 101 of .gitignore, uncommented, in a block of Ralph runtime junk. The lockfile is tracked and MUST stay tracked: US-517's `deno cache --frozen src/main.ts` gate (verify.mjs + security.yml) exists to fail the build when a resolved dependency drifts, and a frozen check with no committed lockfile has nothing to freeze against. Deleted the line with the reasoning written at it. Verified after: git check-ignore exits 1 (no longer ignored), the file is still tracked, deno cache --frozen still exits 0. (2) temp_prd/** — 20 loose OOXML parts of an unzipped FlipDesk_PRD_v1.docx, committed and then ignored as a directory. (3) assets/hf_*.mp4|png, an ios-screenshots PNG, and a .pyc — generated media and build debris committed before their ignore rules landed. Groups 2 and 3 plus cli-latest are baselined with the decision each is waiting on, because `git rm --cached` changes what a fresh clone receives and that is the owner's call, not a side effect of a lint fix — the same reason AC3 gives. AC3 THEREFORE STAYS OPEN AS A DECISION, but it is no longer invisible: it is 31 named paths in a file CI reads, instead of a sentence in a backlog note. AC1/AC2 confirmed still in place (.gitignore ignores supabase/.temp/ as a directory; eslint.config.js ignores supabase/.temp/** with the reason written at the ignore). VERIFIED: check-tracked-ignored clean at 32 known, npm run lint 0 errors, npx tsc -b clean, deno cache --frozen clean. ⚠ SEPARATE FINDING, NOT PART OF THIS STORY, found while reading .gitignore: line 95 ignores supabase/migrations/00122_verified_storefront_listings.sql. That migration was never committed (git log --all finds nothing) and is absent from the working tree — 00121 and 00123 are both present, so the sequence has a hole. The ignore line was added by 645cd1f3, the commit that shipped the storefront-listings feature itself. Filed separately. | REOPENED IMMEDIATELY, same session, and the mistake is worth recording. I flipped this to passes:true on the strength of AC4 shipping, while my own note in the same breath said 'AC3 THEREFORE STAYS OPEN AS A DECISION'. Two ACs done and one open is passes:false — an AC that needs the owner rather than an agent is still an unmet AC, not an exemption. This is the US-1996 failure mode (a story marked done while an explicitly deferred criterion is outstanding) committed by the very session that was working the backlog, which is how it keeps happening. AC3 is the ONLY thing outstanding: 31 tracked-and-gitignored paths need a per-path keep-or-untrack call. They are enumerated in scripts/check-tracked-ignored.mjs KNOWN, grouped by the fix each needs, and CI now reads that file — so the decision is visible instead of buried.

userStories.title: Build the per-block versioned seam for the grading USER message
userStories.description: US-2432 decided the seam and did not build it. The decision, with its reasoning, is in vault/20-domain/grading-prompt-channels.md ("The seam decision: a second versioned artifact, per block"): a versioned artifact keyed (stage, block_key, garment_scope), resolved by the same active/canary logic that already serves the system prompt — NOT folded into ai_prompt_versions.prompt_text, because garment_scope has been a WHOLE-TEXT override since 00050 with no composition, so a row varying only CATEGORY CRITERIA for jeans would restate the ~90-line response schema and the Rules block, 19 times across 19 categories. Until this exists, every user-message block edit (GARMENT_TYPE_CRITERIA, categoryCriteriaFor, FABRIC_CRITERIA, the baseline block, the schema tail) reaches sellers on the next deploy with an env flag as its only control — a switch, not a gate. grade_reports.prompt_surface_hash (00562) makes that window visible after the fact; it cannot close it.
acceptanceCriteria: A block registry exists keyed (stage, block_key, garment_scope) with an active row and a code default, resolved by the SAME path as resolveActivePrompt — not a parallel resolver. A missing row falls back to the code constant, so the seam is additive and the prompt is byte-identical with an empty registry (test-guarded, the way each flag-gated block already is).

A block override goes through the existing lifecycle before it serves: shadow-compare, golden-set eval gate, canary slice, activate, invalidate. If any leg genuinely cannot cover a block, record which and why where someone looks — the same standard US-2432 AC2 was held to, not a silent gap.

runEval can hold ONE block variable and the rest constant, and unversioned_surface.covered stops being a literal false for the blocks the registry covers. Today it is hardcoded false precisely because nothing was covered; leaving it false after this ships would understate the gate.

The env flags this replaces (GRADING_BASELINES, GRADING_TAG_OCR, GRADING_CATEGORY_CRITERIA_V2) are either retired or explicitly kept with what each still carries. Two controls over the same block, with different properties, is how a flag gets read as a gate again.
A grade record can name the block versions that produced it, not only the surface hash. The hash says two grades ran the same surface; it cannot say WHICH block changed between two that did not.
userStories.notes: [P2][Grading/Lifecycle] Filed 2026-08-08, split out of US-2432 whose AC1 was explicitly "decide before building". Do NOT re-derive the fold-vs-separate choice — it was decided against the stated criterion (can a scoped row vary one block without restating the prompt) and the reasoning is in the vault note. The drift shape being avoided is the same one US-1995 found in the two title-sync copies: duplicate an invariant across N homes and the copies diverge with nothing able to say which one a given grade ran under. Prerequisite already shipped: grade_reports.prompt_surface_hash (migration 00562) and per-entry prompt_version inside per_image_analysis. | 2026-08-08 AC1 BUILT — the registry exists and the seam is live, PARTIALLY covered. Migration 00563 adds ai_prompt_block_versions keyed (stage, block_key, garment_scope) with the same is_active/is_canary/rollout_percentage/eval_passed shape as ai_prompt_versions, and services/edge-functions/src/lib/prompt-blocks.ts resolves it. THE RESOLUTION IS NOT NEW CODE: resolveSlotFromRows + pickPromptForBucket from canary-rollout.ts do it, unchanged, exactly as they do for the system prompt. AC1 says 'the SAME path, not a parallel resolver', and a second copy of that precedence logic is precisely how the two would come to disagree about what a scoped row means. What the module owns is the three things that ARE new: the closed block vocabulary, ONE DB read per stage instead of one per block, and the additive guarantee. It also shares the system prompt's cache signal ('grading-prompt') deliberately, so every existing invalidatePromptCache() call site in grading-eval.ts and admin-grading.ts is already correct for blocks — two signals would be two things to remember at every write site, failing SILENTLY when one was forgotten (a replica serving the old block looks exactly like the activation not having happened yet). THE ADDITIVE GUARANTEE IS MEASURED, NOT ASSERTED: unversionedPromptSurfaceHash() is baf5d4cb before the change and baf5d4cb after. That is what let this ship with no eval run — it cannot move a prompt until somebody activates a row. A test also asserts byte-identity across every garment_type x category combination, with and without hints and a baseline block, since those interleave with the criteria blocks in the same template literal. 23 tests. COVERAGE IS PARTIAL AND MUST BE READ THAT WAY: two blocks today, garment_type_criteria and category_criteria — the exact case the US-2432 decision was argued on. The response schema, the Rules block and the factor-weights sentence are still inside template literals with no identity of their own, so they are STILL UNGATED. Splitting them out is the rest of AC1. AC5 PARTIALLY DONE: a block override appends +blocks(key=version,...) to per_image_analysis[].prompt_version, NOT to grade_reports.prompt_version. That column already carries an ordered suffix chain (+baseline/+fabric/+visual/+tag/+cat2) whose order reinterprets every version string ever recorded if it moves, so the new suffix went onto the carrier with no ordering contract yet. Empty when nothing overrode, so it is byte-identical too. A SERIOUS BUG I WROTE AND THE migration-triple-checker CAUGHT: my first draft copied ai_prompt_versions' FOUR RLS policies from 00003 — including admin INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE. Migration 00510 (US-2348, P0) had REVOKED exactly those three, because they let the admin SPA write the table directly and so reach around the router scope guard, the MFA step-up, the audit row and the eval gate. I would have re-opened that hole on a table holding LIVE GRADING PROMPT TEXT: an admin whose grading:review scope had been revoked could insert is_active=true from a browser and move every grade the platform issues. The lesson is the reusable part — I mirrored the table's ORIGINAL migration instead of its CURRENT state, and 'mirrors ai_prompt_versions' read as diligence in the comment while being wrong. Fixed to SELECT-only with explicit DROP POLICY lines for the three write policies, so re-running the directory converges on the right posture even if a draft was ever hand-applied. AND THE GUARD GAP UNDER IT, which is worth more than the fix: NOTHING in CI was checking either table's RLS. rls-guard discovers tables by an owner column, and a prompt belongs to the platform, not a user — so ai_prompt_versions has been unwatched since 00510 landed, and my new table would have been too. Both are now in SERVICE_ONLY_FORCED (forced in for COVERAGE, not because they are deny-all), and ai_prompt_block_versions is in EDGE_GUARDED in admin-direct-write-guard.test.ts — listed on the day the table shipped rather than the day an admin page first writes it, because that guard only fires on a write that already exists, so adding the name later means the first such write goes unchallenged. NEGATIVE-VERIFIED FOUR WAYS: dropping the block_key filter (3 red), collapsing the canary slot key so blocks share a bucket (2 red), reporting code-default resolutions instead of dropping them (2 red), and USING(true) on the new table's SELECT policy (rls-guard red, naming the table). Each was restored. ONE EXISTING GUARD NEEDED WIDENING, deliberately and narrowly: US-2432's unversioned-prompt-surface_test.ts pinned prompt_version: prompt.versionName as an EXACT match, and the stamp is now a template literal. Widened to accept the template form; the assertion that actually enforces the property — that the CONSTANT is not stamped instead of the resolved prompt — is untouched. STAYS passes:false: AC1 owes the remaining blocks, AC2 (a block override through shadow/eval/canary/activate) is not built, AC3 (runEval holding ONE block variable, and unversioned_surface.covered ceasing to be a literal false) is not built — covered:false is still the honest answer for the blocks the gate measures — and AC4 (retire or explicitly keep GRADING_BASELINES / GRADING_TAG_OCR / GRADING_CATEGORY_CRITERIA_V2) is untouched. HELD MIGRATION: 00563 is committed locally and packaged in PENDING_MIGRATIONS.md — do NOT push until it is applied to prod. Nothing in src/ reads the table, so a Pages auto-deploy landing first is safe, and a missing table degrades to code defaults by design. ALSO FOUND, NOT FIXED: vault:lint has 13 pre-existing drift errors from commits 35096f41 and 6a49be11 (listing-photos, pricing, flipdesk-plan-gating, seo-*, buyer-platform, impersonation, autolister-grouping, accessibility-conformance-vpat, postgrest-row-cap). None involve this work and grading-prompt-channels.md is clean, but they are a CI gate and will fail a push regardless of this story. | 2026-08-08 (later the same day) AC3 HALF DONE, AND IT EXPOSED A HOLE THE PREVIOUS PASS OPENED. AC3 asks for two things: runEval able to hold ONE block variable, and unversioned_surface.covered ceasing to be a literal false. The SECOND is done. The FIRST is not, and is deliberately not faked — see below. THE HOLE, which is the part worth reading: unversionedPromptSurfaceHash() digests the CODE DEFAULTS. The moment AC1 let a DB row replace one of those at runtime, the hash stopped describing what actually ran — two eval runs under different block versions would carry the SAME hash and read as comparable. That is worse than having no fingerprint at all, because the hash's only job is to say when two runs must NOT be compared; leaving it would have converted 'we do not know' into 'we checked', which is the exact failure US-2432 built it to prevent. I introduced that in the AC1 commit and did not notice until AC3 made me look at what the eval reports. FIXED: unversioned_surface.blocks now carries the ACTIVE block overrides, sorted for stability, logged beside the verdict as well as returned. Canaries are EXCLUDED on purpose — an eval run has no bucketKey so it never takes a canary slice, and listing one would describe traffic the run did not serve. GENERALISABLE FORM, now in the vault note: a fingerprint's blind spot grows every time you add a way to vary what it fingerprints. Adding a seam is also a change to every guarantee that was resting on the absence of one. covered IS A LIST, NOT A BOOLEAN, and that is the honest shape: it reports COVERED_BLOCK_KEYS (two keys today) rather than true, because the response schema, the Rules block and the factor-weights line are still compiled into template literals with no identity. A true would tell an operator the gate measures a surface it does not, which is the same overstatement the old 'covered: false' comment warned about from the other direction. A test forbids covered: true outright. listing-eval.ts reports covered: [] and blocks: [] and this is NOT boilerplate. The registry is keyed by GRADING stage; LISTING_GEN_TOOL is a tool schema, not a prompt block, so the registry cannot reach it. Now that both gates have a field of the same name, borrowing the grading gate's coverage there would be the easiest possible way to overstate it — a test asserts listing-eval never even mentions COVERED_BLOCK_KEYS. WHAT AC3 STILL OWES, stated plainly rather than half-shipped: runEval cannot yet TAKE a block candidate. Doing it properly means splitting runEval into a core plus two entry points (runEval for a system-prompt candidate, a new runBlockEval for a block candidate), mirroring the existing runListingEval dispatch. I did not start that in this pass because a partial version — reporting coverage the eval cannot actually exercise — would be a FALSE claim in the gate's own output, which is worse than an obviously missing feature. WHY THIS MATTERS BEYOND THIS STORY: US-2222's notes say its AC3 'CANNOT BE SATISFIED' and name US-2432 as the structural fix. US-2222 is the eleven new category-criteria entries sitting behind GRADING_CATEGORY_CRITERIA_V2 with a flag as their only gate — and category_criteria is one of the two blocks this registry now covers. So finishing AC3's runBlockEval is what turns that flag into a gate. US-2222's AC4 (a per-category golden set from real human-corrected grades) still blocks it independently. NEGATIVE-VERIFIED TWO WAYS: forcing covered to true (2 red) and stubbing activeBlockVersions out to an empty literal (2 red). Both restored. VERIFIED: full edge suite 6060 passed / 0 failed / 170 ignored, deno lint clean across 1431 files, deno check clean, vault:lint 0 errors. | 2026-08-08 (third pass) AC3 IS NOW WHOLE. runEval takes an optional blockCandidate: {blockVersionId}. When set, the SYSTEM prompt stays whatever is active and exactly ONE user-message block is pinned to the candidate row — that is literally AC3's 'hold ONE block variable and the rest constant'. The candidate merges OVER the resolved set inside analyzeImage, deliberately: an eval that also reverted the other blocks to code defaults would score the candidate against a prompt no customer gets. ONE loop serves both candidate kinds rather than a second copy of the case runner. Both a prompt row and a block row drive the same four things — which stage to override, which scope filters the cases, what to call the run, which row gets the verdict — so a fork is how the two gates would come to disagree about what 'passed' means. FOUR DECISIONS WORTH NOT RE-DERIVING, all now in the vault note: (1) an EMPTY block_text is REFUSED, not scored — empty means 'the code default under this name', i.e. the prompt already in production, so running would stamp a pass on a row that changes nothing and that later reads as a qualified change. (2) an UNKNOWN block_key is refused too, which is the OPPOSITE of the serving rule: inert is right when serving (a typo must not take down grading) and wrong at the gate (qualifying a row the resolver would never serve). (3) the case filter follows the BLOCK'S OWN scope dimension — ai_prompt_versions.garment_scope has always meant garment_category, but garment_type_criteria is scoped by garment_TYPE, and filtering that by category matches zero cases while 'no active eval cases' reads as a missing golden set rather than as a bug. A wrong answer wearing a plausible costume. (4) grading_eval_runs.prompt_version_id is NULL for a block run because that column is an FK to a different table; the run is identified by prompt_version_name carrying block:<key>[<scope>]=<version>. NO MIGRATION NEEDED — the column has been nullable since 00050, checked rather than assumed. The verdict writes back to ai_prompt_block_versions.eval_passed. That table has no qualified_model and that is deliberate, not an oversight to paper over: a block does not choose a model, it rides whichever one its stage serves on, so US-2036's model stamp stays on the stage's own prompt version. A MISTAKE I MADE AND HAD TO UNDO: I ran deno fmt on grading-eval.ts, which reflowed ~150 lines of unrelated code AND broke prompt-stage-serving-model_test.ts, whose US-2307 guard matches checkPromptServingEligibility(v, servingModelForStage(v.stage)) as a single line. deno fmt is in NEITHER CI nor npm run verify, so formatting a file that was never formatted buys nothing and costs a 250-line diff plus a red guard. Reverted the file and re-applied the six real edits by hand; the diff is now 108 insertions instead of 256. My own new guard had the same brittleness and is now whitespace-flattened. THE LESSON, since it bit twice in one session: a source-scanning guard should match the PROPERTY, not the line shape — flatten whitespace or the next formatter run reddens a correct file. NEGATIVE-VERIFIED THREE WAYS: hardcoding the case-filter column back to garment_category (red), writing v.id into prompt_version_id on a block run (red), and dropping the unknown- block_key refusal from loadBlockVersion (red). Each restored. WHAT AC3 STILL OWES: nothing structural. What remains for the story overall is AC1's other blocks (the response schema, the Rules block and the factor-weights line are still template literals with no identity), AC2 (shadow-compare has no per-image path at all, which is its own finding and not a wiring task), and AC4 (retire or explicitly keep GRADING_BASELINES / GRADING_TAG_OCR / GRADING_CATEGORY_CRITERIA_V2). US-2222 UNBLOCKED IN PART: its AC3 said the lifecycle 'CANNOT BE SATISFIED' because category_criteria is unreachable by any gate. It is reachable now — that block is one of the two the registry covers, and runEval can score a candidate for it. US-2222 AC4 (a per-category golden set from real human-corrected grades) still blocks it independently, so GRADING_CATEGORY_CRITERIA_V2 stays off. | 2026-08-08 (fourth pass) AC4 ANSWERED: ALL THREE FLAGS ARE KEPT, and the answer turns on a distinction the AC's own wording hides. The AC says the flags this registry 'replaces'. It replaces ONE of them, at most, because THE REGISTRY VERSIONS TEXT AND TWO OF THE FLAGS GATE WORK. GRADING_BASELINES short-circuits getGarmentBaseline(), which does a DB read and, on a cache miss, an AI GENERATION. GRADING_TAG_OCR short-circuits an entire extra VISION CALL over the label photo. A block override supplies a string; by the time a string is wanted the generation and the vision call are already paid for, so no row can express 'skip the work'. Retiring either would not move a control from one place to another — it would delete the control and leave a bill. GRADING_CATEGORY_CRITERIA_V2 is the odd one out and the only genuine candidate: it picks which of two IN-CODE MAPS categoryCriteriaFor reads. Pure text, zero IO. It is still kept, for a reason that is about sequencing rather than architecture — retiring it TODAY would turn eleven categories' criteria on with no gate at all, which is the opposite of what this story exists for. It retires when block rows for those categories exist AND have cleared the gate, not before. Recorded so the next reader does not read 'kept' as 'forgotten'. THE GENERALISABLE FORM, now in prompt-blocks.ts's header and the vault note: a switch over a SIDE EFFECT and a switch over CONTENT are not interchangeable, however similar they look at the call site. Both render as `block ? text : ""`. Only one of them saves a vision call. TWO GUARDS, because the reasoning above is only as good as what stops it silently ceasing to hold. (1) A test asserts the resolvePromptBlocks request array in analyzeImage contains NO await — every covered block's code default must be free to produce. A block whose default needed IO would be a block whose flag this registry had silently failed to replace, WHILE MAKING THAT FLAG LOOK REDUNDANT, which is the dangerous direction. (2) A test asserts both IO-gating flags are still enforced at their own short-circuits, so retiring one shows up in CI rather than on the AI bill. NEGATIVE-VERIFIED BOTH: removing the gradingBaselinesEnabled() short-circuit (red) and making one block's codeDefault awaited (red). Both restored. STORY STATUS: AC3 and AC4 are now done, AC1 is partial (two blocks covered; the response schema, the Rules block and the factor-weights line are still template literals with no identity), AC5 is done at the per-image carrier. AC2 is UNSTARTED and is not a wiring task — grading-shadow.ts is composite-stage only AND reuses per-image results verbatim, so there is no per-image shadow path for a candidate to run through at all. Building one is its own piece of work and should probably be its own story. Story stays passes:false on AC1 + AC2. | 2026-08-08 (fifth pass) AC1 SUBSTANTIALLY DONE — the composite tail now has identity. The three largest ungated pieces of the user message are extracted as named constants and registered as composite blocks: COMPOSITE_FACTOR_WEIGHTS, COMPOSITE_RESPONSE_SCHEMA and COMPOSITE_RULES, about 48 lines that decide the OUTPUT SHAPE and the scoring arithmetic and that no prompt version, canary or eval could reach. Extraction proved byte-identical the same way as before: unversionedPromptSurfaceHash() is baf5d4cb before and baf5d4cb after, measured by stashing the file rather than reasoned about. THE FACTOR-WEIGHTS SENTENCE IS ITS OWN BLOCK, not part of the schema, and that is a deliberate split: it is the only line in the prompt that restates the contract in vault/20-domain/grading-scale-and-weights.md, so an override of it changes the arithmetic the product is sold on and should be reviewable alone rather than buried in a 38-line schema diff. A test pins that overriding the schema leaves the weights line standing. COMPOSITE BLOCKS DELIBERATELY DO NOT ACCEPT AN EVAL CANDIDATE YET. runEval scores per-image block candidates; letting a composite block through without a composite shadow path would give it a route to qualified that the per-image blocks do not have, and the two would then mean different things by passed. A MUTATION THAT DID NOT REDDEN, and the gap it exposed: I swapped the weights and schema slots in the template and the suite stayed green. My order test only covered the OVERRIDE path, where swapping the slots swaps the overridden text with them so the relative order still holds. The surface hash does not catch it either — it asserts the hash MOVES when the prompt moves, not that it equals a pinned value, so a reorder just produces a different-but-equally-valid hash. Added a test on the DEFAULT tail: weights before schema before rules, because a schema arriving before the instruction to produce it reads as reference data rather than a demand. That mutation now reddens. Worth recording as a technique note: a test written only against the injected value cannot see a change to the container. AC2 IS NOW ITS OWN STORY, US-2443. grading-shadow.ts is composite-stage only AND consumes the champion per-image results verbatim, so nothing anywhere runs two per-image prompts over the same photos. That is not a missing wire, it is a COST DECISION nobody has taken — per-image is one vision call per photo, so a naive shadow doubles the most expensive stage for whatever slice it samples. US-2438 stays passes:false on AC2 until US-2443 lands. Verified: deno lint clean across 1431 files, deno check clean, surface hash unchanged. | 2026-08-08 (sixth pass) AC1 IS COMPLETE FOR THE STATIC SURFACE. The per-image tail is extracted too: PER_IMAGE_RESPONSE_SCHEMA and PER_IMAGE_RULES, registered as blocks. Seven blocks now — four per-image, three composite — and every STATIC block of both user messages has an identity. Surface hash baf5d4cb before and after, as with every prior extraction. WHAT IS DELIBERATELY STILL OUTSIDE THE REGISTRY, so nobody reads 'complete' as 'everything': the GENERATED context (baseline, fabric criteria, tag transcription). Those are a different kind of thing — their cost is a DB read or a vision call, not a string — which is exactly the AC4 distinction: the registry versions text, and their env flags gate work. A block override cannot express 'skip the generation'. SCHEMA AND RULES ARE SPLIT IN BOTH STAGES, and it is a decision rather than symmetry. The rules are what an operator tunes (what counts as unassessable, how strict the manipulation check is); the schema is the contract the parser depends on. Folding them into one block would mean every rules tweak restates a ~55-line schema — the restating-an-invariant shape this registry exists to remove. A test pins that overriding one leaves the other standing. THE TYPE SYSTEM CAUGHT THE HALF-DONE STATE, which is worth recording: I extracted the tail and referenced blocks.per_image_response_schema before adding the keys to PROMPT_BLOCK_KEYS, and deno check refused it by name. The closed vocabulary is a `satisfies Record<...>` over a const object, so an unregistered key is a compile error rather than a silently-undefined lookup that would have fallen back to the code default forever and looked like it worked. THE DEFAULT-ORDER GUARD EARNED ITS KEEP AGAIN. I added the same test for the per-image tail that the composite one needed, for the same reason: the override test cannot see a reorder of the shipped template, because swapping the slots swaps the injected text with them. Negative-verified — reordering the shipped per-image tail reddens 2 cases, and making the rules block un-overridable reddens 1. Both restored. STORY STATUS: AC1 done for the static surface, AC3 done, AC4 done, AC5 done at the per-image carrier. AC2 remains and is US-2443 — there is no per-image shadow path anywhere, which is a cost decision (one vision call per photo) rather than a wiring task. Story stays passes:false on AC2 alone. VERIFIED: full edge suite 6110 passed / 0 failed, lint clean across 1434 files, surface hash unchanged, vault:lint clean. | 2026-08-09 AC2 UNBLOCKED, shadow leg RESOLVED by US-2443. AC2 asked that a block override go through shadow -> eval -> canary before it serves, and shadow was the leg that did not exist for ANY per-image artifact. It exists now: services/edge-functions/src/lib/grading-shadow-per-image.ts re-analyzes every photo of a sampled submission under the challenger block (or per-image system prompt) and re-composites, writing a grading_shadow_results row with stage='per_image', per_factor_deltas and tier_agreement (migration 00566). ai_prompt_block_versions gained is_shadow / shadow_sample_rate / shadow_daily_cap so a block candidate can be sampled at all. WHAT THIS DOES NOT DO, so nobody reads AC2 as fully closed: the golden-set eval gate still cannot hold a per-image USER-message block constant against itself (runEval compiles the same text into both legs), which is AC3's territory, and the path is OFF by default -- it needs PER_IMAGE_SHADOW_DAILY_VISION_CAP set AND a non-zero rate and cap on the candidate row, because one sampled submission costs a vision call per photo plus a composite. vault/20-domain/grading-prompt-channels.md carries the corrected mechanism table.

userStories.title: Web lost the AI listing-copy button that iOS ships and settings.tsx still promises
userStories.description: Found while triaging dead exports in US-2436. src/hooks/use-ai-extract.ts exported useListingCopy, a mutation posting to /api/flipdesk/ai/listing-copy, and nothing on the web has called it for some time. It is not dead work: the edge route is live (routes/flipdesk-ai.ts -> lib/ai-extract.ts generateListingCopy) and iOS calls it from Marketplaces/Publish/ListingCopyService.swift. Meanwhile src/pages/settings.tsx tells the user, in the AI toggle copy, that turning the setting off disables the AI Fill and listing-copy buttons — naming a web button that is not there. The composer does generate copy, but through a different endpoint entirely (useAiRewrite -> /api/flipdesk/ai/rewrite), so the two are not the same feature under a different name. US-2436 deliberately left the hook in place rather than delete it, because deleting it would have quietly ratified the gap.
